AI.conclusion: CreativityNeuro offers a straightforward, data-free method to enhance divergent thinking and reduce mode collapse in LLMs without data, retraining, or gradient-based fine-tuning, with demonstrated cross-task benefits.

title: MIBE: Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator for Personalized Image Generation
summary: Multi-subject personalized image generation requires the precise rendering of all requested reference identities and their specified interactions based on a guiding prompt. However, state-of-the-art models still struggle with this process, frequently omitting subjects, failing to preserve reference appearances, or misattributing interactions. Furthermore, existing metrics designed primarily for single-subject fidelity cannot reliably capture these errors, suffering severe degradation in ranking separability and failing to align with human preference as the subject count increases. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark and Evaluator (MIBE), a unified framework comprising a Multi-subject Interaction Benchmark (MIB) and a Multi-subject Interaction Evaluator (MIE). MIB systematically covers diverse relation types and scene complexities through a decoupled data regime. This consists of a 60K-pair VLM-labeled Silver Set for scalable metric training and a 4K-pair double-blind Human Evaluation Gold Set covering a diverse range of state-of-the-art generators, with the Silver Set reaching 95.1% cross-VLM preference agreement. To demonstrate the utility of this benchmark, we present MIE, a lightweight, reference-conditioned evaluator trained exclusively on the Silver Set with a dual-head ranking and diagnosis objective. MIE exhibits strong cross-generator generalization on the Gold Set, achieving 0.922 overall pairwise accuracy against human preference, including 0.982 on seen generators and 0.884 on unseen generators. By outperforming a broad spectrum of baseline metrics, including CLIP and DINO variants, MIE demonstrates that diagnostic supervision can preserve ranking separability and human alignment where traditional evaluators collapse.

AI.tldr: Introduces MIBE with MIB and MIE for evaluating multi-subject image generation; uses a Silver VLM-labeled set and a Gold human-evaluated set; MIE achieves strong cross-generator performance and outperforms standard metrics.
AI.motivation: Current multi-subject generation suffers from omissions and misattributions, and existing single-subject metrics fail to rank appropriately as subject count grows. There is a need for a benchmark and a reference-conditioned evaluator that align with human preference.
AI.method: Decoupled data regime: 60K-pair Silver Set labeled by vision-language models for scalable metric training, plus a 4K-pair double-blind Human Evaluation Gold Set across state-of-the-art generators. Train MIE, a lightweight, reference-conditioned evaluator with dual-head ranking and a diagnosis objective, on the Silver Set; evaluate on the Gold Set against human preferences.
AI.result: Silver Set achieves 95.1% cross-VLM preference agreement. MIE attains 0.922 overall pairwise accuracy against human preference on the Gold Set (0.982 seen generators, 0.884 unseen). Outperforms CLIP and DINO variants.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostic supervision preserves ranking separability and human alignment in multi-subject image generation, enabling robust evaluation where traditional evaluators fail; MIE generalizes across generators and demonstrates the utility of MIBE for benchmarking multi-subject interactions.

title: IonSense-QKG: A Quantum-Readiness Metadata Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery Dataset Discovery
comment: 7 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. Code and metadata artifact available at GitHub
summary:
Public lithium-ion battery datasets are increasingly used for state-of-health estimation, remaining-useful-life prediction, anomaly detection, electrochemical diagnostics, second-life analytics, and battery safety research. However, these datasets vary substantially in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, sequence structure, access status, and preprocessing complexity. These differences directly affect whether a dataset is feasible for near-term hybrid quantum-classical machine-learning workflows.
  This paper presents IonSense-QKG, a quantum-readiness metadata framework for lithium-ion battery dataset discovery. Starting from the EV-Battery-IonSense index, the proposed framework enriches public battery dataset records with quantum-relevant metadata, including task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, and NISQ feasibility. A transparent Quantum Readiness Score is introduced to rank datasets as candidate resources for future hybrid quantum-classical battery benchmarks. The score is intended as a dataset-selection heuristic, not as evidence of quantum advantage.
  The framework demonstrates query-based discovery over enriched metadata to identify datasets suitable for compact quantum feature maps, quantum time-series workflows, limited-label anomaly detection, and future battery-health benchmarking. The released artifact includes metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, link-checking utilities, and SQL-style query examples. IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem and provides a reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.

AI.tldr: IonSense-QKG is a metadata framework to assess lithium-ion battery datasets for quantum ML readiness, enabling discovery and ranking via a Quantum Readiness Score.
AI.motivation: Public battery datasets vary in chemistry, modality, scale, label quality, and structure, creating barriers for near-term hybrid quantum-classical workflows; a standardized, queryable readiness metadata framework is proposed.
AI.method: Enrich the EV-Battery-IonSense index with quantum-relevant metadata (task type, sensing modality, chemistry, label availability, sequence type, preprocessing requirements, candidate quantum encodings, estimated qubit range, NISQ feasibility); introduce Quantum Readiness Score as a heuristic; provide artifact with metadata, scoring scripts, and query examples; demonstrate query-based discovery for specific quantum ML tasks.
AI.result: Demonstrates dataset discovery and ranking for compact feature maps, quantum time-series, limited-label anomaly detection, and battery-health benchmarking; releases metadata tables, scoring scripts, robustness checks, and SQL-like query examples; offers reproducible foundation for data-centric quantum battery analytics.
AI.conclusion: IonSense-QKG positions dataset selection as a data-management problem, offering a transparent, reproducible framework and scoring to guide future quantum battery benchmarks; scores are heuristic, not proof of quantum advantage.

title: Path planning for unmanned naval surface vehicles
summary: There nowadays is a myriad of approaches to real-time avoidance of fixed obstacles for unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) and, to a lesser extent, also the task of avoiding moving obstacles such as boats, ships, swimmers, and other USVs, but both topics still present challenges. This paper offers novel approaches to both of these problems. It uses a combination of a global path planner, which finds a path from a start point to a goal point that avoids fixed obstacles (given that their locations are known in advance), and a local path planner, which can circumnavigate a moving obstacle (as well as any previously unknown fixed obstacles). The global planner is novel in that it employs a combination of three path planners, one known in the literature as Grassfire, one that is a new modification of Grassfire, and one that is a new, and arguably more intuitive, version of the well-known Probabilistic Roadmap. The local planner is novel in that it employs a higher-level decision logic based on its observations regarding the direction of movement of the obstacle relative to the USVs global path. This logic enables the USV to determine the best strategy for avoiding the obstacle by systematically routing the vehicle behind the obstacle rather than running parallel to it until the opportunity to pass appears. Simulations are provided that validate these claims. For comparison with other systems, the simulations include an implementation of the well-known D* algorithm, and the discussion covers additional dynamic path planning systems, which, like D*, do not necessarily route the vehicle behind the moving obstacle.

AI.tldr: Hybrid global-local path planning framework for USVs that simultaneously handles fixed and moving obstacles; leverages Grassfire family and a new RRPM-like global planner, plus a local obstacle-aware logic to route behind moving obstacles; simulations validate performance against D* and other dynamic planners.
AI.motivation: Real-time autonomous navigation for unmanned surface vehicles requires robust avoidance of both known fixed obstacles and unknown moving obstacles; existing methods often fail to pass behind moving obstacles or to integrate global and local planning effectively.
AI.method: A three-component global planner combining Grassfire, a modified Grassfire, and a novel, intuitive Probabilistic Roadmap-like planner; a local planner with higher-level decision logic that estimates obstacle direction relative to the global path and routes the USV behind the obstacle; integration with a comparison suite including D* and other dynamic planners; simulation-based validation.
AI.result: Simulations validate that the framework can avoid fixed obstacles and effectively navigate around moving obstacles by routing behind them; performance is contrasted with D* and other dynamic planners.
AI.conclusion: The proposed hybrid global-local planning approach, with the new local decision logic and a triplet of global planners, improves real-time obstacle avoidance for USVs and shows favorable results in simulations against established methods.

title: Discrete Diffusion Language Models for Interactive Radiology Report Drafting
summary: Diffusion language models, which generate text by denoising a token canvas bidirectionally instead of emitting tokens left to right, have become competitive with autoregressive (AR) generation. Medical foundation models, however, remain almost entirely autoregressive. We adapt a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, DiffusionGemma-26B, and benchmark it against its same-size AR sibling Gemma-4-26B under an identical LoRA recipe on medical visual question answering datasets, scored by a verbosity-robust LLM judge. Diffusion matches or exceeds AR on all of them, and the finetuned model (3.8B active) is competitive with frontier vision-language models; its decoding is also 3.5-4.4x faster. Beyond this parity, the diffusion model offers a drafting capability AR lacks: any-order infill. Because the canvas is denoised bidirectionally, a radiologist can fix report fragments and have the model fill the text between them, an operation inherent to diffusion but not to autoregression, which is subpar at it. This suits real reports, which are often terse or inconsistent across clinicians and institutions.

AI.tldr: DiffusionGemma-26B, a mixture-of-experts diffusion language model, matches or exceeds a same-size autoregressive baseline on medical visual question answering with identical LoRA tuning; it decodes 3.5–4.4× faster and enables any-order infill drafting, offering advantages over AR in clinical reporting.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether diffusion language models can outperform autoregressive models in medical NLP tasks, offering faster decoding and novel editing capabilities for clinical reports.
AI.method: Adapt and fine-tune the diffusion LM DiffusionGemma-26B using a LoRA recipe; compare to its autoregressive sibling Gemma-4-26B on medical VQA datasets; evaluate with a verbosity-robust LLM judge; assess decoding speed and any-order infill capability.
AI.result: Diffusion matches or exceeds the AR baseline across evaluated medical VQA tasks; a finetuned 3.8B-active model approaches frontier vision-language models; decoding speed improvements of 3.5–4.4×.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion-based medical LMs can rival AR models in performance while offering unique drafting/drafting-infill capabilities (any-order infill) that align well with real-world radiology reporting needs and heterogeneous clinical text.

title: Rethinking Generic Object Tracking Toward Human-Level Perceptual Intelligence
comment: Ph.D. dissertation, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, 2026. arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2602.14771
summary: At the heart of human visual perception lies the ability to maintain a continuous and coherent understanding of the external world. By integrating observations with accumulated experience, the human visual system can continuously adapt to variations in both the target and its surrounding environment, while preserving robust visual continuity as scene dynamics evolve. Human vision can therefore integrate prior knowledge, spatial geometry, and semantic context to understand complex scenes and their changes. As a core problem in computer vision, visual object tracking aims to bring machine perception closer to human visual perception. These capabilities are central to the task of Generic Object Tracking (GOT). In this task, a visual tracker is initialized only with the bounding box of an arbitrarily specified target in the first frame, and must continuously localize the target in subsequent dynamic visual streams. However, future events, observations, and real-world variations are inherently unpredictable; therefore, the model's generalization and online adaptation capabilities remain bottlenecks. Tracking reliability can deteriorate when the target undergoes severe deformation, is affected by complex distractors, encounters significant environmental changes, or belongs to a category unseen during training. This dissertation aims to narrow the gap between machine visual tracking systems and human visual perception by proposing a series of methods that systematically enhance the target discrimination, robust adaptation, and geometric reasoning capabilities of tracking models.

AI.tldr: A dissertation proposes methods to enhance generic object tracking by improving discrimination, robust online adaptation, and geometric reasoning to close the gap with human vision, addressing generalization under deformation, distractors, scene changes, and unseen categories.
AI.motivation: To bridge the gap between machine visual tracking and human perception by leveraging continuous perception, prior knowledge, geometry, and semantics, and to overcome bottlenecks in generalization and online adaptation in GOT.
AI.method: A series of methods that systematically improve target discrimination, robust adaptation, and geometric reasoning in tracking models.
AI.result: Not specified in abstract.
AI.conclusion: The work aims to narrow the gap to human perception in GOT by proposing methods that enhance discrimination, adaptation, and geometric reasoning.

title: A Novel Machine Learning Approach for Central Nervous System Tumor Classification from DNA Methylation
summary: NA methylation profiling has become a powerful approach for central nervous system (CNS) tumor classification, yet important challenges remain regarding cross-cohort transferability, methodological correctness, and robust multiclass evaluation. In this work, we propose a novel and methodologically rigorous machine-learning approach for methylation-based CNS tumor classification that combines Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction with multinomial logistic regression for classification. We evaluate the proposed approach in the same general experimental setting established by a widely used reference classifier. On the 2,801-sample reference cohort, our method achieves a mean accuracy of 96\% under stratified 3-fold cross-validation. On the independent 1,104-sample clinical evaluation cohort, it reaches 86\% accuracy at the 91-class level and 93\% when predictions are evaluated at the methylation class family level. These results improve upon the corresponding state-of-the-art reference figures of 82\% class-level concordance and 88\% family-level concordance, yielding absolute gains of approximately 4 and 5 percentage points, respectively. This improvement is clinically relevant: in a diagnostic setting, a 5-point increase in correct tumor classification can directly affect cancer subtype assignment and, in turn, influence treatment selection and downstream clinical decision-making. Our results show that the proposed model, grounded in stronger methodological practice in machine learning, consistently outperforms the previous state of the art across evaluation settings and can materially improve the reliability of CNS tumor classification.

AI.tldr: A method for methylation-based CNS tumor classification using Sparse Random Projection and multinomial logistic regression; strong cross-cohort performance with substantial gains over a reference classifier; highlights methodological rigor and potential clinical impact.
AI.motivation: Address cross-cohort transferability and robust multiclass evaluation in methylation-based CNS tumor classification; reduce dimensionality while maintaining predictive power.
AI.method: Sparse Random Projection for dimensionality reduction followed by multinomial logistic regression; evaluated with stratified 3-fold CV on a 2,801-sample reference cohort and an independent 1,104-sample clinical cohort; performance benchmarked against a widely used reference classifier.
AI.result: Mean CV accuracy of 96% on the reference cohort; 86% accuracy at 91-class level and 93% at methylation family level on the independent cohort; outperforms reference figures of 82% (class-level) and 88% (family-level) by ~4–5 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Methodologically rigorous ML approach yields consistent, clinically meaningful improvements over the state of the art in CNS tumor methylation classification; enhanced reliability and potential impact on diagnostic decisions.

title: One Demonstration Is Enough for Real-World Robotic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Learning effective robot control policies on physical hardware is challenging due to costly data collection and the difficulty of reward specification. Prior work has incorporated demonstrations into reinforcement learning (RL), yet existing approaches either require large numbers of demonstrations or depend on continuous human intervention during training. To address these limitations, we present AutoSERL, a framework that leverages a single demonstration to fully automate the intervention process in real-world robot RL. The framework includes three complementary mechanisms to accomplish certain tasks: a sliding window intervention mechanism that continuously guides exploration to prevent local optima and unsafe deviations, a safety recovery mechanism that detects and corrects failure states via predefined trajectory recovery points, and an intervention termination criterion that automatically disables guidance once the policy can independently complete the task, preserving its exploration advantage. We evaluate AutoSERL on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms, spanning insertion, hanging, and hinge-based tasks. AutoSERL consistently outperforms SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES -- a dedicated one-shot imitation learning baseline -- across all tasks while matching HIL-SERL, achieves 100% success rate on insertion tasks, and demonstrates improved robustness to positional variations, all from a single demonstration. Code and videos are available on our project website: https://autoserl.github.io/.

AI.tldr: AutoSERL enables one-shot demonstration-guided real-world RL for robot manipulation via three automated intervention mechanisms, improving data efficiency and safety.
AI.motivation: Reduce data collection costs and reward engineering burden in real-world robot RL while maintaining effective exploration and safety.
AI.method: AutoSERL uses a single demonstration to fully automate the intervention process in real-world robot RL, comprising three components: (1) a sliding window intervention to steer exploration away from local optima and unsafe deviations; (2) a safety recovery mechanism that detects and corrects failure states using predefined trajectory recovery points; (3) an intervention termination criterion that disables guidance once the policy can perform the task autonomously. Evaluated on six contact-intensive manipulation tasks across two robot platforms (insertion, hanging, hinge-based tasks), comparing against SERL with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES, and matching results of HIL-SERL.
AI.result: AutoSERL consistently outperforms SERL initialized with 20 demonstrations, behavior cloning, and MILES across all tasks; it matches HIL-SERL performance, achieves 100% success on insertion tasks, and shows improved robustness to positional variations, all from a single demonstration.
AI.conclusion: A single demonstration with automated interventions suffices to achieve high-performance, robust, real-world robotic RL in contact-intensive manipulation, reducing human labeling effort while preserving exploration and safety advantages; the approach generalizes across multiple tasks and could extend to related manipulation domains.

title: Beyond Next-Token Prediction: An RLVR Proof of Concept for Tool-Use Agents on Atlassian Workflows
summary: Large language models are trained to predict the next token, not to act inside a specific API. In niche enterprise SaaS workflows -- where success means hitting the right endpoint with the right nested arguments in the right order -- this objective mismatch shows up as silent failures: dropped required fields, hallucinated tools, or early stops after a single read. We ask whether Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), applied directly in the target environment, closes the gap. As a proof of concept we build a suite of five synthetic environments emulating the Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs at schema fidelity; rewards are computed entirely from the tool-call trace, with no live API, no learned judge, and no human label in the loop. Scoring prompted Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3.5-4B on the same checkers that drive GRPO training, we find that on the four scenarios whose rewards are non-degenerate the RL-trained policy lifts average reward from a 4B-baseline range of 0.35--0.92 to 0.95--1.00, with the largest single gain on Confluence page creation ($0.35 \rightarrow 1.00$). We position this as a preliminary step toward outcome-optimised small models for niche enterprise APIs, and foreground two limitations a workshop reader should weigh: hand-crafting verifiable rewards does not scale beyond the handful of endpoints reported here, and one of our five scenarios (ticket-transition) has a saturating reward shape that the prompted 4B already maxes out.

AI.tldr: RLVR in synthetic enterprise API environments yields near-perfect task rewards, showing promising outcome-optimization for small models, but relies on handcrafted rewards and exhibits saturation in at least one scenario.
AI.motivation: LLMs trained for next-token prediction misalign with actuation in niche enterprise API workflows, causing silent failures; study investigates whether verifiable, environment-derived rewards can close the gap.
AI.method: Five synthetic environments simulating Jira REST v3 and Confluence v2 APIs with full schema fidelity; rewards computed from tool-call traces only (no live API, no learned judge, no human labels); evaluate on Qwen 3-1.7B and Qwen 3.5-4B; four scenarios with non-degenerate rewards.
AI.result: RLVR-trained policies raise average reward from a 4B baseline of 0.35–0.92 to 0.95–1.00; largest gain on Confluence page creation (0.35 → 1.00); four non-degenerate rewards show consistent improvement.
AI.conclusion: Preliminary step toward outcome-optimized small models for niche enterprise APIs; limitations include non-scalability of handcrafted rewards beyond the reported endpoints and a saturating reward shape in one scenario despite 4B prompting.

title: Computer Vision for Wildlife Monitoring: Detecting Brown Howler Monkeys using YOLO
comment: Accepted on International Conference on Computer Animation, Social Agents, and Extended Reality '26 (CASAXR 26)
summary: Urban expansion threatens global biodiversity, especially affecting arboreal species due to the fragmentation of forest habitats. The movement of arboreal species across disjointed forest patches increases mortality risk and, thus, compromises their conservation. In this context, the installation of canopy bridges can be a viable strategy; yet continuous monitoring of their use by arboreal species is essential for ensuring their effectiveness, typically carried out with the aid of camera traps. However, this method often produces false-positive images that demand time from conservationists for review. In this context, computer vision algorithms can optimize the task of detecting target species using the canopy bridges. In this study, we explored the automatic detection of brown howler monkeys (Alouatta guariba) in videos obtained by camera traps. Given the need for a large number of annotated images of the target animals to train the algorithms, we tested the incorporation of auxiliary data to improve detection models, fine-tuning the YOLOv10 framework using varying proportions of them. The improvement of these automatic detection techniques contributes to conservation efforts, by providing automatic tools to monitor solutions that minimize the impact of human interference in animals habitats.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning YOLOv10 with auxiliary annotated data improves automatic detection of brown howler monkeys in canopy-bridge camera-trap videos, aiding conservation by reducing false positives and reviewer workload.
AI.motivation: Urban expansion fragments forests, threatening arboreal biodiversity. Monitoring canopy-bridge use via camera traps yields many false positives; automated detection is needed to support conservation efforts.
AI.method: Train and fine-tune YOLOv10 using varying proportions of auxiliary annotated data from camera-trap videos of Alouatta guariba to detect monkeys on canopy bridges; compare performance across data fractions.
AI.result: Incorporating auxiliary data improves detection performance; the gains depend on the amount of auxiliary data used, enabling more reliable automatic monitoring of canopy-bridge use.
AI.conclusion: Auxiliary-data-driven fine-tuning of YOLOv10 is a promising approach for scalable, accurate detection of arboreal mammals in fragmented habitats, enhancing conservation monitoring processes.

title: From Approximation to Emergence: A Theory of Deep Learning
summary: Deep learning has outgrown any single mathematical explanation. From Approximation to Emergence develops a unified, proof-oriented account of modern deep learning theory, tracing a path from the classical foundations of approximation, optimization, and generalization to the contemporary mechanisms of overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence. Rather than presenting isolated results, the book organizes a broad literature into a coherent research narrative: each theory is examined through the object it controls, the assumptions that make it valid, and the phenomena it leaves unexplained. Written for researchers, graduate students, and mathematically trained practitioners, this monograph offers a rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands today: powerful, incomplete, and increasingly centered on the question of how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.

AI.tldr: A unified, proof-oriented synthesis of modern deep learning theory linking classical foundations to emergent phenomena; organizes diverse results into a coherent map.
AI.motivation: To organize heterogeneous theoretical work into a coherent narrative and provide a rigorous guide for researchers by showing how learned mechanisms arise from scale, data, architecture, and training.
AI.method: Theoretical synthesis using an object-based lens: for each theory, identify the object controlled, the assumptions under which it holds, and the phenomena it cannot yet explain; integrate topics across approximation, optimization, generalization, overparameterization, robustness, generative modeling, transformers, in-context learning, scaling laws, interpretability, alignment, and emergence.
AI.result: A rigorous map of deep learning theory as it stands, emphasizing that the theory is powerful but incomplete and increasingly centered on emergence from scale, data, architecture, and training.
AI.conclusion: Provides a coherent, rigorous narrative for researchers and graduate students, outlining known results and key gaps, and offering a framework to study how learned mechanisms arise from scaling and design choices.

title: Imagining the Sense of Touch: Touch-Informed Manipulation via Imagined Tactile Representations
summary: Tactile sensing can substantially improve contact-rich robotic manipulation, yet its practical deployment remains limited by the fragility, calibration requirements, and maintenance burden of tactile hardware. This raises a fundamental question: can robots benefit from tactile knowledge without requiring tactile sensors at deployment? We present TacImag, a tactile imagination framework that predicts tactile observations from vision and proprioception and uses the generated signals to guide manipulation policies. Trained from paired visuotactile demonstrations, TacImag enables touch-informed manipulation using only visual observations at test time. We evaluate TacImag on six simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks. Across simulation and real-world experiments, imagined tactile observations consistently improve manipulation performance without requiring tactile hardware. In real-world experiments, imagined force fields improve contact-sensitive tasks by 44.4% on average, whereas imagined tactile images improve texture-sensitive tasks by 23.3%, revealing that the effectiveness of tactile imagination depends strongly on the relationship between tactile representation and task requirements. Our results further suggest that tactile imagination does not simply recover missing tactile measurements. Instead, it acts as a form of contact-aware supervision that transforms subtle visual interaction cues into representations that are easier for manipulation policies to exploit.

AI.tldr: TacImag predicts tactile observations from vision and proprioception to guide manipulation, enabling touch-informed policies using only visual input at test time.
AI.motivation: Deploy robust manipulation without tactile hardware by leveraging tactile knowledge learned from paired visuotactile demonstrations, addressing fragility and maintenance of tactile sensors.
AI.method: Train a model to map vision+proprioception to predicted tactile signals (tactile images and force fields) from paired demonstrations; use imagined tactile signals to supervise vision-based manipulation policies; test with vision/proprioception only.
AI.result: Across six simulated and four real-world tasks, imagined tactile signals improve performance; real-world gains include ~44.4% for contact-sensitive tasks (imagined force fields) and ~23.3% for texture-sensitive tasks (imagined tactile images); gains depend on alignment between tactile representation and task.
AI.conclusion: Tactile imagination serves as contact-aware supervision that enables touch-informed manipulation without tactile hardware, though the benefit depends on how well the tactile representation matches task needs.

title: World Feedback for Clinical Agents: Diagnosing RL in FHIR Environments
summary: Clinical protocol-execution tasks -- checking a lab value, applying a threshold, placing a correctly structured FHIR order -- are natural candidates for RL from world feedback: once clinical SMEs encode decision logic into a verifier, that verifier grades unlimited rollouts without per-episode annotation. But applying RL requires a sound feedback channel and sufficient base capability. We audit MedAgentBench v1/v2, find a 41.7\% silent-finish ceiling that makes inaction the RL dominant strategy, and construct \textbf{MedAgentBench-v3 (MAB-v3)} (508 tasks, 8.9\% ceiling). Training Qwen3-8B exposes two structural barriers: a \emph{capability ceiling} (10/20 task types have 0\% base performance, zero gradient) and a \emph{format-knowledge barrier} (3/20 types require exact clinical codes undiscoverable by exploration). Pure RL reaches 18.2\% pass@1 vs.\ 34.1\% for rule-based SFT; the 15.9~pp gap is attributable entirely to these barriers. A decision/format-knowledge/lookup taxonomy predicts RL learnability and prescribes the fix: SFT to inject codes, RL to learn conditionals.

AI.tldr: RL can learn clinical protocol-execution tasks but faces significant barriers; MedAgentBench-v3 improves base capabilities; hybrid SFT+RL is recommended.
AI.motivation: Assess RL learnability in clinical task settings, identify bottlenecks in MedAgentBench and Qwen3-8B, and propose a corrective taxonomy.
AI.method: Audit MedAgentBench v1/v2 for silent-finish; construct MedAgentBench-v3 with 508 tasks; train Qwen3-8B to evaluate base performance; analyze barriers (capability and format-knowledge); compare RL vs rule-based SFT; develop taxonomy and fixes.
AI.result: Silent-finish ceiling 41.7% in MedAgentBench; MAB-v3 ceiling 8.9%; 10/20 task types have 0% base performance; 3/20 require exact clinical codes; pure RL passes 18.2% vs SFT 34.1% pass@1; 15.9 pp gap due to barriers.
AI.conclusion: A taxonomy of decision/format-knowledge/lookup predicts RL learnability; fix is SFT to inject codes and RL to learn conditionals; hybrid approach recommended.

title: Beyond Heatmaps: Unsupervised Concept-Graph Reasoning for Interpretable Visual Explanation
comment: Accepted at the IJCAI-ECAI 2026 Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), Bremen, Germany. 7 pages, 4 figures
summary: Concept Bottleneck Models (CBMs) provide an intrinsically interpretable alternative to post-hoc explanations. However, existing CBMs often rely on predefined concept vocabularies or supervised annotations, lack explicit concept grounding, and summarize each concept with a single image-level score -- discarding spatial recurrence and inter-concept dependencies. We propose a Graph-based Concept Bottleneck Model (G-CBM), an intrinsically interpretable framework that performs unsupervised concept discovery via Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and represents the discovered concepts as nodes in a per-image concept-graph representation. G-CBM matches region-level features to these concept nodes -- providing concept grounding and capturing concept recurrence across the image -- and applies a \emph{tunable concept filtering threshold} $τ$ to suppress weak region-level features. A Graph Attention Network (GAT) then performs concept-level reasoning by modeling nonlinear dependencies across nodes. Across ImageNet, HAM10000, PH2, and Derm7pt, G-CBM achieves an average relative AUC improvement of 3.7\% over a ResNet-50 baseline. Concept filtering frequently improves predictive performance while inducing selective concept use, achieving peak AUC of $0.96$ on PH2 with only 2 of 10 concepts and 0.92 on HAM10000 with 3.8 of 9 concepts. On dermoscopy benchmarks, G-CBM is competitive with supervised approaches requiring external annotations. Deletion/insertion analyses with random ablation controls show that the learned concept ranking faithfully reflects model predictions.

AI.tldr: G-CBM uses unsupervised NMF to discover concepts, grounds them via region features in a per-image concept-graph, filters weak signals with a tunable threshold tau, and reasons over concepts with a Graph Attention Network, yielding better AUC than ResNet-50 and competitive dermoscopy results.
AI.motivation: Current concept bottleneck models rely on predefined concept vocabularies and single image-level scores, lacking explicit grounding, spatial recurrence, and inter-concept modeling, which hampers interpretability and performance.
AI.method: Unsupervised concept discovery via Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) to obtain per-image concept nodes; align region-level features to these nodes for grounding and capturing recurrence; apply a tunable concept-filtering threshold tau to prune weak region signals; use a Graph Attention Network (GAT) to model nonlinear dependencies among concept nodes for final prediction.
AI.result: Average relative AUC improvement of 3.7% over a ResNet-50 baseline across ImageNet, HAM10000, PH2, and Derm7pt. Concept filtering yields selective concept use, with peak AUC of 0.96 on PH2 using only 2 of 10 concepts and 0.92 on HAM10000 with 3.8 of 9 concepts. On dermoscopy benchmarks, G-CBM is competitive with supervised approaches requiring external annotations. Deletion/insertion analyses with random ablation indicate the learned concept ranking faithfully reflects model predictions.
AI.conclusion: G-CBM enhances interpretability by grounding concepts and capturing recurrence, while leveraging inter-concept dependencies through a GAT; demonstrates consistent improvements across diverse datasets and maintains competitive performance with supervised methods.

title: Black-Box Inference of LLM Architectural Properties with Restrictive API Access
summary: In practice, most commercial LLM providers do not publicly release details of underlying LLM architectures. However, prior work has shown that given limited API access to an LLM (namely, top-$k$ logits and/or a logit bias function), one can recover certain architectural details of an LLM, such as the hidden dimension of the feed-forward network. Perhaps in response to these results, most commercial LLM providers have restricted their APIs to expose only the single logit for each decoded token, and they no longer give users the ability to bias logits. We show that even under current restrictive APIs, several architectural parameters are still recoverable. We present NightVision, an attack that uses restrictive black-box API access to estimate the hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count of an LLM. Algorithmically, NightVision relies on a novel common set prompting technique in which multiple prompts expose log probabilities for the same set of output tokens; a spectral analysis of these results is used to infer hidden dimension. NightVision additionally uses end-to-end time to first token (TTFT) measurements and the estimated hidden dimension to estimate depth and parameter count. We empirically evaluate NightVision on 32 open-source LLMs, recovering hidden dimension to within 23% average relative error across all models (9% on MoE models), and depth and parameter count to within 53% for models exceeding three billion parameters. We run extensive ablations to demonstrate how these accuracies scale with token budget and model properties. Overall, our results suggest that current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restricted to fully obfuscate the architectural details of their underlying models.

AI.tldr: NightVision is a black-box API attack that infers core architecture of LLMs (hidden dimension, depth, and parameter count) from restrictive API access. It achieves ~23% average relative error in hidden dimension (9% on MoE models) and ~53% error for depth/parameter count on models above 3B parameters, showing that current APIs still leak architectural details.
AI.motivation: Despite API restrictions, attackers can extract architectural details of underlying LLMs. Understanding what is still inferable helps assess security risks and informs defenses to obfuscate model internals.
AI.method: 3-part approach: (1) a common-set prompting technique to reveal log-probabilities for the same tokens under different prompts; spectral analysis of these log-probabilities to estimate hidden dimension; (2) end-to-end time-to-first-token (TTFT) measurements combined with hidden-dimension estimates to infer depth and parameter count; (3) extensive evaluation on 32 open-source LLMs, with ablations showing scaling behavior with token budget and model properties.
AI.result: Empirically, NightVision recovers hidden dimension within 23% average relative error across models (9% on MoE models), and estimates depth/parameter count within 53% for models >3B parameters; results hold under restricted API access and reveal robust leakage of architecture.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM APIs are not sufficiently restrictive to fully obfuscate underlying architectural details; this has implications for model security and motivates development of mitigation strategies to protect model internals.

title: CoRe: Combined Rewards with Vision-Language Model Feedback for Preference-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reward design remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning (RL). Hand-crafted rewards are often difficult to specify and may lead to suboptimal policies, while learned rewards from preferences can suffer from inefficiency and unstable training. Inspired by the dual nature of human learning explored in cognitive science, we decompose rewards into two complementary components: Formal Rewards (FR), explicitly designed based on task knowledge, and Residual Rewards (RR), learned from observations to capture implicit and nuanced preferences. Based on this decomposition, we propose CoRe, a hybrid framework that integrates FR and RR with vision-language models (VLMs) feedback to achieve preference-aligned policies without human involvement. Our contributions are twofold: (1) We propose a Formal Reward Module (FRM) that leverages VLMs to iteratively design and optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback, enabling the continual improvement of policy during training; (2) We introduce a Residual Reward Module (RRM) that learns RR from video-level preference by employing VLMs to generate preference labels and capturing nuanced rewards that complement FR, ensuring alignment with human intent. Through the synergy of FRM and RRM, CoRe enables the automatic construction of reliable rewards that are efficient and preference-aligned. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CoRe outperforms existing approaches in terms of policy learning effectiveness and efficiency on ten robotic manipulation tasks in simulation and five real-worlds. Videos can be found on our project website: https://core-2026.github.io/

AI.tldr: CoRe blends Formal Rewards and Residual Rewards using vision-language model feedback to automate preference-aligned RL without human input.
AI.motivation: Crafting effective rewards in RL is hard: hand-designed rewards may constrain performance, while learned rewards from preferences can be inefficient or unstable. A hybrid approach leveraging vision-language models can capture explicit task structure and implicit preferences.
AI.method: CoRe proposes a dual-module framework: (1) Formal Reward Module (FRM) that uses VLMs to iteratively design/optimize FR based on task knowledge and preference feedback; (2) Residual Reward Module (RRM) that learns RR from video-level preferences, using VLMs to generate preference labels and extract nuanced rewards.
AI.result: CoRe outperforms baselines in policy learning effectiveness and efficiency on ten simulated robotic manipulation tasks and five real-world tasks.
AI.conclusion: A hybrid FR+RR framework guided by VLM feedback yields reliable, efficient rewards and better alignment with human intent without manual reward design.

title: Procedural Memory Distillation: Online Reflection for Self-Improving Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), along with recent selfdistillation variants such as SDPO, evaluates each rollout against a verifier and updates the policy from that episode-level signal. However, the richer procedural information in the rollout is rarely retained or reused. Across episodes and epochs, the model repeatedly encounters related problems under a changing policy, producing cross-episode signals that episode-local updates cannot capture: which strategies consistently pass verification, which failure modes persist, which patterns recur. We propose Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD), which converts these crossepisode signals into reusable procedural memory and distills it into the policy's weights during training. This memory functions as a training scaffold, absorbed into the policy itself, yielding a memory-free model at inference. PMD organizes the memory at three levels of abstraction: raw trajectories, self-reflected strategies and lessons, and higher-level behavioral patterns that recur across problems, all extracted online from the model's own trajectories. A memory-conditioned self-teacher draws on the accumulated experience to supervise the student on its own rollouts, enabling student to progressively internalize procedural knowledge within its parameters. The central design principle is co-evolution: the policy generates rollouts that update the memory, and memory shapes the supervision that updates the policy. Empirically, across Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B, PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8-5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9-13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH. Co-evolution powers these gains: freezing either the memory or the policy trails PMD by more than 10% across SCIKNOWEVAL domains.

AI.tldr: Procedural Memory Distillation (PMD) augments RLVR/SDPO by capturing cross-episode procedural signals into a reusable memory that co-evolves with policy; the memory is distilled into weights, yielding a memory-free policy at inference.
AI.motivation: To exploit richer cross-episode information in rollouts that is ignored by episode-local updates, enabling agents to learn stable, reusable procedures across changing policies and problem instances.
AI.method: PMD builds a three-tier memory: (1) raw trajectories, (2) self-reflected strategies/lessons, and (3) higher-level recurring behavioral patterns. A memory-conditioned self-teacher supervises the student on its own rollouts, with online extraction from agent trajectories. The policy and memory co-evolve: rollouts update memory, memory guides supervision that updates the policy, producing a memory-integrated policy without requiring memory at inference.
AI.result: PMD improves over SDPO by 3.8–5.5% on SCIKNOWEVAL and 7.9–13.6% on LIVECODEBENCH on QA/PL benchmarks using Qwen3-8B and OLMo3-Instruct-7B. Ablations show that freezing either memory or policy reduces gains by over 10%, highlighting the importance of co-evolution.
AI.conclusion: Cross-episode procedural signals can be captured as procedural memory and distilled into the policy, enabling improved performance with a memory-free policy at inference; co-evolution of memory and policy is critical for PMD's gains.

title: Sign in the Air to Unlock: An Interface for authentication in Virtual and Augmented Reality Powered by Point-Voxel Cross-Attention Network
summary: Significant advancement of immersive technologies such as Virtual and Augmented Reality (VR/AR) and their integration into diverse aspects of modern life need authentication interfaces that are secure, intuitive, and compatible with embodied interaction. Traditional methods such as passwords, PINs, and device-based logins, break immersion and rely on external hardware. Recent 3D-specific behavioral approaches, such as hand-gesture, eye-tracking, and electroencephalography (EEG)-based methods, offer promising alternatives but often require specialized sensors or constrain natural movement, limiting usability in dynamic environments. We present Sign in the Air to Unlock, an in-air signature interface that enables users to authenticate by signing naturally in 3D space which is a familiar, personal, and reproducible gesture. To realize this interface, we design a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network (PV-Net) that jointly models local motion dynamics and global spatial structure from 3D trajectories. The model is evaluated on two datasets: the public DeepAirSig dataset (1,800 signatures from 40 users) and ImmAirsig, a new dataset collected using Meta Quest 2 in immersive VR (880 samples from 22 users). PV-Net achieves an Equal Error Rate of 2.5% on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig. These findings highlight the potential of 3D behavioral interfaces for seamless, user-centric authentication that merges security with natural interaction in immersive environments.

AI.tldr: PV-Net enables 3D in-air signature authentication using point-voxel cross-attention; strong results on DeepAirSig (2.5% EER) and ImmAirSig (76% accuracy).
AI.motivation: Need secure, immersion-preserving authentication for VR/AR without external sensors, avoiding passwords or device-based logins that break immersion; existing 3D biometrics often require special hardware or constrain movement.
AI.method: Introduce PV-Net, a point-voxel Cross-Attention Network that jointly models local motion dynamics (point data) and global spatial structure (voxelization) from 3D trajectories. Evaluated on two datasets: DeepAirSig (1,800 signatures, 40 users) and ImmAirsig (880 samples, 22 users) collected with Meta Quest 2.
AI.result: PV-Net achieves 2.5% Equal Error Rate on DeepAirSig and 76% classification accuracy on ImmAirSig, demonstrating the feasibility of natural, device-free authentication in immersive environments.
AI.conclusion: 3D behavioral interfaces like in-air signatures hold promise for seamless, user-centric authentication in VR/AR, though further work is needed on generalization, robustness, real-time deployment, and privacy considerations.

title: Multi-modal Rail Crossing Safety Analysis
summary: Given one or more images of a railway crossing, can we leverage visual cues that allow us to robustly estimate how safe it is? Can we improve our ability to do so by introducing structured data (such as official accident reports) about the accident history of that crossing into our models? In this work, we explore how to best answer those questions towards building an AI system that can ingest multi-modal data for railway crossings and provide safety assessment and scores that align with expert opinion and with safety scoring used by the Federal Railroad Administration (FRA). To that end, we propose a proof-of-concept pipeline that delivers on that goal, while at the same time exploring and tackling a number of critical research challenges that pertain to different parts of the pipeline, from data preparation to different learning paradigms that can allow us to realize such a system. Indicatively, our proposed system identifies HIGH-RISK and LOW-RISK crossings with a macro F1 score of 0.757 and estimates FRA-based safety scores with an RMSE of 0.078 and correlation of 0.492 using a routed fine-tuned compact VLM pipeline, while producing qualitative results that align with domain-expert assessment.

AI.tldr: A multimodal safety-assessment pipeline for railway crossings using images and structured data (accident history) to predict expert-aligned FRA scores; demonstrates feasibility with notable but imperfect performance.
AI.motivation: Improve safety evaluation of railway crossings by leveraging both visual cues from images and official accident-history data, aligning AI scores with expert opinions and FRA metrics.
AI.method: A proof-of-concept pipeline with data preparation, learning paradigms, and a routed fine-tuned compact Vision-Language Model (VLM) to ingest multi-modal data and produce safety assessments and scores.
AI.result: High/Low risk classification macro F1 = 0.757; FRA-based safety scores: RMSE = 0.078, correlation = 0.492; qualitative results align with domain experts.
AI.conclusion: Multi-modal ingestion is feasible for railway-crossing safety scoring and can align with FRA-like metrics, though performance gaps (e.g., correlation) point to areas for further research and refinement.

title: Lightweight Safe Reinforcement Learning for End-to-End UAV Navigation
summary: With the rapid development of autonomous aerial systems, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are increasingly deployed in applications such as inspection, environmental monitoring, and rescue, creating growing demand for reliable autonomous navigation. However, autonomous UAV navigation in dense environments remains challenging under sparse perception and dynamic constraints. Most reinforcement learning (RL) methods lack explicit safety mechanisms, leading to unsafe exploration, unstable training, and risky behaviors, especially during high-speed flight. Even in safe RL approaches, safety is often enforced by projecting policy outputs onto a safe action set, which may introduce instability. Meanwhile, many learning-based methods rely on dense inputs or large networks, increasing computational burden and limiting lightweight onboard deployment. Facing the above challenges, we propose a safety-constrained perception-control integrated framework for UAV navigation. A lightweight network encodes sparse observations into collision-risk-aware features using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. We formulate the task as a constrained Markov decision process within a hierarchical control architecture and solve it using a Lagrangian-based safe PPO algorithm. Curriculum learning further improves training stability. Experiments with varying obstacle densities and flight speeds demonstrate higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency than existing reinforcement learning baselines.

AI.tldr: A lightweight, safety-constrained framework for UAV navigation in dense environments using sparse observations, a constrained MDP with a Lagrangian-safe PPO, and curriculum learning; achieves higher success, safety, and efficiency than baseline RL methods.
AI.motivation: Autonomous UAVs require reliable navigation in cluttered environments with limited sensing. Conventional RL often risks unsafe exploration; safe RL methods can be unstable if policy outputs are projected onto a safe set; heavy perception models hinder onboard deployment.
AI.method: A safety-constrained perception-control framework where a lightweight encoder creates collision-risk features from sparse data using asymmetric and depthwise separable convolutions. The task is formulated as a constrained MDP within a hierarchical control architecture and solved with a Lagrangian-based safe PPO. Curriculum learning is employed to stabilize training.
AI.result: Across varying obstacle densities and flight speeds, the approach yields higher success rates, improved safety, and better efficiency compared with existing RL baselines.
AI.conclusion: The integrated safety-constrained framework enables safer and more efficient UAV navigation under sparse perception, with curriculum learning enhancing training stability and suitability for lightweight onboard deployment.

title: The Agentic Garden of Forking Paths
summary: Empirical research rarely admits a unique analysis. Different analytical choices can lead to different conclusions from the same data, yet these hidden forking paths are difficult to observe. We show that AI agents capture much of the analytical variation among human researchers while making these paths explicit. Across four high-stakes domains, assigning different personas is sufficient for AI agents to report divergent, often opposing, conclusions from the same data and question, with findings systematically aligned with those beliefs. In a study in which 42 human research teams analyzed the same immigration dataset, AI agents reproduced 72% of the human ideological gap in reported effect estimates. Despite reaching opposing conclusions, it is difficult to identify clear issues in each analysis based on the final AI reports: 86% passed independent AI review and 78% passed majority human expert review. These findings suggest that the central challenge is often not flawed analyses, but selective exploration and reporting from a large space of methodologically defensible analyses. AI agents may amplify this longstanding problem by making such exploration inexpensive and scalable. To address this, we introduce the m-value (multiverse value), the probability that an analysis path would produce a claim at least as extreme as the reported one. We further introduce Agentic Bootstrap, which estimates the m-value by using AI agents to sample plausible analysis paths. Applied to the human immigration study, 13.5% of reported human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05). Scientific evidence should therefore be evaluated not only by a single reported analysis but also by its position within the distribution of analyses that could reasonably have been reported. Agentic Bootstrap makes this distribution observable and turns it into a criterion for scientific credibility.

AI.tldr: AI agents reveal and quantify the analytic choice variance (multiverse) in empirical research, introducing m-value and Agentic Bootstrap to assess credibility across plausible analyses; applied to immigration data, showing substantial alignment with human ideological gaps and highlighting the risk of selective reporting.
AI.motivation: Empirical analyses involve many defensible paths (the “multiverse”). Hidden forks can drive divergent conclusions. The work aims to reveal, quantify, and guard against this variability by using AI agents to sample plausible analyses and measure credibility.
AI.method: Use AI agents with varying personas to conduct parallel analyses across four high-stakes domains. Compare agent-reported conclusions to those of 42 human teams analyzing the same immigration dataset. Introduce m-value (probability an analysis path yields as extreme a claim) and Agentic Bootstrap (AI-assisted sampling of plausible analysis paths to estimate m). Apply to immigration study to assess distribution of analyses.
AI.result: AI agents reproduced a large portion of human ideological gaps (e.g., 72% of the human gap in reported effect estimates). Despite opposing conclusions, many AI reports pass independent AI and majority human expert reviews (86% and 78%, respectively). 13.5% of human analyses fell in the most extreme 5% of the analysis space (m<0.05).
AI.conclusion: The credibility of scientific claims should be assessed relative to the entire distribution of plausible analyses, not a single result. Agentic Bootstrap operationalizes this by exposing the analysis distribution via AI sampling, making for a broader criterion of scientific credibility and highlighting that selective exploration can be a key driver of reported conclusions.

title: How Much Future Helps? A Controlled Study of Future-Privileged Supervision for Causal Egocentric Gaze Estimation
comment: Accepted to the 7th International Workshop on Eye and Gaze in Computer Vision (GAZE 2026), CVPR 2026. Best Paper Award
summary: Egocentric gaze estimation is commonly studied using models that process the full video with access to future frames, while real-world applications require strictly causal, online prediction. This discrepancy raises key questions: Does future context inherently provide valuable signals for gaze estimation? If so, how much future look-ahead optimally supervises a causal model during training? To investigate, we propose a controlled framework featuring a future-aware branch that accesses a tunable look-ahead horizon during training but is discarded at inference. This design isolates the impact of future context while keeping the inference architecture fixed and strictly causal. Across EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D, we find that future-privileged supervision consistently improves causal gaze prediction, confirming its utility. However, performance gains do not increase monotonically with longer look-ahead, but rather peak within a bounded temporal regime. Specifically, optimal performance corresponds to roughly 1.7--3.3 seconds of future context ($H{\in}[5, 10]$) on EGTEA Gaze+ and 2.7 seconds ($H{=}10$) on Ego4D. Our results demonstrate that lightweight causal models can effectively absorb future-aware signals, providing practical guidance for real-time egocentric gaze modeling.

AI.tldr: Future-aware supervision helps causal egocentric gaze models, but gains peak at a finite look-ahead; longer horizon does not guarantee more improvement.
AI.motivation: To determine whether future context provides useful signals for strictly causal, online gaze estimation and to identify the optimal training look-ahead horizon.
AI.method: A controlled framework with a future-aware branch that accesses a tunable look-ahead horizon H during training but is discarded at inference, preserving a strictly causal model at test time; evaluated on EGTEA Gaze+ and Ego4D.
AI.result: Future-privileged supervision improves causal gaze prediction on both datasets; gains saturate at a bounded horizon: ~1.7–3.3 seconds (H in [5,10]) for EGTEA Gaze+ and ~2.7 seconds (H=10) for Ego4D.
AI.conclusion: Training with future context is beneficial for causal gaze estimation, but the benefit peaks at a finite horizon; provides practical guidance for real-time egocentric gaze modeling and suggests that lightweight causal models can effectively leverage future signals.

title: How Should Transformers Encode Numeric Values in Electronic Health Records?
comment: 16 pages, 15 figures, 3 tables, accepted to ICML 2026, to be published in Proceedings of Machine Learning Research
summary: How do we encode numeric values in transformer-based sequence processing, particularly in electronic health record (EHR) data? We systematically compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encoding strategies using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded within real-world EHR data, as well as real-world clinical prediction tasks. Our study reveals trade-offs between numeric precision, optimisation stability, and architectural flexibility. We find that approaches that explicitly model value-concept interactions perform best on precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when architectural constraints permit. Hybrid token-based approaches that retain numeric values but apply binning prior to projection provide a more robust and broadly applicable alternative, with the optimal number of bins following a simple empirically derived power-law in dataset size. Across tasks, models consistently exhibit reliable "good enough" numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic, while clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent. This suggests that robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision in practice, motivating hybrid token-based approaches as a practical default.

AI.tldr: Systematic comparison of encoding strategies for numeric values in transformer-based EHR sequence models; hybrid token-based encoding with binning offers robust, scalable performance, while explicit value-concept interactions improve precision when architecture allows; good-enough numeric computation often prevails over exact arithmetic; clinical gains from lab values are task-dependent.
AI.motivation: Address how to encode numeric values in transformer models handling EHR data, comparing discrete, continuous, and hybrid strategies to assess precision, stability, and deployability.
AI.method: Systematic evaluation using synthetic arithmetic tasks embedded in real-world EHR data and real clinical prediction tasks; compare discrete, continuous, and hybrid value encodings; investigate bin counts and resulting performance; derive empirical guidance (power-law) for optimal bin numbers.
AI.result: Trade-offs between numeric precision, optimization stability, and architectural flexibility; value-concept interactions boost precision-sensitive arithmetic tasks when feasible; hybrid token-based approaches with pre-bin projections offer robust, broadly applicable performance; optimal number of bins follows a simple power-law with dataset size; models tend to perform reliable 'good enough' numeric computation rather than exact arithmetic; clinical gains from incorporating laboratory values are task-dependent.
AI.conclusion: Robustness and deployability often outweigh maximal numeric precision; hybrid token-based encoding is a practical default for EHR transformer tasks, though task-specific considerations remain important for clinical gains.

title: VLA-Corrector: Lightweight Detect-and-Correct Inference for Adaptive Action Horizon
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) foundation models have recently achieved strong progress in embodied intelligence. To reduce policy-call frequency while preserving temporal coherence, most generative policies adopt an action chunk mechanism, executing multiple future actions in an open-loop manner under a fixed action horizon. However, this "predict-then-blindly-execute" paradigm sacrifices closed-loop reactivity: in contact-rich physical interactions, even small local perturbations can rapidly amplify within the open-loop blind spot, leading to compounding errors and ultimately task failure. To address this limitation, we propose VLA-Corrector, a lightweight corrective inference framework for action-chunked VLA policies. Without modifying the backbone policy weights, VLA-Corrector introduces a lightweight Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) that continuously compares predicted and actual visual feature evolution, enabling online detection of visual dynamics deviations. Once persistent deviation is detected, the system triggers a truncation event, discards the remaining stale actions, and invokes corrective replanning via Online Gradient Guidance (OGG). The detect-and-correct mechanism of VLA-Corrector naturally induces an event-triggered adaptive action horizon: it preserves long-horizon execution when the current chunk remains reliable, and invokes short-horizon corrective replanning when execution begins to drift. In doing so, VLA-Corrector mitigates the trade-off imposed by static horizons between execution robustness and policy-call frequency. It can be integrated into different VLA models without further retraining the VLA backbone, interrupting compounding errors while preserving much of the efficiency benefit of action chunking and substantially improving robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich robotic manipulation tasks.

AI.tldr: A lightweight corrective inference framework (VLA-Corrector) enhances action-chunked VLA policies by online visual monitoring and corrective replanning to adapt action horizons on the fly.
AI.motivation: Action chunking improves efficiency but sacrifices closed-loop reactivity, risking drift and failure in contact-rich manipulation; an online mechanism is needed to detect deviations and correct without retraining.
AI.method: Introduce Latent-space Vision Monitor (LVM) to compare predicted vs actual visual features; detect persistent deviations; trigger truncation of remaining actions; use Online Gradient Guidance (OGG) for corrective replanning; adaptive event-triggered horizon; backbone unchanged; compatible with various VLA models.
AI.result: Improved robustness in long-horizon, contact-rich tasks; reduces compounding errors; preserves efficiency benefits of chunking; demonstrates plug-in improvement without backbone retraining.
AI.conclusion: VLA-Corrector provides a plug-in, lightweight mechanism to interrupt drift and perform online correction, achieving a better trade-off between robustness and policy-call frequency in VLA systems.

title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
comment: Code and data released on GitHub: https://github.com/GraceBrigham/Janus
summary: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains under explored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user input is critical and can significantly strengthen privacy and security, that AI augmentation of user decisions can help reduce cognitive load, and that realistic user behavior including permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.

AI.tldr: Janus provides a modular framework (Janus-Core) and evaluation harness (Janus-Harness) for user-involved agentic permission management, showing no one-size-fits-all design and highlighting the value of user input, AI augmentation, and realistic user behavior in permission decision-making.
AI.motivation: To address how users should participate in agentic permission management as AI agents autonomously perform tool calls, and to provide a principled, testable design space.
AI.method: 1) Develop Janus-Core: a modular agentic system with a spectrum of permission-management designs. 2) Build Janus-Harness: automated evaluation across three scenarios and three synthetic responders. 3) Ground design in a conceptual model of design axes for user involvement. 4) Implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them.
AI.result: Found that user input significantly strengthens privacy and security; AI augmentation can reduce cognitive load; realistic user behavior (e.g., permission fatigue) must be considered. No single design dominates across contexts; context-sensitive approaches are needed. Janus is publicly available for future work.
AI.conclusion: A principled, context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants is necessary; user involvement is beneficial but must be tailored to context, and evaluation frameworks like Janus are crucial to compare designs and drive progress in agentic permission management.

title: A Cost-Aware, Paired Protocol for Auditing Dynamic Tool Synthesis in Agentic Video Question Answering
summary: Agentic Video Question Answering (VideoQA) systems invoke tools during inference, but their tool libraries are fixed, so recurring procedures are rebuilt from primitives on every question. Synthesizing composite tools could remove this overhead, but whether such expansion helps is hard to assess: final-answer accuracy, the standard metric, ignores inference effort, so it cannot reveal how a system shifts cost. We propose a cost-aware, paired protocol for auditing tool-augmented video agents. The protocol pairs two complete systems on the same input for each question and reports their net difference across accuracy and cost jointly. For each question, it sorts the paired outcome into one of six groups defined by joint correctness and by the change in visible tool calls, separating accuracy-preserving efficiency gains from harmful regressions. Significance is reported with McNemar's test and paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We instantiate the protocol on Dynamic-SAGE, an agentic VideoQA framework that synthesizes, validates, and persistently registers executable composite tools for reuse on unseen questions, and evaluate it against the SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench. The audit reveals a multi-axis profile that a scalar accuracy comparison would miss: Dynamic-SAGE improves accuracy by 7.5 points (p < 0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by roughly 28%, while shifting rather than reducing inference cost, as token usage rises 34% and cost 26%. Gains are largest on visual and open-ended questions and neutral on verbal and multimodal ones, and residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended questions where the pipeline does the most work. By measuring accuracy and cost jointly, the protocol shows where the pipeline-level difference is reliable and where it is not. The code is available at https://github.com/KurbanIntelligenceLab/Dynamic-SAGE.

AI.tldr: A cost-aware paired auditing protocol for tool-augmented VideoQA, demonstrating Dynamic-SAGE outperforms SAGE on accuracy while changing but not reducing overall cost; paired evaluation reveals multi-axis trade-offs ignored by scalar accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard accuracy metrics hide inference cost shifts when evaluating tool-augmented systems. There is a need to audit both accuracy and resource usage to understand true efficiency and reliability of composite-tools pipelines.
AI.method: Introduce a paired evaluation: for each question, compare two complete systems on the same input. Classify outcomes into six groups by joint correctness and by changes in visible tool calls. Use McNemar's test and paired bootstrap CIs to report significance. Instantiate on Dynamic-SAGE (synthesizes/validates composite tools) vs SAGE baseline on SAGE-Bench, measuring accuracy, reasoning turns, visible tool calls, token usage, and monetary cost.
AI.result: Dynamic-SAGE increases accuracy by 7.5 points (p<0.001) and reduces reasoning turns and visible tool calls by ~28%, but raises token usage by 34% and overall cost by 26%. Gains are strongest on visual/open-ended questions and neutral on verbal/multimodal ones; residual failures concentrate on hard, open-ended queries where the pipeline does most work. The protocol reveals a multi-axis profile that scalar accuracy would miss; code is publicly available.
AI.conclusion: Joint accuracy-cost auditing provides reliable insight into when tool synthesis helps or harms overall performance, revealing trade-offs and guiding development of tool-augmented agents. The approach is applicable to other multi-component AI systems and emphasizes cost-aware evaluation.

title: NeuroBridge: Bridging Multi-Task MRI Knowledge for Neurodegenerative Disease Diagnosis
summary: INTRODUCTION: Accurate MRI-based identification of Alzheimer's disease (AD), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and related dementias remains challenging because disease-related structural changes are often subtle and heterogeneous. We developed NeuroBridge, a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis. METHODS: NeuroBridge integrates large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, and reconstruction objectives, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning. Performance was evaluated across ADNI and OASIS cohorts, including cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening. RESULTS: NeuroBridge achieved the highest performance across evaluated classification tasks, reaching 88.17% accuracy for AD versus cognitively normal controls in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. The largest gains occurred in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. The framework demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization, systematic associations between predicted-class probability and accuracy, and the feasibility of probability-based opportunistic screening. DISCUSSION: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning improves neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond conventional single-task approaches. NeuroBridge provides a robust and scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

AI.tldr: NeuroBridge is a clinically guided multi-task MRI framework that combines self-supervised pretraining with hippocampal segmentation, atrophy classification, and reconstruction, followed by gated fusion fine-tuning, achieving high accuracy in AD vs CN and good cross-cohort generalization.
AI.motivation: MRI-based dementia diagnosis is hampered by subtle, heterogeneous disease-related changes. A robust, scalable framework that leverages multi-task learning and self-supervised pretraining could improve accuracy and generalization, enabling opportunistic screening.
AI.method: Large-scale self-supervised MRI pretraining integrated with three tasks (hippocampal segmentation, hippocampal atrophy classification, reconstruction) and a gated fusion mechanism for fine-tuning. Evaluation on ADNI and OASIS cohorts with cross-cohort transfer, probability-based analysis, and opportunistic screening.
AI.result: Achieved 88.17% accuracy for AD vs CN in ADNI and 82.78% in OASIS. Notable gains in MCI-related and mixed-diagnosis settings. Demonstrated strong cross-cohort generalization and relevance of predicted-class probabilities for accuracy and opportunistic screening.
AI.conclusion: Clinically guided multi-task representation learning enhances neurodegenerative MRI diagnosis beyond single-task approaches. NeuroBridge offers a robust, scalable framework for dementia assessment and MRI-based opportunistic screening.

title: DL-SLAM: Enabling High-Fidelity Gaussian Splatting SLAM in Dynamic Environments based on Dual-Level Probability
summary: Recent advances in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) have enabled significant progress in dense dynamic Simultaneous Localization And Mapping (SLAM). Prevailing methods typically discard predefined dynamic objects, ignoring that transiently static objects offer valuable geometric constraints for pose estimation. A recent work attempts to leverage this potential by employing per-pixel uncertainty maps to quantify the magnitude of motion. While this approach enables transiently static objects to enhance pose estimation, it erroneously integrates these objects into the static map, resulting in persistent artifacts. Moreover, its reliance on purely geometric information leads to ambiguous object boundaries in the uncertainty maps. To overcome these limitations, we present DL-SLAM, a monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM system built upon a novel dual-level probabilistic framework. Our method computes dynamic probability maps by combining semantic and geometric information. These pixel-level probabilities are lifted to 3D and aggregated to derive an object-level dynamic probability for each instance. Object-level probability enables the categorical pruning of dynamic Gaussians, resulting in an artifact-free static map. The static map, in turn, provides a geometrically consistent guidance to refine the pixel-wise probabilities, enhancing their reliability. Experimental results demonstrate that DL-SLAM outperforms existing approaches, improving tracking accuracy by up to 13\% while generating high-fidelity semantic maps.

AI.tldr: DL-SLAM introduces a dual-level probabilistic framework for monocular Gaussian Splatting SLAM that fuses semantic and geometric cues to separate dynamic objects from the static map, enabling artifact-free maps and improved tracking.
AI.motivation: Prevailing dynamic-SLAM methods either discard dynamic objects (losing useful geometric constraints) or rely on uncertain per-pixel motion maps that produce artifacts by embedding dynamic elements into the static map.
