A robust approach should leverage transiently static objects while avoiding artifacts.
AI.method: Compute dynamic probability maps by combining semantic and geometric information at the pixel level, lift these probabilities to 3D and aggregate per object instance to obtain object-level dynamic probabilities, prune dynamic Gaussians based on object-level probabilities to produce an artifact-free static map, and iteratively refine pixel-level probabilities using the robust static map to enhance reliability.
AI.result: DL-SLAM outperforms existing methods, achieving up to ~13% improvement in tracking accuracy and delivering high-fidelity semantic maps.
AI.conclusion: A dual-level probabilistic framework effectively separates dynamic and static components in 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM, leveraging object-level dynamics to prune dynamic elements and using the consistent static map to refine probabilities, yielding better pose estimation and semantic mapping.

title: Revisiting Chain-of-Thought Reasoning under Limited Supervision: Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning has emerged as an effective approach for activating latent reasoning capabilities in large language models. However, most existing CoT methods use reasoning chains mainly as inference-time prompts, while the generated reasoning traces are rarely reused as semi-supervised learning signals. In this report, we define \textbf{Semi-supervised Chain-of-Thought Learning} and propose \textbf{Semi-CoT}, a simple framework that uses unlabeled questions to construct pseudo reasoning supervision. Semi-CoT samples multiple pseudo-CoTs for each unlabeled question, estimates answer-level semantic entropy, and selects low-entropy reasoning chains as reliable pseudo-CoT demonstrations. This extends the self-training view of CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised pseudo-supervision. Pilot experiments on AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith show that the entropy gate selects high-precision pseudo-CoTs, with pseudo-answer precision ranging from $91.36\%$ to $100\%$. Semi-CoT also gives small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, while AQuA shows negative transfer and MultiArith reaches a ceiling. These results suggest that unlabeled questions can provide reliable pseudo reasoning signals, but their effective use still requires stronger demonstration selection or student training.

AI.tldr: Semi-CoT introduces semi-supervised CoT by generating multiple pseudo-CoTs for unlabeled questions, then using an entropy-based gate to select low-entropy, high-precision pseudo reasoning traces as demonstrations for training. It extends CoT from inference-time prompts to semi-supervised signals, showing high pseudo-CoT precision but mixed downstream impact across datasets.
AI.motivation: To leverage unlabeled questions to produce reliable pseudo reasoning demonstrations, shifting CoT from inference-time refinement to semi-supervised learning and potentially reducing labeling effort.
AI.method: Generate multiple pseudo-CoTs per unlabeled question. Estimate answer-level semantic entropy to gauge reliability and select low-entropy reasoning chains as pseudo-CoT demonstrations. Use these pseudo-CoTs to train the model in a semi-supervised loop, extending self-training of CoT from inference-time use to training-time supervision.
AI.result: On AQuA, SVAMP, GSM8K, and MultiArith, the entropy gate yields high-precision pseudo-CoTs (pseudo-answer precision 91.36%-100%). Downstream gains are dataset-dependent: small gains on SVAMP and GSM8K, negative transfer on AQuA, and a ceiling on MultiArith.
AI.conclusion: Unlabeled data can provide useful pseudo reasoning signals, but effective use requires stronger demonstration selection criteria or student training. Semi-CoT is promising for semi-supervised CoT, yet robustness across tasks remains an open challenge.

title: Anti-Prompt: Image Protection against Text-Guided Image-to-Video Generation
summary: Recent advances in Image-to-Video generation allow a single image to be animated into a convincing video under text guidance, raising serious copyright and privacy risks. We propose Anti-Prompt, an image protection approach that injects imperceptible perturbations into an image, inducing visible inconsistencies and structural failures in text-guided I2V generation. Our method is motivated by a simple empirical observation. When text guidance is removed from modern I2V models, generation quality degrades markedly, not only in motion realism but also in subject preservation, structural coherence, and temporal consistency. Building on this insight, Anti-Prompt exploits the model reliance on textual guidance by attenuating text-conditioned interactions during denoising while strengthening visual-only pathways. To further systematically evaluate protection effectiveness, we introduce a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol that provides interpretable, frame-grounded analyses of generation artifacts and inconsistencies. Experiments on two representative I2V architectures demonstrate that our method achieves strong protection performance while improving efficiency and cross-model transferability.

AI.tldr: Proposes Anti-Prompt: imperceptible image perturbations that disrupt text-guided image-to-video generation by weakening text-conditioned interactions and enhancing visual pathways; introduces a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol; shows protection across two I2V architectures with improved efficiency and cross-model transferability.
AI.motivation: Rising copyright and privacy concerns in text-guided image-to-video generation demand protective techniques. The approach leverages the model's reliance on textual guidance to suppress text-conditioned synthesis while preserving visual pathways.
AI.method: Inject imperceptible perturbations into the input image. During denoising, attenuate text-conditioned interactions and strengthen visual-only pathways. Introduce a Video-LLM-assisted evaluation protocol for frame-grounded analyses of artifacts and inconsistencies.
AI.result: Empirical results on two representative I2V models show strong protection performance, with improvements in efficiency and cross-model transferability.
AI.conclusion: Anti-Prompt offers an effective defense against I2V-enabled copyright/privacy risks, supported by a systematic evaluation protocol; the approach may generalize to other modalities and paves the way for robust content protection.

title: Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics Enable Complete and Scalable $\mathrm{E}(3)$-Equivariant Networks
summary: $\mathrm{E}(3)$-equivariant networks are promising for 3D atomistic system modeling, yet their scalability is limited by the $O(L^6)$ complexity of the Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP). The recently proposed Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) reduces the complexity but is unable to capture the antisymmetric paths, resulting in incomplete expressivity. In this work, we present SpinGTP, an approach to overcome the GTP incompleteness by generalizing from scalar functions to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH). By relying on the algebraic properties of SWSH, SpinGTP recovers the missing antisymmetric interactions while maintaining the asymptotic efficiency of GTP. It also allows for a more expressive equivariant basis that naturally accounts for the parity-odd components of tensor products. We evaluate SpinGTP across diverse benchmarks, including Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, and OC20. Our results show that SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP. Notably, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, SpinGTP exhibits superior performance in tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries. This work provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous path toward high-order equivariance in large-scale 3D atomistic system simulations.

AI.tldr: SpinGTP generalizes from scalar to Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics to recover antisymmetric interactions in E(3)-equivariant networks, achieving CGTP-like accuracy with lower complexity and enhanced parity-odd expressivity, enabling scalable high-order equivariant modeling of 3D atomistic systems.
AI.motivation: To overcome the expressivity gaps and scalability limits of existing Clebsch-Gordan Tensor Product (CGTP) and Gaunt Tensor Product (GTP) approaches, particularly the inability of GTP to capture antisymmetric paths and parity-odd components in high-order equivariant models.
AI.method: Introduce SpinGTP by replacing scalar basis with Spin-Weighted Spherical Harmonics (SWSH), leveraging their algebraic properties to encode antisymmetric interactions and parity-odd tensor products, while preserving the asymptotic efficiency close to GTP.
AI.result: SpinGTP achieves accuracies comparable to full CGTP across benchmarks (Tetris, 3BPA, SPICE-MACE-OFF, OC20) and, by explicitly capturing antisymmetric paths, shows superior performance on tasks involving chiral materials and non-centrosymmetric geometries.
AI.conclusion: SpinGTP provides a complete, scalable, and mathematically rigorous pathway to high-order E(3)-equivariant representations in large-scale 3D atomistic simulations, addressing both expressivity gaps and computational efficiency.

title: SPLC: Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation
summary: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) holds significant potential for crowd robot navigation in human-robot coexistence applications. However, the inherent complexity of pedestrian motion renders the design of effective reward functions for promoting socially compliant robot behaviors a persistent challenge. This paper proposes a Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) algorithm to eliminate the need for detailed reward design. Its core innovation lies in the introduction of a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data through principled preference evaluation criteria. By explicitly accounting for the intricacies of pedestrian dynamics, the pipeline mitigates the reward bias and facilitates the systematic quantification of broad social norms, thereby fostering socially compliant behaviors. Extensive experiments integrating SPLC with offline RL methods demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across standard performance metrics. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the TurtleBot4 further validate the effectiveness of SPLC in practical human-robot coexistence settings. Our code and video demos are available at https://github.com/sklus949/SPLC.

AI.tldr: SPLC: an offline RL framework for crowd robot navigation that uses a social preference feedback mechanism to automatically generate preference data, removing the need for hand-crafted reward functions; validated in simulations and on TurtleBot4 with code published.
AI.motivation: Reward design for socially compliant navigation is difficult due to complex pedestrian dynamics and the need to encode broad social norms; an automated, preference-based learning approach can reduce reward bias and improve learning of social behavior.
AI.method: Introduce Social Preference Learning for Crowd Robot Navigation (SPLC) with a social preference feedback mechanism that heuristically evaluates and converts pedestrian- and scene-level interactions into preference data; integrate this with offline RL methods to learn policies that are socially compliant without explicit reward engineering; test in standard benchmarks and real-world TurtleBot4 experiments; release code at GitHub.
AI.result: SPLC-consistently improves over state-of-the-art offline RL baselines across standard performance metrics in simulations; real-world TurtleBot4 experiments validate practicality in human-robot coexistence scenarios; code and demos provided.
AI.conclusion: SPLC offers a practical, reward-design-free pathway to learn socially compliant crowd navigation policies via synthetic preference data derived from pedestrian dynamics; demonstrated effectiveness in both offline and real-world settings and with available code for reproduction.

title: OPINE-World: Programmatic World Modeling with Ontology-error-Prioritized Interactive Exploration
summary: Learning how an environment behaves from interaction is central to building agents that adapt to unfamiliar tasks. World models learned with deep networks are flexible but data-hungry and transfer poorly beyond their training distribution. Program-synthesized world models, written as source code by LLMs and refined through counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS), are instead data-efficient and reusable, yet they have been demonstrated mainly on structured-state worlds with a given object vocabulary, and a single program search does not scale to pixel-rendered environments whose object structure must be hypothesized flexibly. We introduce OPINE-World, an LLM agent that learns an object-centric programmatic world model online from interaction. OPINE-World couples two cooperating agents in a loop of hypothesis and test, one acting in the environment and one synthesizing the model in code with replay verification and model-based planning, and it steers exploration with a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy we call ontology error. We evaluate OPINE-World on ARC-AGI-3, a benchmark for skill-acquisition efficiency in which the object vocabulary, the goal, and the action semantics are withheld. OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and reaches an action-efficiency score of 78.4 against the human baseline.

AI.tldr: OPINE-World learns an online, object-centric, programmatic world model via an LLM and CEGIS, enabling data-efficient, reusable learning in pixel environments; evaluated on ARC-AGI-3, obtaining 20/25 games solved and 78.4 action-efficiency.
AI.motivation: Data-efficient, reusable world models are needed because deep networks are data-hungry and transfer poorly. Prior program-synthesized models work on structured-state worlds with fixed vocabularies and struggle to scale to pixel-based environments where object structure must be hypothesized.
AI.method: Two-agent loop: an environmental actor and a model-synthesis agent that writes object-centric world-model code with an LLM, refined by replay verification and counterexample-guided inductive synthesis (CEGIS); model-based planning is used for control; exploration guided by ontology error, a Bayesian measure of object-type adequacy.
AI.result: On ARC-AGI-3, OPINE-World solves 20 of 25 games without per-game training and achieves an action-efficiency of 78.4 compared to human baseline.
AI.conclusion: OPINE-World demonstrates a data-efficient, reusable, object-centric world-modeling approach based on programmatic models synthesized by LLMs and refined via CEGIS, scalable to pixel-based worlds, with ontology-error-guided exploration and strong skill acquisition performance.

title: Disentangling Pictorial Cue Understanding from Language Bias in VLMs via Depth Ordering Task
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, accepted to ECCV 2026 (30 pages, 13 figures, supplementary materials included)
summary: In this paper, we study depth perception of vision-language models (VLMs) to isolate the effects of pictorial depth cues and disentangle vision and language influences on model performance. To this end, we combine depth-ordering and odd-one-out psychophysical tasks: the VLMs are presented with images where one object is at different depth relative to other, otherwise identical, objects, and must determine whether the odd-one-out target is closer or farther to the observer. To create stimuli, we generate 2D views from simulated and real 3D scenes while controlling the presence of individual pictorial depth cues, enabling a fine-grained analysis of cue-level contributions. Language effects are examined by varying referring expression clarity. We also introduce a novel metric to quantify vision-vs-language sensitivities. Applying this methodology, we create the Odd-One-Out Depth (O3-D) dataset with 37K real and synthetic images and 147K image-question pairs. Evaluation of 12 open-source and commercial models on O3-D shows under-utilization of depth cues and depth-ordering accuracies between 47% and 56%, with no model above chance level. At the same time, our metric reveals strong linguistic bias in the answers. Neither chain-of-thought (CoT) nor in-context learning (ICL) significantly improves performance, suggesting that static image data alone may be insufficient for depth understanding. All code, the image generation pipeline, and the O3-D dataset are publicly released at https://github.com/lyiqian/o3-d.

AI.tldr: A study on depth perception in vision-language models using controlled pictorial cues and language manipulation, introducing the O3-D dataset to quantify vision vs. language contributions in depth tasks.
AI.motivation: To disentangle how VLMs rely on visual depth cues versus language cues, and to assess whether current models truly understand depth from static images.
AI.method: Use depth-ordering and odd-one-out tasks with stimuli derived from real and synthetic 3D scenes; systematically enable/disable individual pictorial depth cues; vary referring expression clarity; introduce a vision-vs-language sensitivity metric; evaluate 12 models on the resulting O3-D dataset (37k real/synthetic images; 147k QA pairs).
AI.result: Depth cues are under-utilized; depth-ordering accuracy ranges 47–56% with no model above chance; strong linguistic bias in answers; CoT/ICL do not improve performance; static images alone may be insufficient for depth understanding.
AI.conclusion: O3-D reveals substantial gaps in current VLMs’ depth reasoning and highlights the need for datasets and methods that separately probe visual depth understanding from language biases; authors provide code, generation pipeline, and dataset publicly.

title: The Rollout Infrastructure Tax in Coding-Agent Reinforcement Learning
comment: Preprint. 6 pages, 6 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to ACM SoCC 2026
summary: Coding-agent reinforcement learning treats execution infrastructure as a background implementation detail, despite relying on large numbers of interactive software rollouts. This is a missed opportunity: measuring infrastructure overhead can reveal practical efficiency gains for RL post-training, where small per-rollout savings compound at scale. We present a comparative study of four execution substrates: single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-orchestrated containers, and cloud virtual machines. We find up to $110\times$ variation in cold-start latency and a $1.8\times$ spread in projected worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories. Our results suggest that future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training system itself, not merely as deployment plumbing.

AI.tldr: Comparative analysis of four execution substrates for coding-agent RL shows large startup-time and training-cost variation; infrastructure choices materially affect training efficiency, arguing for treating execution substrate as part of the training system.
AI.motivation: Execution infrastructure is a hidden but significant cost in coding-agent RL; measuring and optimizing substrate performance can yield large efficiency gains when scaling with many rollouts.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing four substrates (single containers, hosted sandboxes, Kubernetes-managed containers, cloud VMs); measure cold-start latency and project worker-hours for one million 150-step trajectories; analyze variation and implications for training efficiency.
AI.result: Observed up to 110x variation in cold-start latency and about 1.8x spread in projected worker-hours for large-scale trajectories, indicating substantial efficiency gaps across substrates.
AI.conclusion: Future coding-agent RL systems should optimize execution substrates as part of the training loop, integrating substrate decisions into the training architecture rather than treating it as deployment plumbing.

title: PhysMani: Physics-principled 3D World Model for Dynamic Object Manipulation
comment: ECCV 2026. Code and data are available at: https://github.com/vLAR-group/PhysMani
summary: Manipulating fast and dynamically moving targets in unstructured 3D environments remains challenging for embodied AI. Existing visual-language-action models and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting. We propose PhysMani, a framework that couples a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy model. The world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast and physically grounded future dynamics prediction. The policy model integrates the predicted 3D scene future dynamics through a learnable token based cross-attention module. We introduce PhysMani-Bench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark with 16 tasks, and demonstrate a superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.

AI.tldr: PhysMani proposes a physics-principled 3D Gaussian world model with a future-aware action policy for dynamic manipulation; introduces PhysMani-Bench with 16 tasks and shows superior success in simulation and real robots.
AI.motivation: Current visual-language-action and world models struggle with accurate 3D geometry and physically meaningful forecasting for fast-moving targets in unstructured 3D environments; a physically grounded, future-aware framework is needed for robust dynamic manipulation.
AI.method: A world model learns a divergence-free Gaussian velocity field via online optimization for fast, physically consistent future dynamics; a policy model uses a learnable token-based cross-attention module to integrate predicted 3D scene dynamics; framework is named PhysMani; evaluation includes PhysMani-Bench with 16 tasks.
AI.result: Superior success rate over strong baselines in both simulation and real-world robot experiments.
AI.conclusion: PhysMani provides a physically grounded, future-aware approach to dynamic 3D manipulation, with a dedicated benchmark validating performance across diverse tasks.

title: Scaling Trends for Lie Detector Oversight in Preference Learning
summary: Deceptive behavior in LLMs is costly to monitor and prevent, motivating approaches such as Scalable Oversight via Lie Detectors (SOLiD) (Cundy & Gleave, 2025), which uses lie detectors to identify responses for review by high-cost labelers. In this paper, we scale SOLiD to larger models and evaluate it in more diverse and realistic preference-learning settings. We find favorable scaling: undetected deception drops from 34% for 1B-parameter models to 14% for 405B-parameter models at a detector true positive rate of 99%, and expensive human labelers can be removed entirely from the fine-tuning phase without a statistically significant increase in deception. However, SOLiD is sensitive to distribution shift between detector training and preference-training data, which can drive detector false positive rates to impractical levels.

AI.tldr: Scaling SOLiD for deception detection in LLMs shows improved detection with larger models; human labeling can be dropped during fine-tuning with little deception increase; however, distribution shift between detector training and preference training causes higher false positives.
AI.motivation: To provide scalable oversight for LLMs by detecting deceptive responses at scale and reducing reliance on expensive human review; extend SOLiD to larger models and more realistic settings.
AI.method: Scale SOLiD to up to 405B-parameter models; evaluate in varied preference-learning contexts; measure undetected deception at detector TPR=99%; compare 1B vs 405B; test removing expensive labelers during fine-tuning; assess robustness to distribution shift.
AI.result: Undetected deception dropped from 34% (1B) to 14% (405B) at 99% TPR; removing humans from fine-tuning did not yield a statistically significant increase in deception; distribution shift increases detector FP rates to impractical levels.
AI.conclusion: SOLiD scales favorably with model size and can reduce reliance on human labeling in fine-tuning, but robustness to distribution shift remains a challenge; future work should address FP control under domain shift.

title: Hidden-Shot: Towards One-Shot Task Generalization for Low-Level Vision Generalist Models
summary: Despite the intense engagement surrounding low-level vision generalist models, their effectiveness in zero/few-shot scenarios beyond learned tasks remains unverified. The primary challenge of developing an ideal generalist lies in achieving the ability to generalize from new unseen tasks, which also can be assessed by matched quantitative criteria. Existing methods have made some progress in prompt engineering but have not systematically explored this gap across a wide range of low-level visual tasks. Stimulated by the problem, we propose Hidden-Shot, an implicit prompt mechanism aimed at exploring low-level task adaptation in a vision generalist model. Specifically, the method extracts implicit visual task-based information, utilizes a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merges implicit information with in-task processing information to enhance one-shot capabilities in new tasks. The overall design performs direct injection in a cost-effective manner, while minimally altering the architecture of the original generalist model. Additionally, we introduce a data-driven evaluation framework termed C/U assessment to cover two basic scenarios, 3C4U (3 conventional and 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models and 3C7U (3 conventional and 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch, as a comprehensive assessment to systematically test the generalization ability of low-level generalist models. Experiments on seven and ten datasets outperform the state-of-the-art vision generalist model, respectively verified by 3C4U and 3C7U framework. Our presented Hidden-Shot approach demonstrates superior performance on one-shot new tasks while maintaining consistent performance on existing tasks.

AI.tldr: Hidden-Shot: an implicit prompt mechanism to improve one-shot generalization for low-level vision generalist models, using a global task-aware textural prompt and selective information merging; introduces C/U assessment with 3C4U/3C7U to evaluate generalization across conventional/unconventional tasks; shows state-of-the-art gains on seven/ten datasets under respective frameworks.
AI.motivation: Evaluate and improve generalization of low-level vision generalist models beyond learned tasks, addressing the gap in one-shot and zero-shot adaptation to unseen tasks and the lack of systematic evaluation across a broad task spectrum.
AI.method: Extract implicit task-based information, employ a global task-aware textural prompt, and selectively merge implicit information with in-task processing to enable one-shot adaptation; injects prompts in a cost-effective, minimally invasive manner; introduces data-driven C/U assessment frameworks: 3C4U (3 conventional, 4 unconventional tasks) for retraining existing models, and 3C7U (3 conventional, 7 unconventional tasks) for training from scratch.
AI.result: Outperforms the state-of-the-art vision generalist model on seven datasets (3C4U) and ten datasets (3C7U), validating improved one-shot generalization on new tasks while maintaining performance on existing tasks.
AI.conclusion: Hidden-Shot provides an effective, lightweight mechanism to enable rapid adaptation of vision generalists to unseen tasks; the C/U assessment framework offers a comprehensive, data-driven evaluation protocol for broad generalization across conventional and unconventional tasks.

title: Conditional Inference Trees and Forests for Feature Selection
summary: Conditional inference trees (CIT) and conditional inference forests (CIF) reduce split-selection bias by testing features before choosing split thresholds, but repeated permutation tests and threshold searches can make these methods computationally expensive. We study CIT and CIF as top-$k$ feature-ranking methods for downstream prediction using real-data benchmarks, runtime ablations, and synthetic feature-recovery experiments. At a fixed node, if the features and permutation budget do not depend on the node responses, Bonferroni-corrected $+1$ Monte Carlo permutation $p$-values control nodewise rejection under the complete permutation null. CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. With Bonferroni correction held fixed, the CIF runtime ablations indicate that adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest measured effect on runtime: turning off adaptive stopping and using exact threshold search increase fitting time by 4.0--8.4$\times$ and 1.9--10.8$\times$, respectively, while downstream score changes are at most 0.011. Sparse high-$p$ simulations indicate that forest feature sampling can leave informative features out of many split decisions. Overall, the results support CIF as a top-$k$ feature-ranking method in the evaluated downstream prediction benchmarks.

AI.tldr: CIF/CIT reduce split-selection bias but can be computationally expensive; CIF ranks competitively as a top-k feature-ranking method; runtime is driven by adaptive stopping and threshold search; sparse high-p simulations can miss informative features; overall CIF is effective for downstream prediction benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Assess the practical value of CIT/CIF as top-k feature-ranking tools by quantifying bias reduction, computational cost, and downstream predictive utility on real and synthetic data.
AI.method: Per-node permutation testing with Bonferroni-corrected +1 Monte Carlo p-values under a complete permutation null when features and permutation budget do not depend on node responses. Benchmark CIF/CIT against a broad suite of methods across 22 classification datasets and 8 regression datasets; perform runtime ablations (adaptive stopping and threshold search) and synthetic feature-recovery experiments; also examine sparse high-p scenarios to assess feature sampling impact.
AI.result: CIF ranks 4th among 17 classification methods on 22 datasets and 3rd among 18 regression methods on 8 datasets. When Bonferroni correction is fixed, adaptive stopping and the number of thresholds searched have the largest runtime impact (4.0–8.4× and 1.9–10.8× increases, respectively) with downstream score changes ≤0.011. Sparse high-p simulations show forest feature sampling can omit informative features from many split decisions.
AI.conclusion: CIF is a strong top-k feature-ranking method for downstream prediction in the evaluated benchmarks; runtime can be significantly reduced with fixed adaptive stopping and threshold search settings, albeit with minimal loss in downstream performance; beware potential loss of informative features in very sparse high-p regimes.

title: A Stereo Visual SLAM System Using Object-Level Motion Estimation and Geometric Filtering Based on Cross Disparity
summary: This paper presents OCD SLAM, a dynamic stereo visual SLAM framework that extends ORB-SLAM2 by jointly addressing dynamic objects and dynamic features in the scene. Usual visual SLAM systems operating in dynamic environments often fail in the presence of moving objects, due to the static-world assumption used in pose estimation and mapping. To address this predicament, we introduce a novel geometric approach based on the discrepancy between disparity and a newly proposed notion called ``cross disparity'', which exploits both temporal and stereo inconsistency to identify dynamic feature points. Complementary to this feature-level motion analysis, OCD SLAM integrates a 3D object detection module (SMOKE) with Kalman filter-based object tracking to perform object-level motion classification, enabling robust separation of static and dynamic scene elements for accurate pose estimation. The proposed approach has been evaluated on various sequences from the KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw datasets. Results demonstrate that OCD SLAM achieves significant improvement in trajectory accuracy compared to ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods. Ablation studies further demonstrate the effectiveness of the cross disparity module in the KITTI Raw dataset and show that this method is able to detect dynamic features that are missed by the 3D object detection scheme alone.

AI.tldr: Dynamic stereo SLAM OCD-SLAM extends ORB-SLAM2 by introducing cross disparity for feature-level dynamic detection and integrating SMOKE-based 3D object detection with Kalman tracking for object-level motion classification, improving pose/trajectory accuracy in dynamic scenes.
AI.motivation: Standard SLAM assumes a static world; moving objects cause feature and map corruption, requiring joint handling of dynamic features and objects to maintain accurate camera pose and map.
AI.method: Proposes cross disparity: a discrepancy between disparity and cross disparity that uses temporal and stereo inconsistencies to identify dynamic feature points. Combines a 3D object detector (SMOKE) with Kalman-filter-based tracking for object-level motion classification. Integrates these with the mapper to exclude dynamic elements from pose estimation and mapping.
AI.result: Evaluated on KITTI Odometry and KITTI Raw sequences; shows significant trajectory accuracy improvement over ORB-SLAM2 and several state-of-the-art dynamic SLAM methods. Ablation confirms effectiveness of cross disparity in KITTI Raw and its ability to detect dynamics missed by 3D object detection alone.
AI.conclusion: Cross-disparity-based feature exclusion together with object-level motion classification yields robust dynamic SLAM performance, enabling more accurate trajectory estimation in dynamic environments and validating the approach on standard KITTI datasets.

title: EO-Agents: A Three-Agent LLM Pipeline for Earth Observation Hypothesis Generation
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 AI for Science Workshop
summary: Large language models have recently been explored for scientific hypothesis generation, but most prior work relies on unstructured literature and free-form textual claims. We present a pipeline for Earth observation that grounds hypothesis generation directly in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph. A heterogeneous graph neural network trained on historical co-usage relations ranks candidate dataset pairings, and a three-agent LLM pipeline filters, generates, and evaluates structured research hypotheses. Applied to 1,475 NASA datasets, the system produces 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains, including ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol--cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry. Model-predicted novel dataset pairings are rated nearly as plausible as held-out real co-usages from the literature, indicating that the pipeline surfaces scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations. A 2*2*2 factorial experiment across GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 shows that hypothesis rankings remain stable, while absolute scores depend strongly on judge identity, highlighting limitations of single-judge LLM evaluation.

AI.tldr: A graph-based, multi-agent LLM pipeline grounds Earth observation hypothesis generation in the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph, ranks dataset pairings with a heterogeneous graph neural network, and uses a three-agent LLM system to filter, generate, and evaluate hypotheses; applied to 1,475 NASA datasets to produce 160 coherent, novel hypotheses across Earth-science domains; evaluation shows new pairings nearly as plausible as real co-usages, but LLM scores are sensitive to judge identity, indicating evaluation variability.
AI.motivation: To move hypothesis generation away from unstructured text toward structured knowledge graphs, enabling coherent, data-grounded discovery of novel dataset pairings in Earth observation.
AI.method: Construct and train a heterogeneous graph neural network on historical co-usage relations to rank candidate dataset pairings from the NASA Earth Observation Knowledge Graph; deploy a three-agent LLM pipeline (filter, generate, evaluate) to produce and assess structured hypotheses; validate on 1,475 NASA datasets yielding 160 hypotheses across ecohydrology, glaciology, aerosol-cloud interactions, vegetation phenology, and stratospheric chemistry; perform a 2x2x2 factorial test comparing GPT-5.2 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 to test stability of rankings versus absolute scores.
AI.result: Generated 160 hypotheses spanning multiple Earth-science domains; model-predicted novel dataset pairings receive plausibility ratings close to those of held-out real co-usages, suggesting scientifically coherent yet unexplored combinations; rankings are stable across LLMs, but absolute scores vary by judge identity.
AI.conclusion: A promising knowledge-graph-grounded framework for hypothesis generation in Earth observation, combining graph-based ranking with multi-agent LLM reasoning; results show coherence and novelty but highlight evaluation variability across judges and potential domain-dependent performance.

title: Boosting Infrared Small Target Detection via Logit-Domain Contrast and Adaptive Shape Refinement
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication
summary: Infrared small target detection (IRSTD) remains challenging due to tiny target size, low signal-to-noise ratio, severe foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries in complex scenes. Existing methods usually rely on post-activation probability-domain supervision for discrimination, where weak targets and strong clutter may produce saturated and close probabilities, limiting weak-target discrimination. Meanwhile, blurred boundaries and halo-like predictions mainly stem from thermal diffusion, tiny target scale, boundary uncertainty, and insufficient explicit contour constraints. To address these issues, we propose Adaptive-Contrastive SLSIoU (AC-SLSIoU), a plug-and-play discriminative and shape-aware loss for IRSTD. Specifically, a Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) is introduced to enlarge the response gap between targets and informative hard negatives in the logit space, thereby enhancing weak-target discrimination. Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applies scale-aware annular penalties to refine target contours and suppress halo-like overflow responses. In addition, False-Alarm Focal Loss assigns larger weights to high-probability negative samples, further penalizing persistent high-confidence false alarms. Without introducing extra inference overhead, the proposed method can be seamlessly integrated into existing detectors and consistently improves both detection accuracy and shape quality. Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations demonstrate the effectiveness, robustness, and generalization ability of the proposed method for infrared small target detection.

AI.tldr: A plug-and-play, shape-aware loss (AC-SLSIoU) for infrared small target detection that combines LDMC, ABS, and False-Alarm Focal Loss to improve discrimination of weak targets and contour quality without extra inference cost.
AI.motivation: Infrared small target detection faces tiny targets, low SNR, foreground-background imbalance, and blurred boundaries. Post-activation supervision can saturate probabilities for weak targets and halo-like predictions arise from diffusion and boundary uncertainty, necessitating explicit logit- and contour-level guidance.
AI.method: Introduce AC-SLSIoU loss with three components: (1) Logit-Domain Margin Constraint (LDMC) to widen the logit gap between targets and hard negatives; (2) Adaptive Boundary Suppression (ABS) applying scale-aware annular penalties to refine contours and suppress halo-like responses; (3) False-Alarm Focal Loss to increase weight on high-probability negatives. The loss is plug-and-play and does not add inference overhead, applicable across backbones.
AI.result: Extensive experiments and cross-backbone evaluations show consistent improvements in detection accuracy and shape quality, demonstrating robustness and generalization of AC-SLSIoU across diverse IRSTD detectors.
AI.conclusion: AC-SLSIoU provides an effective, robust, and generalizable discriminative and shape-aware training objective for infrared small target detection, enhancing weak-target discrimination and contour accuracy without increasing inference cost.

title: On the Utility and Factual Reliability of Pruned Mixture-of-Experts Models in the Biomedical Domain
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models offer inference speedups via selective activation but impose substantial memory requirements because the whole network must remain loaded. Structured expert pruning is a practical approach for reducing deployment costs in resource-constrained settings. However, prior studies primarily evaluate benchmark utility, leaving the effect of pruning on factual reliability underexplored, particularly in high-stakes domains such as biomedicine. In this paper, we investigate how domain-specific expert pruning affects both utility and reliability. We assess four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks under in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings. Results reveal that moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility without immediate reliability decline, although hallucination risks increase at extreme pruning ratios. When shifting to the general domain, both utility and reliability degrade rapidly. These findings indicate that safe compression depends heavily on the task and domain. Evaluating pruned MoE models solely on utility is inadequate for high-stakes deployment without reliability assessment.

AI.tldr: Moderate domain-specific pruning can preserve biomedical MoE utility with limited reliability loss, but extreme pruning increases hallucinations; cross-domain transfer degrades both utility and reliability, signaling that safe compression is highly task- and domain-dependent.
AI.motivation: To address the gap where pruning studies optimize utility while neglecting reliability in high-stakes domains like biomedicine; evaluate how domain-specific expert pruning impacts both utility and reliability of Mixture-of-Experts models.
AI.method: Empirical study evaluating four MoE models, six pruning methods, and multiple pruning ratios across generation and classification tasks, conducted in-domain (biomedical) and cross-domain settings to measure utility and reliability.
AI.result: Moderate pruning preserves in-domain utility with no immediate reliability decline; hallucination risk increases at extreme pruning; cross-domain transfer leads to rapid degradation in both utility and reliability; overall, safe compression depends heavily on task and domain.
AI.conclusion: Reliability assessment is essential alongside utility when deploying pruned MoE models in high-stakes domains; solely optimizing for utility is insufficient for safe deployment.

title: Cross-Platform Control for Autonomous Surface Vehicles via Adaptive Reinforcement Learning
summary: Autonomous surface vehicles vary widely in hydrodynamic and actuation characteristics, yet most controllers are designed for single-platform deployment. We present an adaptive reinforcement learning approach for trajectory tracking that enables zero-shot cross-platform deployment using a single policy. Since the deployment platform's dynamics are unknown to the policy, we address cross-platform generalization with the standard partial-observability approach of conditioning on interaction history, employing a teacher-student architecture in which a learned module infers a latent representation of the platform dynamics. The policy is trained in simulation under randomized vessel dynamics and is deployed zero-shot to two real-world platforms without any fine-tuning, despite relying on a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator. In real-world experiments on two different platforms, the adaptive policy outperforms non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error while approaching the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.

AI.tldr: An adaptive reinforcement learning approach enables zero-shot cross-platform trajectory tracking for autonomous surface vehicles. It uses partial observability and a teacher-student latent dynamics module to generalize across platforms. Trained in simulation with randomized dynamics, it transfers to two real platforms without fine-tuning, outperforming non-adaptive baselines by up to 58% MAE and approaching a platform-specific controller, despite relying on a simple analytical dynamics model.
AI.motivation: Autonomous surface vehicles exhibit wide variability in hydrodynamic and actuation characteristics. Controllers are typically tuned for a single platform, hindering generalization. A policy that generalizes across platforms and requires no per-platform tuning would simplify deployment and reduce reliance on high-fidelity simulators.
AI.method: A reinforcement learning policy is trained under partial observability by conditioning on interaction history. A teacher-student architecture infers a latent representation of platform dynamics to adapt to different platforms. The policy is trained in simulation with randomized vessel dynamics and deployed zero-shot to two real platforms without fine-tuning, using a simple analytical dynamics model rather than a high-fidelity hydrodynamic simulator.
AI.result: In real-world experiments on two platforms, the adaptive policy outperformed non-adaptive learning-based baselines by up to 58% in position mean absolute error and approached the tracking accuracy of a platform-specific tuned controller.
AI.conclusion: The study demonstrates cross-platform generalization and zero-shot deployment for ASV trajectory tracking using an adaptive RL framework that infers latent platform dynamics, achieving substantial performance gains without platform-specific tuning, even with a simple dynamics model.

title: Hawk: Harnessing Hardware-Aware Knowledge for High-Performance NPU Kernel Generation
summary: Developing high-performance kernels for Neural Processing Units (NPUs) is a critical industry bottleneck, requiring developers to manually navigate implicit hardware constraints and strict memory hierarchies. While large language models offer immense automation potential, they fail catastrophically on NPUs due to a fundamental lack of hardware-specific priors. Naively transplanting code snippets from similar NPU kernels may pass the compiler, but it consistently triggers runtime crashes and performance degradation by blindly violating underlying hardware constraints. To overcome this, we introduce Hawk, a training-free framework that harnesses hardware-aware knowledge through three core modules: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module, which employs a Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to inherently couple the error context with executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module, which implements a 2D-Retrieval paradigm to project queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; and (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module, which leverages LLM-driven semantic arbitration to continuously distill the knowledge by pruning errors and consolidating redundancies based on the empirical execution feedback. Extensive evaluations on real-world NPU workloads demonstrate that Hawk elevates generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0%, while achieving up to a 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Hawk is a training-free framework for NPUs that combines run-time knowledge synthesis, hardware-aware 2D knowledge retrieval, and effect-driven knowledge distillation to improve kernel generation reliability and performance, achieving substantial accuracy and speed gains on real NPU workloads.
AI.motivation: Developers face hardware-specific constraints and memory hierarchies when writing high-performance NPU kernels. LLMs lack hardware priors and naive porting often fails at runtime. A training-free, hardware-aware system is needed to bridge this gap.
AI.method: (1) Run-Time Knowledge Synthesis Module using Triple-Part Executable Knowledge Representation to tie error context to executable semantics; (2) Bottleneck-Aware Knowledge Retrieval Module with 2D-Retrieval projecting queries into orthogonal syntactic and hardware-aligned semantic spaces; (3) Effect-Driven Knowledge Distillation Module employing LLM-driven semantic arbitration to distill knowledge via empirical execution feedback and prune errors.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on real-world NPU workloads shows Hawk increases generation accuracy from 49.4% to 80.0% and provides up to 2.2x execution speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: Hawk demonstrates that hardware-aware, training-free knowledge integration can significantly improve both the correctness and performance of NPU kernel generation, suggesting a viable path toward automated, robust NPU development without heavy retraining of models.

title: Mind the Gap: Standard 3DGS Evaluation Primarily Measures Near-Trajectory Interpolation
summary: Standard MipNeRF360-style 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) evaluation holds out every N-th frame -- but these frames have trained neighbors on both sides, so the metric measures near-trajectory interpolation rather than spatial generalization. We introduce a fair matched-count protocol that isolates this effect: both arms train on the same number of images and differ only in whether the holdout is spread evenly (interpolation) or forms a contiguous spatial sector (extrapolation). Our primary finding is a large, consistent interpolation-extrapolation gap of 3~12dB -- several times the differences typically reported between competing methods. The gap is robust to training noise, is in two cases large enough to flip a method ranking under multi-seed confirmation, and -- crucially -- persists across three representation families, including a non-Gaussian volumetric neural radiance field (NeRF), so it reflects spatial coverage rather than any one representation. Diagnostically, it is dominated by a diffuse/geometry-proxy component and tracks each view's angular distance to its nearest training view, a zero-cost signal that also guides capture planning; loss-side regularization yields only marginal gains. Standard holdouts remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but should not, alone, be read as evidence of spatial generalization. Prior work notes protocol sensitivity; ours is, to our knowledge, the first to combine matched-count paired holdout, cross-representation quantification, and a diagnostic analysis Table 1. We describe a spatial-holdout benchmark toolkit with standardized splits and baselines for 16 scenes, which we are preparing for public release.

AI.tldr: A matched-count, spatial-holdout protocol reveals a substantial interpolation–extrapolation generalization gap (3–12 dB) across 3D Gaussian Splatting, NeRF variants, and non-Gaussian representations, indicating spatial generalization is weaker than standard holdouts suggest; a diagnostic of angular distance to training views explains much of the gap; the work provides a benchmark toolkit for standardized spatial splits across 16 scenes.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation protocols for 3D scene representations blend interpolation with spatial extrapolation, obscuring true spatial generalization; to measure spatial generalization independently, a matched-count holdout protocol is proposed that separates interpolation from extrapolation.
AI.method: Two training arms with equal image counts but different holdout layouts: (i) interpolated holdout spread evenly across views; (ii) extrapolated holdout as a contiguous spatial sector. Evaluate across 3DGS, NeRF variants, and a non-Gaussian representation. Compare interpolation vs extrapolation gaps (in dB). Assess robustness to training noise and seeds. Diagnose with angular distance to nearest training view; analyze geometry proxy vs diffuse components. Develop diagnostic toolkit and benchmarks for 16 scenes.
AI.result: Consistent 3–12 dB interpolation–extrapolation gap observed across representation families; robust to noise and seeds; persists across three representation families; main driver is a geometry proxy component correlated with angular distance to nearest training view; loss-regularization provides marginal gains; standard holds remain useful for near-trajectory rendering but not for asserting spatial generalization.
AI.conclusion: Spatial generalization is substantially overestimated by standard holdout protocols; a matched-count, spatial-holdout benchmark reveals a sizable interpolation–extrapolation gap and should be used for evaluating spatial coverage; a cross-representation evaluation and diagnostic analysis support that the gap reflects true spatial generalization, guiding capture planning and benchmark standardization across 16 scenes.

title: Geometry-Aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
summary:
We propose a novel hybrid neural architecture, the Geometry-aware R-Structured Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (GRS-KAN), which integrates V.L.Rvachev's R-functions into the Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (KAN) framework. The proposed approach combines two complementary modeling mechanisms: smooth nonlinear structure is learned by KAN branches, while known geometric or logical constraints are encoded analytically using differentiable R-functions. This enables explicit representation of discontinuities, feasible regions, and implicit geometric boundaries within a trainable neural architecture.
  The framework implements differentiable logical operations through R-conjunctions and R-disjunctions, allowing complex geometric supports to be represented analytically and incorporated directly into regression models. Several GRS-KAN variants are introduced, including additive, multiplicative, and agnostic branch-weighted architectures.
  The method is demonstrated on regression problems involving discontinuities with circular and rectangular supports. Numerical experiments show that explicit geometric encoding substantially improves predictive accuracy and boundary localization compared with standard KANs. In the considered benchmarks, geometry-aware GRS-KAN models reduce test RMSE by up to 67% while simultaneously improving interpretability through explicit analytical representation of the learned geometric structure. The agnostic variant further demonstrates the ability to automatically determine whether geometric priors are beneficial for a given learning task.

AI.tldr: Hybrid geometry-aware neural network combining R-functions with Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (GRS-KAN) to encode explicit geometric priors and differentiable logic, yielding improved regression performance on discontinuous problems and enhanced interpretability; includes additive, multiplicative, and agnostic variants with up to 67% RMSE improvement.
AI.motivation: Leverage explicit geometric and logical priors within a trainable architecture to better capture discontinuities and boundaries, improving accuracy and interpretability while maintaining differentiability.
AI.method: Integrate V.L. Rvachev's differentiable R-functions into the KAN framework to implement differentiable logical operations (R-conjunctions/disjunctions); develop multiple branch-weighted variants (additive, multiplicative, agnostic); train on regression tasks with circular/rectangular supports and discontinuities; compare against standard KAN baselines.
AI.result: GRS-KAN variants achieve substantial performance gains, reducing test RMSE by up to 67% and improving boundary localization; explicit geometric encoding enhances interpretability via analytical representation of learned geometry; agnostic variant can automatically assess the utility of geometric priors.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware GRS-KAN combines smooth learned structure with analytic geometric priors for improved regression accuracy and interpretability; the agnostic variant offers a data-driven approach to adopting priors. Further evaluation across tasks and ablations could solidify the method's generality.

title: Guided Action Flow: Q-Guided Inference for Flow-Matching Vision-Language-Action Policies
summary: Flow-matching vision-language-action policies generate robot action chunks through an iterative transport process, creating an opportunity for test-time guidance without retraining the base policy. We study this opportunity in Guided Action Flow, an inference-time framework that keeps a pretrained SmolVLA policy frozen and uses a learned action-chunk critic to guide its reverse-time flow sampler. The critic is trained from real success and failure rollouts, can condition on task-description features from the frozen SmolVLA language pathway, and is used only through action gradients during sampling. We evaluate the approach on LIBERO manipulation tasks. A single-task critic improves success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improves validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, while the locked held-out test gain is positive but modest, from 65.0% to 67.5%. These results support the feasibility of Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies, while showing that critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain the central bottlenecks.

AI.tldr: Test-time Q-guided inference improves frozen flow-matching VLA policies on LIBERO tasks by training an action-chunk critic to steer reverse-time sampling; substantial gains but critic generalization/uncertainty remain bottlenecks.
AI.motivation: To enable performance improvement for flow-matching vision-language-action policies without retraining the base policy, by introducing a learned action-chunk critic that guides test-time reverse-time sampling.
AI.method: Freeze the base SmolVLA policy and train an action-chunk critic from real success/failure rollouts. The critic can condition on task-description features from the frozen language pathway and is used only through action gradients during sampling. Evaluate the approach on LIBERO manipulation tasks using single-task and multi-family critics.
AI.result: Single-task critic improves success from 68.0% to 82.0% on one seed window and from 82.0% to 86.0% on another. A multi-family task-description critic improves validation success from 46.0% to 56.0%, while the locked held-out test gain is positive but modest, from 65.0% to 67.5%.
AI.conclusion: Q-guided inference for frozen flow-matching VLA policies is feasible; however, critic generalization and uncertainty-aware guidance remain the central bottlenecks to address.

title: Safe and Adaptive Cloud Healing: Verifying LLM-Generated Recovery Plans with a Neural-Symbolic World Model
summary: As the scale and complexity of cloud-based AI systems continue to escalate, ensuring service reliability through rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery has become a critical challenge. While existing approaches integrate Large Language Models (LLMs) for semantic understanding and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) for policy optimization, they often rely on sequential, loosely coupled architectures that underutilize the generative and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. In this paper, we propose a paradigm shift with PASE, a Planning-Aware Semantic self-healing engine, a novel fault self-healing framework that reconceptualizes recovery as a neuro-symbolic program synthesis task. PASE employs an LLM as a core Plan Synthesis Engine to generate structured recovery plans from a library of semantic primitives. A Neural-Symbolic World Model verifies plan feasibility through simulation, while a Meta-Prompt Optimizer, trained via DRL, learns to generate optimal prompts that guide the LLM's planning process. This tight reason-plan-verify-adapt loop enables dynamic, context-aware recovery strategy generation beyond predefined action spaces. Experiments on a real-world cloud fault injection dataset demonstrate that PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average system recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios. Our framework advances autonomous system management by unifying LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance.

AI.tldr: PASE reframes cloud self-healing as neuro-symbolic planning using LLMs, a world model, and DRL-tuned meta-prompts to generate and verify adaptive recovery plans, achieving ~40% faster recovery and better fault detection.
AI.motivation: Escalating scale and complexity of cloud AI systems necessitate rapid fault detection and adaptive recovery beyond sequential, loosely coupled architectures.
AI.method: Use an LLM as Plan Synthesis Engine to generate recovery plans from semantic primitives; a Neural-Symbolic World Model simulates/verifies plan feasibility; a Meta-Prompt Optimizer (trained via DRL) learns to generate optimal prompts guiding the LLM; tight plan-verify-adapt loop.
AI.result: On real-world cloud fault injection data, PASE significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, reducing average recovery time by over 40% and improving fault detection accuracy in unknown fault scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Unifies LLM-based reasoning with model-assisted verification and meta-learned guidance to enable dynamic, context-aware recovery strategies beyond predefined action spaces.

title: MVFusion-GS: Motion-Variance Guided Temporal Attention for High-Quality Dynamic Gaussian Splatting
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time novel view synthesis for static scenes. Extending it to dynamic scenes via deformation fields has recently attracted significant attention, particularly for dynamic scene reconstructionband distractor-free. However, existing deformation networks lack explicit motion awareness: they neither capture long-term motion intensity nor exploit short-term temporal coherence, leading to inaccurate foreground deformation and pseudo-static residuals in the background. We present MVFusion-GS, a method that enhances deformation networks with two complementary motion-aware mechanisms. The Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics across time to estimate motion variance and uses it to guide dynamic-static separation during deformation prediction. The MotionFormer Temporal Attention module applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency. Extensive experiments on both dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, showing that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.

AI.tldr: MVFusion-GS enhances dynamic 3D Gaussian Splatting with motion-aware mechanisms (variance-guided refinement and temporal attention) to improve foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction, achieving state-of-the-art results on dynamic and distractor-free benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing deformation networks for dynamic NeRF-like methods lack explicit motion awareness, failing to capture long-term motion and short-term temporal coherence, leading to inaccurate foreground deformation and residual background motion.
AI.method: Two mechanisms: (1) Motion-Variance Guided Refinement aggregates per-Gaussian deformation statistics over time to estimate motion variance and guides dynamic-static separation during deformation; (2) MotionFormer Temporal Attention applies Transformer self-attention over neighboring timesteps to model local motion dependencies and improve temporal consistency.
AI.result: Experiments on dynamic scene reconstruction and distractor-free reconstruction benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating that explicit motion awareness improves both foreground motion modeling and static background reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Explicit motion awareness via MVFusion-GS yields improved dynamic scene reconstruction; the two mechanisms complement each other; suggests broader applicability to dynamic NeRF-like models and potential reductions in distractor artifacts.

title: Token Geometry
summary: Language models learn continuous programs over discrete symbols, with the embedding table and LM-head acting as the read/write interface between them. We show that this interface has gradient geometry distinct from dense hidden weights which can be exploited to improve the Pareto frontier across supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining, while only utilizing kilobytes of optimizer state. We introduce Ember, a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that utilizes O(V + D) VRAM, instead of Adam's O(2VD), and forgoes the need to shard both token table optimizer states. We provide empirical evidence that Ember scales effectively across batch size and parameter count. We show that the optimization trajectory of tokens can be well described by a simple 1D ray, counter to the popular belief that neural net parameters navigate a heavily nonconvex landscape. We provide a principled view on the surprisingly narrow space of optimizers that suffice for Transformer training. Finally, we open-source our distributed Ember implementation that merges cleanly with existing ZeRO/FSDP setups to support further research at https://github.com/katop1234/ember

AI.tldr: Ember is a lightweight optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices that dramatically reduces memory footprint (O(V+D) VRAM) while maintaining or improving the Pareto frontier across Finetuning, RL, and pretraining, using kilobytes of optimizer state; integrates with ZeRO/FSDP.
AI.motivation: Reduce optimizer memory and compute for training language models, focusing on the embedding table and LM-head as the primary read/write interface between discrete tokens and dense weights; challenge the assumption that dense hidden weights dominate optimization dynamics.
AI.method: Introduce Ember, an O(V+D) VRAM optimizer for embedding and LM-head matrices, avoiding Adam-like shardings and reducing state overhead; provide empirical evidence across batch sizes and parameter counts; analyze token optimization trajectory as a 1D ray; open-source implementation compatible with ZeRO/FSDP.
AI.result: Ember achieves favorable Pareto improvements in supervised finetuning, RL, and pretraining configurations; scales with batch size and parameter count; simplification of optimizer state to kilobytes; token optimization follows a simple linear trajectory; open-source integration with existing distributed training stacks.
AI.conclusion: Embedding/LM-head optimization can be significantly decoupled from dense parameter optimization; a narrow set of optimizers suffices for Transformer training; Ember provides a practical, scalable solution and invites further research into the geometry of optimizer dynamics and interface-based optimization.

title: Choreographing the Way of Water: A Computational Framework for Aquatic Robotic Art
summary: Robotic choreography in open water is governed by nonlinear fluid dynamics, which impose significant challenges due to environmental disturbances and nonlinear system dynamics. This paper presents the cyber-physical architecture of Way of Water, a vertically integrated framework that orchestrates a fleet of autonomous surface vessels as a distributed choreographic platform. Moving beyond the surface-pixel paradigm, these vessels use laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend their expressive range from the 2D water plane into the 3D volumetric domain. Our primary contribution is the Way of Water Studio, a browser-based, timeline-compositing authoring paradigm that treats the fleet as a DAW-like instrument for music-responsive choreography. The Studio encapsulates Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection presented through a visual timeline, broadening access to high-performance aquatic robotics for non-programmer artists. Grounding the Studio is the full cyber-physical stack: a custom holonomic chassis, a state-estimation and control stack tuned for the aquatic domain, and an LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS time synchronization. We report on the system's validation across two distinct deployments: an 18-vessel Swan Lake interpretation at Lake Zurich and an 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale demonstration at Forte Marghera, establishing a foundational reference for the design and deployment of fluidic robotic swarms.

AI.tldr: A cyber-physical, browser-based studio orchestrates a swarm of autonomous surface vessels for expressive water choreography, integrating trajectory optimization and disturbance rejection to operate in nonlinear aquatic dynamics, and validated on two large-scale performances.
AI.motivation: To enable high-performance, fluid-robotic choreography in open water while making it accessible to non-programmers, addressing environmental disturbances and nonlinear dynamics that challenge aquatic swarms.
AI.method: Way of Water Studio: a browser-based, timeline-centric authoring environment that uses Sequential Convex Programming for trajectory generation and Model Predictive Control for disturbance rejection, backed by a full cyber-physical stack (custom holonomic chassis, aquatic-tuned state estimation/control, LTE/MQTT fleet link with RTK-GPS synchronization). The vehicles deploy laminar nozzles and multi-zone lighting to extend expression into 3D. Validations include two deployments: 18-vessel Swan Lake at Lake Zurich and 8-vessel Time Space Existence 2025 Venice Biennale at Forte Marghera.
AI.result: Demonstrated scalable, music-responsive choreography across 18 and 8-vessel deployments, establishing a reference architecture for fluidic robotic swarms and providing a framework to bridge artistic intent with high-performance aquatic robotics.
AI.conclusion: The framework makes high-performance aquatic robotics more accessible to artists and researchers, enabling expressive, robust, and scalable swarm choreography in three-dimensional aquatic environments, and sets a canonical approach for design, validation, and deployment of fluidic robot swarms.

title: SemHash-LLM: A Multi-Granularity Semantic Hashing Framework for Document Deduplication
summary: Large scale document deduplication must preserve semantic equivalence while remaining efficient over massive corpora. We present SemHash LLM, a multi granularity framework that unifies semantic projection hashing, attention weighted MinHash, contrastive boundary learning, and selective LLM based adjudication. The method combines character, token, and document level signals through gated fusion, then applies a cascaded filtering pipeline for efficient candidate reduction. Semantic projection hashing learns compact binary codes in distilled LLM embedding space, while attention weighted Min- Hash suppresses boilerplate and emphasizes informative content. Adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation further improve robustness across template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments. Experiments show that SemHash LLM achieves strong duplicate detection quality with less than one percent neural verification cost.

AI.tldr: A multi-granularity SemHash LLM framework for scalable semantic deduplication, combining semantic projection hashing, attention-weighted MinHash, boundary learning, and selective LLM adjudication to achieve high accuracy with minimal neural verification.
AI.motivation: To perform large-scale document deduplication while preserving semantic equivalence efficiently on massive corpora, addressing noise and boilerplate content.
AI.method: Fuse character, token, and document signals via gated fusion; apply semantic projection hashing in distilled LLM embedding space; use attention-weighted MinHash to suppress boilerplate; cascaded filtering for candidate reduction; adaptive decision boundaries and uncertainty estimation; selective LLM-based adjudication.
AI.result: Demonstrates strong duplicate detection quality with less than 1% neural verification cost; shows robustness to template pollution, short text perturbation, containment, and viral fragments across experiments.
AI.conclusion: The SemHash LLM framework provides an efficient, robust solution for large-scale semantic deduplication with dramatically reduced neural verification needs.

title: VLAFlow: A Unified Training Framework for Vision-Language-Action Models via Co-training and Future Latent Alignment
summary: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) have recently advanced robotic manipulation, yet the effects of different robot-data pre-training paradigms remain difficult to compare because existing models often differ in architecture, data, action space, and evaluation protocol. We present VLAFlow (Vision-Language-Action Flow), a unified flow-matching framework for controlled comparison of VLA training objectives. Using a heterogeneous robot corpus, OXEMix, containing approximately 5,000 hours of data from DROID, OpenX-Embodiment, OpenX-Augmented, and RoboCOIN, we evaluate four paradigms under the same pi0-style architecture, shared VLM backbone, action expert, and 14-dimensional action space: action-only modeling (MindPI), language-supervised co-training (MindLPI), future latent alignment (MindWPI), and their combination (MindLWPI). Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv show that action-only pre-training is sensitive to heterogeneous data. In contrast, language supervision helps preserve vision-language generalization, while future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling. By combining both signals, MindLWPI achieves the most stable overall transfer performance across benchmarks. These results suggest a meta-action space view: language and future latent representations provide complementary intermediate constraints that make heterogeneous action supervision smoother and more transferable.

AI.tldr: Unified evaluation of vision-language-action pretraining paradigms (VLAFlow) shows language supervision and latent alignment provide complementary benefits; combining them yields best transfer under a standardized framework (OXEMix) across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, SimplerEnv.
AI.motivation: Difficult to compare VLA pre-training due to varying architectures, data, action spaces, and protocols; need a controlled, unified framework to isolate objective effects on transfer performance.
AI.method: Propose VLAFlow, a flow-matching framework; use homogeneous pi0-style architecture, shared VLM backbone, 14-dim action space, action expert; evaluate four paradigms MindPI (action-only), MindLPI (language-supervised co-training), MindWPI (future latent alignment), MindLWPI (combination); dataset OXEMix (~5k hours from DROID, OpenX-Embodiment, OpenX-Augmented, RoboCOIN); evaluation on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv.
AI.result: Action-only pretraining is sensitive to data heterogeneity; language supervision preserves vision-language generalization; future latent alignment improves state-transition and action-outcome modeling; combining signals MindLWPI yields the most stable overall transfer; meta-action space view: language and future latent representations provide complementary constraints that smooth heterogeneous action supervision and improve transferability.
AI.conclusion: Integrating language and latent dynamics within a unified framework yields robust transfer and supports a meta-action-space perspective; future work could further explore their interaction and data-efficiency.

title: Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum and Faster Hyperparameter Exploration to Tackle Class Imbalance in Federated Learning
summary: Class imbalance poses a critical challenge in federated learning (FL), where underrepresented classes suffer from poor predictive performance yet cannot be addressed by standard centralized techniques due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints. We propose FedCGNM (Federated Class-Grouped Normalized Momentum), a client-side optimizer in FL that partitions classes into a small number of groups based on minimum within-group variance, maintains a momentum per group, normalizes each group momentum to unit length, and uses the summation of the normalized group momentums as an update direction. This design both equalizes gradient magnitude across majority and minority groups and mitigates the noise inherent in rare-class gradients. We further provide a theoretical convergence analysis explicitly accounting for time-varying resampling-rates. Additionally, to efficiently optimize these rates in small-client regimes, we introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit (XAB) based algorithm that exploits federated parallelism that evaluates many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset demonstrates that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines, with FedHOO yielding further gains in small-scale federations.

AI.tldr: FedCGNM introduces a class-grouped, normalized momentum optimizer for federated learning to combat long-tailed data, with per-group momentum and normalization, plus a FedHOO X-armed-bandit to tune resampling rates; together, they achieve improved convergence and performance, especially in small-client federations.
AI.motivation: Address severe class imbalance in federated learning where minority classes perform poorly due to privacy and heterogeneity constraints that prevent standard centralized balancing.
AI.method: Partition classes into a small number of groups by minimum within-group variance. Maintain per-group momentum, normalize to unit length, and update with the sum of normalized group momenta. Converge analysis accounts for time-varying resampling rates. Introduce FedHOO, an X-armed-bandit algorithm that exploits federated parallelism to efficiently search combinations of two candidate resampling rates per client at linear cost.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on four public long-tailed benchmarks and a proprietary chip-defect dataset shows that FedCGNM consistently outperforms baselines; FedHOO provides additional gains in small-scale federations.
AI.conclusion: Class-grouped normalized momentum effectively equalizes gradient magnitudes across majority/minority groups and reduces noise from rare-class gradients, with theoretical convergence guarantees; FedHOO further improves rate optimization in small federations, contributing to robust FL performance on imbalanced data.

title: Bridge-WA: Predicting Where and How the World Changes for Robotic Action
summary: General-purpose vision-language-action models benefit from large vision-language priors, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating action-relevant scene changes. Existing world-action models often rely on large generative world models or dense future rollouts, which are expensive and spend capacity on visual details weakly coupled to control. We present Bridge-WA, a lightweight world-action framework that distills a frozen future-change teacher into three compact priors: future tokens for intended outcomes, change maps for intervention support, and motion-flow maps for local transition direction.
