title: Wind-Aware Reinforcement Learning Control of a Small Quadrotor Using Learned Onboard Wind Estimation in Simulated Atmospheric Turbulence
summary: Small multirotor aircraft are increasingly tasked with operations in the atmospheric boundary layer, where turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and can defeat conventional feedback control. This work illustrates a two-stage learning pipeline that first estimates the local wind from onboard kinematics and dynamics and then exploits that estimate inside a reinforcement learning (RL) flight controller. The wind estimator, an attention-augmented gated recurrent network trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer, recovers the horizontal wind vector with a per-flight root-mean-square error of 0.40 m/s and a direction error of 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes, an accuracy near the floor imposed by unresolved turbulence, and generalizes to vertical ascent profiles with a skill score of 0.861 over a constant-wind reference. A proximal policy optimization controller receiving the frozen estimator's output reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% relative to a wind-blind proportional-derivative baseline across mean winds of 4 m/s to 12 m/s, winning on 100% of evaluation episodes. A three-way ablation decomposes this improvement into a kinematic component, available without wind information, and a wind-perception component; the perception share rises with wind speed, from small in light winds toward roughly half the total benefit in strong winds, consistent with the quadratic scaling of aerodynamic drag. The controller degrades gracefully on out-of-distribution winds of 13 m/s to 15 m/s, where the baseline fails catastrophically.

AI.tldr: Two-stage learning for wind-aware control of small multirotors: a wind estimator plus a PPO controller using the estimate improves trajectory tracking in atmospheric boundary layer turbulence; robust to out-of-distribution winds, with ablation showing wind perception contributes more at higher winds.
AI.motivation: In the atmospheric boundary layer, turbulent winds comparable to the vehicle's airspeed degrade trajectory tracking and challenge conventional feedback control; inferring local wind from onboard data could enable proactive compensation.
AI.method: Stage 1: an attention-augmented gated recurrent network wind estimator trained on thousands of simulated flights through von Karman turbulence with power-law shear and veer. Stage 2: a proximal policy optimization (PPO) controller that consumes the estimator's wind output (frozen during control) and uses a three-way ablation to separate kinematic and wind-perception benefits.
AI.result: Wind estimator achieves horizontal RMSE 0.40 m/s and direction error 3.2 degrees on unseen wind regimes; accuracy near turbulence floor and generalizes to vertical ascent with a skill score of 0.861. PPO controller with the frozen estimator reduces horizontal trajectory tracking error by 48% versus a wind-blind PD baseline across mean winds 4–12 m/s, succeeding in 100% of evaluation episodes. Three-way ablation shows perception gain increases with wind speed (from small in light winds to ~half the total benefit in strong winds); out-of-distribution winds (13–15 m/s) cause graceful degradation for the proposed method while the baseline fails catastrophically.
AI.conclusion: A two-stage wind-aware control framework—wind estimation from onboard kinematics plus wind-perception in a RL controller—substantially improves robustness of small multirotors in turbulent boundary-layer winds, with the perception component becoming more critical at higher wind speeds and graceful degradation under unseen wind regimes.

title: ACID: Action Consistency via Inverse Dynamics for Planning with World Models
summary: Decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models has become a popular paradigm for embodied control. However, the standard planning cost judges a candidate solely by how close its predicted terminal state lies to the goal, leaving the realizability of the intermediate transitions unchecked -- a predicted trajectory can look convincing while the environment rollout drifts away from it. In this paper, we propose ACID, a decision-time planning framework that introduces cycle action consistency: the action inferred backward from a predicted transition by an inverse dynamics model should recover the one that was conditioned on. We fold this per-step residual into the planning cost via a scale-invariant adaptive weight. Across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks spanning rigid and deformable manipulation, articulated control, and visual navigation, ACID consistently improves planning and matches the baseline's accuracy with substantially less planning compute.

AI.tldr: ACID introduces cycle action consistency to decision-time planning with action-conditioned world models, improving planning efficiency while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Standard planners optimize terminal state proximity but neglect realizability of intermediate steps, risking drift between predicted trajectories and actual rollouts.
AI.method: Incorporates cycle-consistency by inferring backward actions from predicted transitions via an inverse dynamics model and penalizing deviations from the original conditioned actions; combines this per-step residual into the planning cost with a scale-invariant adaptive weight.
AI.result: Evaluated across four action-conditioned world models and six tasks (rigid/deformable manipulation, articulated control, visual navigation), ACID improves planning performance and matches baseline accuracy with substantially less planning compute.
AI.conclusion: Cycle-action consistency provides a general, scalable enhancement to decision-time planning, tightening alignment between imagined trajectories and real dynamics without increasing planning burden.

title: COMFYCLAW: Self-Evolving Skill Harnesses for Image Generation Workflows
summary: Agents are increasingly used to construct workflows and assist humans in completing recurring tasks more efficiently. As these workflows become repeated and domain-specific, agent memory and reusable skills become increasingly important: agents should be able to recall workflow patterns, execution constraints, and user preferences from previous runs. We study this problem in workflow-based image generation and introduce COMFYCLAW, an agentic skill evolution harness for controlling ComfyUI workflows. COMFYCLAW formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing, exposes tools organized by construction stage, automatically reverts invalid edits, and uses a region-level vision-language model (VLM) verifier to translate visual failures into actionable repair suggestions. The framework further evolves a progressively disclosed skill library, where trajectories, execution errors, and verifier feedback from previous runs are distilled into reusable Agent Skills. Across four benchmark splits, three agent models, and two image backbones, COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across all six agent configurations, outperforming a verifier-only baseline without skill evolution. Human annotations further show that annotators prefer COMFYCLAW over variants without skill evolution. Our results suggest that skill evolution is an effective mechanism for improving agent reliability and performance in recurring visual workflow construction.

AI.tldr: COMFYCLAW: an agentic skill-evolution framework for controlling ComfyUI workflows that learns from past runs to improve recurring visual workflow construction via typed graph editing, region-level VLM verification, and progressively disclosed agent skills.
AI.motivation: To address the memory and reuse gaps of agents operating in recurring, domain-specific workflows, where remembering patterns, constraints, and user preferences improves efficiency and reliability in image-generation tasks.
AI.method: Formulates workflow construction as typed graph editing; provides stage-organized tools; automatically reverts invalid edits; uses a region-level vision-language model verifier to map visual failures to repair actions; builds a progressively disclosed skill library by distilling trajectories, errors, and verifier feedback into reusable Agent Skills; evaluates across multiple benchmarks, models, and backbones.
AI.result: COMFYCLAW achieves the best average image-generation evaluation score across six agent configurations, beating a verifier-only baseline and receiving favorable human annotations relative to variants without skill evolution.
AI.conclusion: Skill evolution effectively enhances agent reliability and performance for recurring visual workflow construction.

title: Domain Generalization via Text-Anchored Information Bottleneck
summary: Visual recognition models often fail when deployed in new environments. Domain Generalization (DG) addresses this by learning representations that remain invariant to environment-specific variations. Recent approaches increasingly rely on large vision-language models, assuming that preserving their expressive visual representations improves robustness. However, we show that such visual expressiveness can instead propagate spurious cues that tie representations to the training environments, hindering invariant learning. We therefore discard visual guidance and instead treat the language embedding space as the primary source of domain invariance, naturally acting as an information bottleneck that preserves core semantics while suppressing domain-specific variations. Extensive experiments across diverse backbones exhibit state-of-the-art performance and further analyze what makes guidance effective for robust generalization. These findings shift the focus of DG from improving representations to designing supervision that enforces invariance.

AI.tldr: Language-space supervision acts as an invariance bottleneck for domain generalization, outperforming visual-guidance methods by suppressing spurious cues tied to training environments.
AI.motivation: Domain Generalization aims to generalize to unseen environments, but highly expressive visual representations can encode environment-specific cues that hinder invariance. A language-based bottleneck could enforce core semantics while discarding domain-specific variation.
AI.method: Treat the language embedding space as the primary supervision signal for representation learning, reducing reliance on visual guidance and using it to enforce invariance across domains. Evaluate across diverse backbones to demonstrate robustness.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art DG performance across multiple backbones and provides analysis on when language-guided supervision is effective for robust generalization.
AI.conclusion: DG should prioritize supervision that enforces invariance over merely enhancing representation expressiveness; language-grounded supervision provides a robust bottleneck to suppress domain-specific cues and preserve core semantics.

title: Certified World Models as Sensing Clocks: Drift-Aware Deadlines for Active Perception
summary: Certified world models estimate how long their predictions remain valid. We turn this validity horizon into an operational sensing clock: a rule for when an agent should stop coasting and re-sense. Starting from an audited equivariant world model, we derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals and show that deployable deadlines in learned world models must be drift-aware: on-manifold Lyapunov rates alone overestimate coasting validity, while calibrated native rollout-drift envelopes carry the deployed guarantee. On a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model, the resulting clock controls held-out interval-simultaneous certificate violation across seeds and data shards. In a cue-conditioned theorem-bed (a synthetic bench where all schedulers share the exact model, isolating the scheduling rule), the clock remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations relative to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling at matched sensing budget. We also report limits: in the short-horizon frozen VN-JEPA regime, empirical conformal horizons match the deployed clock on validity and budget, and a partial-reset exploration finds no clean budget-matched advantage for the spectral term. Thus the contribution is a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, not a claim that spectral clocks empirically dominate all non-spectral schedulers.

AI.tldr: A certified sensing clock for world models that uses a drift-aware validity horizon to trigger re-sensing, with guarantees across seeds/shards and deployment distributions, validated on VN-JEPA; shows reductions in eventful-tail violations but does not claim spectral clocks dominate all schedulers.
AI.motivation: To provide formal guarantees on how long predictions of learned world models remain valid and to convert that validity horizon into an actionable sensing policy that minimizes unnecessary sensing while preserving deployment guarantees.
AI.method: Start from an audited equivariant world model; derive a deadline for no-sensing intervals; show that deployable deadlines must be drift-aware because on-manifold Lyapunov rates overestimate validity; calibrate native rollout-drift envelopes to carry deployment guarantees. Evaluate on a frozen 3D VN-JEPA model; test across seeds/data shards; use a cue-conditioned theorem-bed to isolate the scheduling rule and compare to exact-mixture expected-belief scheduling; assess validity on deployment distribution and eventful-tail violations; explore short-horizon regime and partial-reset experiments.
AI.result: The clock controls hold-out interval-simultaneous certificate violations across seeds/shards; remains valid on the deployment distribution and substantially reduces eventful-tail violations vs a matched budget baseline. In short-horizon experiments, empirical conformal horizons align with the deployed clock; partial-reset exploration shows no budget-matched advantage for the spectral term.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers a certified sensing-clock primitive and drift-aware deployment method, rather than a general claim that spectral clocks outperform all non-spectral schedulers.

title: LIME: Learning Intent-aware Camera Motion from Egocentric Video
summary: Autonomous robots often need to move their camera before they can act: to inspect an object, reveal an occluded region, or obtain a view that responds to a user's intent. While vision-language navigation translates instructions to base motion and vision-language-action policies map instructions to manipulation actions, language-conditioned camera motion remains comparatively underexplored as a first-class action. We formulate language-conditioned camera motion generation: given a current RGB observation and a free-form natural-language intent, predict a relative target camera pose for the next observation. This task is inherently non-trivial: viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intentions, and a valid motion may operate at different semantic granularity, from entering a room to looking around a corner, inspecting a visible object, or revealing an occluded detail. To model this structure, we mine multi-intention camera-motion supervision from egocentric video, pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative SE(3) target poses. We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching pose head. This design lets the model jointly predict what the next view should reveal while representing multi-hypothesis target views. Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, we show that LIME can learn to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.

AI.tldr: We propose LIME, a vision-language camera-motion generator that predicts the next camera pose conditioned on the current observation and a natural-language intent, enabling multi-hypothesis viewpoint planning for active perception.
AI.motivation: Language-conditioned camera motion is underexplored as a first-class action. Viewpoint changes are driven by latent perceptual intents and can operate at multiple semantic granularities. The authors seek to endow robots with intent-aware camera motion by learning from egocentric video supervision of multi-intent observations and gains.
AI.method: LIME combines an auto-regressive observation-gain output with a continuous flow-matching SE(3) pose head. It mines multi-intention supervision from egocentric video by pairing plausible intents and observation-gain descriptions with relative target poses. The model jointly predicts the next view content and a distribution of target poses to reflect multiple hypotheses, enabling active view selection.
AI.result: Across experiments and downstream robotic tasks, LIME learns to actively choose camera poses from passive human video, turning ordinary egocentric recordings into supervision for intent-aware active perception.
AI.conclusion: Language-conditioned camera motion generation is viable and scalable: LIME demonstrates how intent-aware camera motion can be learned from passive video, enabling robots to actively plan camera views aligned with natural-language goals.

title: Generic Expert Coverage for Pruning SparseMixture-of-Experts Language Models
summary: Sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models contain substantial structured redundancy among routed experts, but pruning them without downstream calibration data remains challenging. Existing expert-pruning methods typically rely on a single aggregated importance score, which can bias the retained set toward experts favored by dominant calibration patterns. We propose \textbf{Generic TB-Coverage}, a coverage-aware expert pruning method that uses only generic text corpora (WikiText2 and C4) for calibration. Instead of collapsing expert utility into one score, our method profiles per-expert utility separately on each corpus and enforces a fixed-budget coverage rule that preserves high-utility experts from each corpus before constructing the final pruning mask. Across Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base at 25\%, 50\%, and 75\% retention budgets, our method improves average accuracy on six common zero-shot benchmarks over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity, while also reducing perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. The gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25\% and 50\% retain), suggesting that preserving cross-corpus expert coverage is an effective generic-data prior for MoE pruning. Our improvements hold with fixed pruning budgets and no downstream calibration data.

AI.tldr: Proposes Generic TB-Coverage, a coverage-aware MoE pruning method that profiles per-expert utility on multiple corpora and enforces cross-corpus coverage under fixed budgets, improving zero-shot accuracy and reducing perplexity degradation without downstream calibration.
AI.motivation: Single aggregated importance scores bias pruning toward experts aligned with dominant calibration patterns; there is a need for a calibration-free, generic-data-prior approach that preserves diverse expert coverage.
AI.method: Profile per-expert utility on two generic corpora (WikiText2 and C4) separately, enforce a fixed-budget coverage rule to preserve high-utility experts from each corpus, and construct the final pruning mask without using downstream calibration data.
AI.result: With Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B and DeepSeek-MoE-16B-Base, at 25%, 50%, and 75% retention, the method improves average zero-shot accuracy over random pruning, REAP, and ExpertSparsity across six benchmarks; also reduces perplexity degradation on WikiText2 and C4. Gains are largest under aggressive pruning (25% and 50% retain).
AI.conclusion: Cross-corpus, coverage-aware pruning using generic data is an effective prior for MoE pruning, enabling improvements with fixed budgets and no downstream calibration data.

title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models What to See and Where to Look
comment: The paper has been accepted by ECCV 2026
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing VLAs' training relies heavily on text-centric visual question answering and chain-of-thought reasoning data, which emphasizes linguistic reasoning rather than action-grounded planning. As a result, the learned representations capture semantic knowledge but lack spatial dependencies crucial for reliable trajectory prediction. We propose DriveTeach-VLA, a framework that explicitly teaches VLAs what to see and where to look. Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving-specific perceptual priors into the vision encoder, while 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Together, they form a vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO). DriveTeach-VLA achieves the state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ShivaTeam/DriveTeach-VLA.

AI.tldr: DriveTeach-VLA enhances Vision-Language-Action models for autonomous driving by combining driving-specific vision distillation with 2D trajectory-guided prompts to align perception with feasible trajectories, achieving state-of-the-art on NAVSIM and nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Traditional VLA training relies on text-centric VQA and chain-of-thought reasoning, prioritizing linguistic cues over action-grounded perception. This leads to semantic knowledge but weak spatial dependencies needed for reliable trajectory prediction.
AI.method: DriveTeach-VLA framework: Driving-aware Vision Distillation (DVD) injects driving priors into the vision encoder; 2D Trajectory-Guided Prompts (2D-TGP) provide spatial conditioning aligned with feasible driving trajectories. Vision-guided learning pipeline: what to see (DVD pretraining) - where to look (TGP-guided SFT) - how to act (TGP-guided GRPO).
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on NAVSIM and nuScenes datasets. Code released at the provided GitHub link.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly teaching VLA models what to see and where to look improves action-grounded perception and trajectory prediction, yielding superior driving performance.

title: Evolutionary Feature Engineering for Structured Data
comment: 9 page main content, 41 pages in total
summary: Large language models are increasingly used as open-ended search operators in evolutionary optimization. We introduce Evolutionary Feature Engineering (EFE), a framework for using LLM-based evolution to discover preprocessing transformations for structured data. EFE represents transformations as Python programs with a standardized fit/transform interface, allowing them to be inserted directly into existing machine learning pipelines. During evolution, candidate programs are refined using dataset context, summary statistics, and downstream performance feedback on validation set. We instantiate EFE in two settings. For time-series forecasting, EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations that improve off-the-shelf time-series foundation models. It reduces forecasting errors (MASE, WQL, MAE) 3% or more when averaged across datasets and improvements are as much as 19% on the COVID-Deaths dataset. Notably, these improvements occur with recent TSFMs such as Chronos-2. For tabular prediction, EFE-Tab evolves compact feature programs that add useful interpretable features and remove redundant ones, improving or matching existing LLM-based feature-engineering methods. We found EFE-Tab to be particularly effective on classical decision trees, where small sets of evolved features yield competitive accuracy while preserving interpretability. Overall, EFE demonstrates that LLM-based evolution can improve both accuracy and interpretability when automatically tackling structured data.

AI.tldr: LLM-guided evolutionary feature engineering discovers Python preprocessing programs to improve structured-data pipelines, boosting accuracy and interpretability in time-series and tabular tasks.
AI.motivation: Address manual, static feature engineering by leveraging LLMs to explore and refine transformations using dataset context and validation feedback.
AI.method: Transformations are Python programs with fit/transform interfaces evolved via context-aware evaluation. Two instantiations: EFE-Time learns invertible, dataset-specific normalizations for time-series foundation models; EFE-Tab evolves compact, interpretable features improving tree-based models.
AI.result: Time-series: average reductions in forecasting errors (MASE/WQL/MAE) of ~3% across datasets; up to 19% on COVID-Deaths; compatible with Chronos-2. Tabular: evolved features improve or match existing LLM-based feature engineering, notably for classical decision trees and preserving interpretability.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based evolution can enhance both accuracy and interpretability for structured-data pipelines.

title: WorldSample: Closed-loop Real-robot RL with World Modelling
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) can overcome the demonstration-coverage limitation of imitation learning (IL) by allowing robots to improve through trial-and-error interaction beyond the states observed in demonstrations. However, deploying RL on real robots remains constrained by high interaction costs, since each physical rollout is costly and reflects only one realized action-outcome path. To address this challenge, we propose WorldSample, a physically grounded data augmentation framework for real-robot RL that closes a real-synthetic loop between physical rollouts, world-model generation, and policy improvement. Grounded on real rollouts, WorldSample generates high-fidelity synthetic transitions through a post-trained world model, which greatly lowers the visual hallucination. Specifically, rather than simply using these transitions as real-world experience, WorldSample introduces Policy-Paced Learning (PPL) to regulate the training process through sample selection and scheduling, balancing useful augmentation against value overestimation and mitigating the hallucination-induced noise. Experiments on robot manipulation tasks involving contact-rich and precise tasks show that WorldSample improves policy success rate by 28% while reducing training steps by 59% compared with baselines. Furthermore, WorldSample improves world model visual fidelity by 19.4dB in PSNR and 0.47 in SSIM over demonstration-only post-training, validating the effectiveness of the real-synthetic loop for both policy and world model performance.

AI.tldr: WorldSample creates a closed real-synthetic loop for real-robot RL by learning a post-trained world model from real rollouts to synthesize transitions, using Policy-Paced Learning to balance augmentation and mitigate hallucination, yielding data-efficient policy improvement and better world-model fidelity.
AI.motivation: Real-robot RL suffers from high interaction costs and limited demonstration coverage; reducing sample complexity and controlling model hallucination are essential to practical deployment.
AI.method: Grounded world-model trained on real rollouts; generate high-fidelity synthetic transitions; Policy-Paced Learning via sample selection and scheduling; integrate into an iterative loop for policy improvement; evaluation on contact-rich manipulation tasks.
AI.result: Policy success rate up by 28%; training steps reduced by 59% vs baselines; world-model visual fidelity improved by 19.4 dB PSNR and 0.47 SSIM over demonstration-only post-training.
AI.conclusion: The real-synthetic loop with PPL effectively enhances policy performance and world-model fidelity in real-robot RL and demonstrates substantial gains in data efficiency.

title: Distributionally Robust Listwise Preference Optimization
summary: Existing robust preference optimization for language-model alignment mainly studies pairwise supervision and places robustness at the dataset, prompt, or preference-pair level. We instead study listwise preference optimization under ranking-label uncertainty: given a prompt and a candidate list, the observed ranking over that list may be ambiguous due to annotator inconsistency, near-ties, lossy rankwise feedback, or reward-model noise. We propose a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett--Luce objective that directly robustifies the ranking label conditional on the candidate list. The robust loss admits an exact decomposition into the nominal PL loss plus a worst-case PL correction, and the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current implicit scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from $K!$ enumeration to $O(K\log K)$. This tractable structure yields strong offline and online optimization guarantees. In the offline fixed-list setting, the robust objective is convex and projected stochastic subgradient reaches global $ε$-suboptimality with $O(ε^{-2})$ sample complexity. In the online policy-induced setting, where candidate lists are generated by the current policy, we establish weak convexity and $\widetilde O(ε^{-2})$ Moreau-envelope stationarity. Experiments in offline LLM alignment show that the proposed robust correction largely preserves performance under clean labels and improves robustness under noise. In online alignment, it makes reward-model-ranked candidate expansion more reliable and improves both reward-model and external GPT-4 judge metrics.

AI.tldr: Proposes a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce objective for listwise ranking under label uncertainty; derives tractable worst-case correction and provides offline/online optimization guarantees; empirically improves robustness in offline and online LLM alignment.
AI.motivation: Address robustness in listwise rankings for language-model alignment where observed rankings can be inconsistent or noisy due to annotator variability, near-ties, lossy feedback, or reward-model noise; extend beyond pairwise robustness to a full listwise treatment.
AI.method: Introduce a pointwise total-variation robust Plackett–Luce loss that conditions on the candidate list. The objective decomposes into a nominal PL loss plus a worst-case correction; the worst-case ranking is obtained by sorting current scores in ascending order, reducing the inner maximization from O(K!) to O(K log K). This yields a tractable, closed-form-like robust objective.
AI.result: Offline fixed-list: the robust objective is convex; projected stochastic subgradient achieves global ε-suboptimality with O(ε^{-2}) samples. Online policy-induced setting: weak convexity and O~(ε^{-2}) Moreau-envelope stationarity. Empirically, robustness gains under noisy labels with little loss on clean data; improved reward-model-ranked candidate expansion and better metrics from reward-models and GPT-4 judge in online alignment.
AI.conclusion: A tractable, provably robust listwise ranking framework for LLM alignment under label uncertainty that offers strong offline and online guarantees and practical empirical benefits.

title: Unified Panoramic-Gaussian Representation for Monocular 4D Scene Synthesis
summary: 4D scene synthesis from monocular videos has made significant progress in recent years. However, existing methods are typically constrained by view interpolation. As a result, they struggle to infer unseen regions beyond the observed views. In this paper, we reformulate the task as 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions, which extends beyond traditional interpolation settings. Camera-conditioned video generation enables unseen region synthesis by guiding generation along specified cameras. However, these methods lack explicit 3D priors and are optimized with random camera trajectories. This design leads to severe inconsistencies under large trajectory deviations. To address this limitation, we build a unified training and inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance. While this design improves cross-view consistency, the panoramic representation alone fails to model dynamic content effectively. Object motion in panoramic space introduces scale and shape distortions. To address this, we propose PanoGaussian, a unified Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic representation into an explicit dynamic Gaussian representation to capture dynamic physical priors of the 4D scene. Experiments demonstrate that PanoGaussian achieves consistent 4D scene synthesis even under large viewpoint variations.

AI.tldr: Introduces PanoGaussian for 4D scene synthesis with unseen regions by combining panoramic trajectory guidance with a dynamic Gaussian representation to maintain cross-view consistency under large camera deviations.
AI.motivation: To enable 4D scene synthesis beyond view interpolation and unseen regions, addressing lack of explicit 3D priors and instability from random camera trajectories. Panoramic representations improve cross-view guidance but distort dynamic content.
AI.method: Proposes a unified training/inference framework with panoramic trajectory guidance and introduces PanoGaussian, a Panoramic-Gaussian representation that distills the panoramic view into an explicit dynamic Gaussian to capture motion priors and dynamic content.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate consistent 4D scene synthesis under large viewpoint variations and improved cross-view consistency, mitigating distortions from panoramic motion.
AI.conclusion: PanoGaussian combines panoramic guidance with an explicit dynamic representation to robustly synthesize 4D scenes with unseen regions across broad camera trajectories.

title: X-LogSMask: Expand Transformer for Graph-Structured Data
summary: Transformers have become general-purpose architectures, but their all-to-all self-attention is poorly matched to graph data, whose interactions are sparse, structured and multi-scale. Existing Graph Transformers address this mismatch through structural encodings, hybrid message-passing modules or learned attention constraints, often introducing additional complexity and limited interpretability. Here we introduce X-LogSMask, an explainable multi-head logarithmic structural mask that injects symmetrically normalized graph topology directly into attention logits. The logarithmic transform converts structural connectivity into a topology-aware gating signal, suppressing unsupported node interactions while preserving feature-dependent attention. By assigning different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different attention heads, X-LogSMask gives each head a defined structural radius and supports multi-hop information propagation within a single layer. We further show that a standard Transformer encoder can be interpreted as one-step message passing on a complete graph, motivating X-LogSMask as a topology-constrained alternative to unrestricted self-attention. Across 20 node-, edge- and graph-level benchmarks, Transformers equipped with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in a lightweight one-layer configuration. These results show that simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention an effective graph-learning operator without changing the Transformer architecture. The code is available at https://github.com/LiLeyan-0120/X-LogSMask.

AI.tldr: X-LogSMask introduces an explainable, topology-aware masking mechanism for self-attention in Transformers to better handle graph-structured data. By applying a logarithmic transform to a symmetrically normalized adjacency matrix and using per-head powers to define structural radii, it constrains attention to multi-hop, sparse interactions while preserving feature-driven signals. This yields strong performance across many benchmarks with a simple architectural plug-in and enhanced interpretability.
AI.motivation: Graph data are sparse, structured, and multi-scale, making all-to-all self-attention inefficient and often misaligned. There is a need for a simple, interpretable mechanism that injects topology into attention without altering the Transformer core.
AI.method: Introduce X-LogSMask: a multi-head, logarithmic structural mask that multiplies the attention logits by a topology-derived gating signal. Normalize adjacency, apply a log transform, and assign different powers of the normalized adjacency matrix to different heads to set a structural radius. Interpretable as one-step message passing on a complete graph, enabling topology-constrained self-attention within a single layer.
AI.result: On 20 benchmarks spanning node, edge, and graph levels, Transformers with X-LogSMask achieve state-of-the-art performance on 13 datasets and remain competitive in lightweight, one-layer configurations.
AI.conclusion: Simple, interpretable structural masks can make self-attention effective for graph learning without modifying Transformer architecture, offering clearer topology integration and competitive performance.

title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are fundamentally bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations -- triplets of observations, instructions, and actions that are costly to collect at scale. We argue that this bottleneck stems from conflating two distinct learning objectives: acquiring physical competence (how to move) and acquiring semantic alignment (what to do). Crucially, only the latter requires language supervision. Building on this Decomposition Hypothesis, we propose Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP), a two-stage framework that first learns transferable motor priors from cheap, unlabeled interaction data -- including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play -- via a self-supervised Inverse Dynamics objective. A lightweight second stage then grounds these priors in language using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, TAP matches models trained on over 1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, yielding a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. On a real-world WidowX platform, TAP retains 25% success under camera perturbations where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining produces robust, transferable physical representations and offers a scalable path forward for Embodied AI.

AI.tldr: TAP decouples physical competence from semantic alignment, using two-stage task-agnostic pretraining to achieve data-efficient, robust VLA models.
AI.motivation: VLA models hinge on scarce expert demonstrations (observation–instruction–action triplets). Distinguishing physical skill from semantic understanding reduces labeling burden, leveraging unlabeled interaction data to learn motor priors before language grounding.
AI.method: Stage 1: self-supervised inverse dynamics on unlabeled interaction data (including discarded off-task trajectories and autonomous robot play) to learn transferable motor priors. Stage 2: lightweight language grounding with minimal expert data to align priors with task semantics.
AI.result: On SIMPLER, TAP matches models trained on >1M expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, achieving a 10% absolute improvement over standard behavior cloning. On WidowX, TAP maintains 25% success under camera perturbations, where internet-scale baselines collapse to 0%, demonstrating robust, transferable physical representations.
AI.conclusion: Task-agnostic pretraining provides a scalable path for Embodied AI by learning robust motor priors from unlabeled data and only then grounding them with language using limited demonstrations.

title: DRL-CLBA: A Clean Label Backdoor Attack for Speech Classification via DDPG Reinforcement Learning
summary: Deep learning models for speech classification are vulnerable to backdoor attacks, where malicious triggers cause misclassification at inference time. While sample-specific attacks can bypass many defenses, they often rely on poisoned label attack, making them detectable via manual data defense. In this paper, we propose DRL-CLBA, a novel clean label backdoor attack for speech classification that leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning. We also utilize deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The proposed reinforcement learning framework effectively optimizes target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's deep latent space, enabling label-migration-free poisoning of target samples. Experimental results across three datasets and four different DNNs demonstrate that DRL-CLBA achieves a high attack success rate, effectively bypassing some backdoor defenses. The attack demonstrates strong resistance against fine-tuning, pruning, and spectral signature defenses, exposing critical vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces DRL-CLBA, a clean-label backdoor attack for speech classification using DDPG reinforcement learning and deep audio steganography to embed triggers, achieving high attack success and defense resistance across multiple datasets and models.
AI.motivation: Speech-classification systems are vulnerable to backdoors. Clean-label attacks minimize suspicious data edits, making defenses harder. The goal is a stealthy, label-migration-free method that can target samples without suspicious labels.
AI.method: Leverages Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) reinforcement learning to optimize target samples toward trigger-bearing anchor points in the model's latent space. Uses deep audio steganography to embed sample-specific triggers into source audio, creating feature-space anchors. The framework steers target samples to anchor points to induce misclassification without label poisoning.
AI.result: Experimental results on three datasets and four DNNs show high attack success and the ability to bypass several defenses (e.g., fine-tuning, pruning, spectral signature defenses). Demonstrates strong robustness and exposes vulnerabilities in speech-controlled systems.
AI.conclusion: The work reveals critical vulnerabilities of speech-classification systems to clean-label, anchor-based backdoor attacks and underscores the need for defenses tailored to latent-space manipulation and steganographic triggers.

title: Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for Enhanced Audiovisual Video Captioning
summary: While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have advanced video understanding, achieving precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning remains a formidable challenge. Most existing approaches suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence, failing to accurately bind auditory events to visual entities or capture complex causal dynamics. To address these deficiencies, we propose TCA-Captioner, a framework specifically engineered to enhance Temporal and Cross-Modal Alignment for audiovisual video captioning. We first introduce the Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) framework, an iterative refinement strategy that generates high-fidelity, meticulously grounded training data. Leveraging a curated high-density human interaction dataset, TCA-Captioner is optimized to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions. Furthermore, we present TCA-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark utilizing a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate and quantify model proficiency in audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning. Extensive experiments demonstrate that TCA-Captioner sets a new standard for temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives.

AI.tldr: Presents TCA-Captioner with OCC iterative refinement for precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual captioning, plus TCA-Bench for decoupled evaluation; achieves state-of-the-art temporal coherence and audiovisual binding.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of precise temporal and cross-modal alignment in audiovisual video captioning, where multimodal LLMs often suffer from modality detachment and temporal incoherence.
AI.method: Observer-Checker-Corrector (OCC) iterative refinement to generate high-fidelity, grounded training data using a high-density human interaction dataset; train TCA-Captioner to model sophisticated audiovisual interactions; introduce TCA-Bench with a Decoupled Evaluation Protocol to isolate audiovisual binding and temporal reasoning.
AI.result: Empirical results demonstrate that TCA-Captioner achieves temporally-coherent and synchronized audiovisual narratives, setting a new performance standard.
AI.conclusion: TCA-Captioner advances temporally aligned audiovisual captioning through OCC-driven data refinement and a targeted diagnostic benchmark, enabling improved audiovisual binding and temporal relational reasoning.

title: Geometric Signatures of Reasoning: A Spectral Perspective on Task Hardness
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning enables large language models (LLMs) to solve complex problems by generating intermediate reasoning steps. While much attention has been paid to the length and content of these reasoning chains, far less is known about their internal geometry. We study the \emph{geometry} of CoT trajectories in the hidden state space of transformer models, formalizing each reasoning chain as a discrete curve in $\mathbb{R}^d$ and characterizing it through spectral, positional, and kinematic geometric functionals. We introduce the effective dimension $d_ρ$ as a measure of trajectory complexity and show theoretically that trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks, as they explore more of the hidden dimensions. Lastly, we explore how kinematic features of the trajectory, mean position, positional dispersion, initial and current hidden states, mean velocity, mean speed, and speed dispersion, can be used to predict solution correctness before generation is complete, and may inform future early-stopping strategies. Experimentally, on mathematical reasoning problems from the MATH500 dataset, $d_ρ$ achieves $0.93$ AUC in distinguishing easy from hard problems, while kinematic features potentially can predict correctness from only the first $20\%$ of generated tokens. These correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty, establishing that the shape of a model's internal reasoning trajectory is a principled window into both task hardness and solution quality.

AI.tldr: Models chain-of-thought as trajectories in hidden state space; introduces effective dimension d_ρ and geometric/kinematic diagnostics to predict task hardness and solution correctness; achieves high AUC and early predictability on MATH500; generalizes across questions.
AI.motivation: Fill the gap in understanding the internal geometry of chain-of-thought, linking trajectory structure to problem difficulty and answer quality, with potential for early stopping and diagnostic tools.
AI.method: Formalize CoT as discrete curves in R^d; compute spectral functionals (eigenvalue spectra of trajectory-related operators), positional metrics (mean position, positional dispersion), and kinematic metrics (mean velocity, mean speed, speed dispersion); define effective dimension d_ρ; develop theoretical link between spectral flatness and task hardness; evaluate on MATH500 with analysis of early-prediction signals.
AI.result: Theoretical result: trajectories with flatter eigenvalue spectra correspond to harder tasks due to broader exploration of hidden dimensions. Empirical: d_ρ achieves 0.93 AUC in distinguishing easy vs hard problems; kinematic features can predict correctness from the first 20% of generated tokens; these correctness signatures transfer across questions of varying difficulty.
AI.conclusion: Internal geometry of CoT trajectories is a principled indicator of task hardness and solution quality, enabling potential early stopping and robust cross-question generalization; establishes a new diagnostic framework for analyzing LLM reasoning.

title: Learning Agile Intruder Interception using Differentiable Quadrotor Dynamics
summary: This paper presents a methodology for learning a control policy to intercept an intruder using the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor state. Prior deep reinforcement learning approaches assume either relative position or distance to the intruder is available, but this information is not readily accessible in real-world applications that employ passive, monocular camera sensors. Instead, we propose a solution that leverages an analytical policy gradient method using differentiable quadrotor dynamics to learn agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s. The proposed approach outperforms baseline methods that utilize simplified point mass dynamics by an average of 30%.

AI.tldr: Proposes differentiable quadrotor dynamics with an analytical policy gradient to learn interception policies that rely on the 3D direction to the intruder and the interceptor state, suitable for monocular sensing; achieves agile interception up to 10 m/s and outperforms simplified point-mass baselines by ~30%.
AI.motivation: Real-world interception tasks with passive monocular cameras cannot readily provide relative position or distance to the intruder. A policy that uses the observable 3D direction to the intruder and the interceptor’s state can enable robust interception without exact depth information.
AI.method: Use an analytical policy gradient method applied to differentiable quadrotor dynamics. The policy takes as input the 3D direction unit vector to the intruder and the interceptor’s state and outputs control actions, training to maximize interception performance under monocular sensing constraints.
AI.result: The approach enables agile interception at speeds up to 10 m/s and achieves approximately 30% improvement over baselines that use simplified point-mass dynamics.
AI.conclusion: Analytical policy gradient with differentiable quadrotor dynamics effectively enables interception under monocular sensing, offering a viable alternative to methods requiring full relative-state information.

title: Reformalization of the Jordan Curve Theorem
summary: We present a case study in reformalization, a variant of autoformalization in which the input proof is not natural language but a formal development in a different proof assistant. Concretely, we report three reformalizations of the Jordan Curve Theorem: from Mizar to Lean, from HOL Light to Lean, and from HOL Light to Agda. We analyse the results and identify pipeline design choices that matter for practical reformalization tasks.

AI.tldr: Case study of reformalization: translating Jordan Curve Theorem proofs across Mizar, HOL Light, Lean, and Agda; analyzes pipeline design choices for practical cross-system reformalization.
AI.motivation: Assess practical cross-system reformalization to identify design decisions, bottlenecks, and best practices for translating formal proofs between proof assistants.
AI.method: Three reformalizations are performed: Mizar -> Lean, HOL Light -> Lean, and HOL Light -> Agda. The study analyzes translation strategies, library mappings, naming conventions, proof scripts, and tooling interactions to extract design choices that impact feasibility and effort.
AI.result: The work identifies several key pipeline design choices that influence success, including handling foundational notions and library compatibility, translation of proof styles, automation potential, and maintainability of the cross-system artifacts. Porting effort varies with source-target pair; certain mappings require substantial adaptation of libraries and proof strategies to fit the target system.
AI.conclusion: Reformationalization is viable and yields actionable guidance for cross-system interoperability. The findings inform pipeline design, resource estimation, and the development of reusable translation components to improve future reformalizations.

title: HistoSeg++: Delving deeper with attention and multiscale feature fusion for biomarker segmentation
comment: Published in the Proceedings of ICBBE 2025. The Version of Record is available at https://doi.org/10.1145/3794209.3794211
summary: Segmentation of biomarkers in medical images is frequently viewed as a first step towards medical image analysis in any bioinformatics or biomedical application. Despite progress, existing methods still struggle to capture information at multiple scales and to perform upsampling effectively across different datasets. These shortcomings often result in suboptimal generalization capabilities. Recently, architectures belonging to the Nested-UNet family excel in capturing multiscale contextual information and upsample them effectively. In this work, We propose a novel Nested-UNet architecture that effectively captures multi-scale contextual information. It includes inner and outer attention units to enhance focus during upsampling, along with channel-wise feature recalibration using squeeze-and-excitation modules, leading to improved segmentation performance. Additionally, the architecture integrates an edge-aware loss to emphasize boundary accuracy by assigning greater importance to edge regions. Tested extensively on three publicly available benchmark datasets. Our method demonstrates a generalization performance superior to existing Nested-UNet methods. Code: https://github.com/saadwazir/histosegplusplus

AI.tldr: A novel Nested-UNet variant for biomedical image segmentation that integrates inner/outer attention, squeeze-and-excitation, and an edge-aware loss to improve multiscale feature extraction and boundary accuracy, achieving stronger generalization on three public datasets; code available on GitHub.
AI.motivation: Biomedical biomarker segmentation demands robust multiscale feature representation and reliable upsampling across diverse datasets. Standard UNet variants often struggle with generalization due to limited multiscale context and boundary precision. A Nested-UNet with attention, channel recalibration, and edge-focused loss aims to address these gaps.
AI.method: Develop a Nested-UNet architecture with inner and outer attention units to refine features during upsampling, incorporate squeeze-and-excitation (SE) modules for channel-wise recalibration, and apply an edge-aware loss that emphasizes boundary regions. Evaluate on three public benchmark datasets, comparing against existing Nested-UNet baselines; provide code implementation.
AI.result: The proposed architecture yields improved segmentation performance and better generalization across the tested datasets relative to existing Nested-UNet methods.
AI.conclusion: Integrating multiscale attention, SE recalibration, and edge-focused loss within a Nested-UNet framework enhances boundary accuracy and cross-dataset generalization for biomarker segmentation in medical imaging; code is released for reproducibility.

title: BOUNDARY_SYNC: Measuring Communication-Induced Representational Coupling in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
summary: As large language models (LLMs) are deployed as communicating agents, does inter-agent communication cause outputs to converge? We introduce BOUNDARY_SYNC, a protocol measuring representational coupling via the Coupling Amplification Factor (CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline), where CAF < 1 indicates homogenization and CAF > 1 indicates diversification. In controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9,900 API calls), we measure coupling in text and image communication. Key findings: (1) text communication causes significant homogenization (CAF=0.803 [0.740, 0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001), confirmed by no-communication ablation and prompt-perturbation controls; (2) image communication also homogenizes under within-modality baselines (CAF=0.834 [0.811, 0.858]), with comparable proportional effect; (3) group size moderates coupling direction -- K=5 produces homogenization while K=3 yields CAF > 1.0 (point estimates 1.14 and 1.06, CI pending), suggesting a directional shift toward diversification; (4) cross-model replication shows extreme variation (CAF 0.034-0.803), with DeepSeek dominated by format artifacts; (5) coupling is stateless -- driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updating, with continuous consensus producing monotonic convergence. These results establish LLM agent coupling as real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with direct implications for multi-agent system design.

AI.tldr: BOUNDARY_SYNC introduces CAF (coupling amplification factor) to quantify how inter-agent LLM communication affects output similarity; results show text and image channels homogenize outputs (CAF<1), modulated by group size; cross-model replications show variability and format artifacts; coupling appears prompt-context driven and stateless, implying controllability for multi-agent system design.
AI.motivation: to determine whether inter-agent dialogue among LLMs leads to convergent (homogenized) or divergent outputs, with implications for reliability, safety, and coordination in AI agent ecosystems.
AI.method: controlled GPT-4o experiments (N=30, ~9.9k API calls) measuring coupling via CAF = JSD_cond / JSD_baseline across modalities (text, image). Includes no-communication ablations, prompt-perturbation controls, different group sizes (K=3 vs K=5), cross-model replication, and statelessness tests to isolate prompt-context effects.
AI.result: Text communication yields homogenization (CAF=0.803; 95% CI [0.740,0.873], d=1.30, p<0.001). Image communication also homogenizes (CAF=0.834; 95% CI [0.811,0.858]). Group size shifts coupling direction (K=5: homogenization; K=3: CAF>1.0, indicating diversification). Cross-model replication shows extreme variability (CAF range 0.034–0.803) with format artifacts dominating some models. Coupling appears stateless and driven by prompt context rather than cumulative updates, with continuous consensus yielding monotonic convergence.
AI.conclusion: LLM agent coupling is real, measurable, and controllable at the prompt level, with clear design implications for multi-agent systems to manage homogenization/diversification through prompt strategy and group composition.

title: QuadRocket: An Aerial Robotic Testbed for Adaptive Thrust-Vector Control of Rocket-Like Vehicles
comment: Paper accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Aerospace and Electronic Systems
summary: This paper presents QuadRocket, a quadrotor-based rocket prototype that provides a low-cost, low-risk platform for validating advanced thrust-vector control strategies for launch vehicle-type systems. The prototype consists of a cylindrical main body mounted on top of a quadrotor through a universal joint, forming a flying inverted pendulum with non-negligible inertia. For control design, the coupled system is modeled as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored force applied along its longitudinal axis. A reduced-attitude representation on the two sphere is adopted to explicitly exploit the vehicle's axial symmetry and to decouple yaw from the thrust-vector direction. On this model, we derive an adaptive backstepping controller that achieves almost global trajectory tracking in the presence of unknown constant disturbances, while a control-point transformation mitigates non minimum-phase behavior. The quadrotor is then treated as a thrust vector actuator, and a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller is designed to track the desired thrust-vector, accounting for actuation dynamics and avoiding explicit differentiation of virtual control signals. The complete architecture is evaluated in simulation and validated experimentally in an indoor motion-capture arena. Results demonstrate accurate trajectory tracking, effective disturbance compensation, and confirm the suitability of the QuadRocket as a versatile testbed for thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles.

AI.tldr: A low-cost quadrotor-based rocket prototype (QuadRocket) enables validation of thrust-vector control for launch-like systems using adaptive backstepping and dynamic-surface attitude control, confirmed by simulation and indoor experiments.
AI.motivation: Provide a safe, affordable testbed to develop and validate thrust-vector control strategies for rocket-like platforms, decoupling yaw from thrust direction and addressing non-minimum-phase dynamics and disturbances.
AI.method: Model the system as a single axisymmetric rigid body actuated by a vectored force along the longitudinal axis. Use a reduced-attitude representation on the two-sphere to exploit axial symmetry and decouple yaw from thrust-direction. Derive an adaptive backstepping controller for trajectory tracking under unknown constant disturbances, with a control-point transformation to mitigate non-minimum-phase behavior. Treat the quadrotor as a thrust-vector actuator and design a dynamic-surface-based attitude controller that accounts for actuation dynamics without differentiating virtual controls.
AI.result: Simulation and indoor-motion-capture experiments show accurate trajectory tracking and effective disturbance compensation, validating QuadRocket as a versatile thrust-vector control testbed.
AI.conclusion: QuadRocket is a suitable, versatile platform for validating thrust-vector-controlled robotic vehicles, with a robust control framework combining reduced-attitude, adaptive backstepping, and dynamic-surface control to handle disturbances and actuation dynamics.

title: Meta-Benchmarks for Financial-Services LLM Evaluation
summary: Public LLM leaderboards optimise for global average performance and do not capture the specific cognitive demands of financial-services work: a model that leads on MMLU-Pro may underperform on document-grounded compliance reasoning, and a coding leader may handle multi-turn customer interactions poorly. We present a meta-benchmarking framework that organises 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and aggregates those into 38 BIAN banking business domains spanning sales, operations, risk, and support work. A multiplicative weighting scheme (discrimination x coverage x recency), computed over a rolling model window, rewards benchmarks that still separate the best models, are widely reported, and remain in active use, suppressing saturated legacy tests automatically. These weights scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, producing cross-benchmark-comparable work-activity scores without raw score normalisation; business-domain scores are weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos. We demonstrate the framework on a point-in-time public snapshot covering 288 models across 25 organisations as of June 2026, and describe the methodology, full taxonomy, design decisions, and limitations with the aim of making the approach reproducible for institutions facing similar selection and governance challenges.

AI.tldr: Introduces a meta-benchmark framework that reweights 452 public benchmarks mapped to work activities and 38 banking domains, using a multiplicative discrimination x coverage x recency score and Elo-based K-factors to produce cross-benchmark comparable scores for financial services work; demonstrated on 288 models across 25 organizations as of June 2026 with reproducibility-focused design.
AI.motivation: Public LLM leaderboards optimize global averages and often miss domain-specific cognitive demands of financial services; there is a need for governance-oriented, reproducible benchmarks that reflect actual work activities and can guide model selection in institutions.
AI.method: Aggregate 452 publicly reported benchmarks into 41 O*NET Generalized Work Activities and 38 BIAN banking domains. Apply a multiplicative weight (discrimination x coverage x recency) over a rolling model window to reward benchmarks that remain informative and widely used. Use these weights to scale the K-factor in a pairwise Elo tournament, enabling cross-benchmark comparability without raw score normalization. Compute domain scores as weighted averages of the constituent work-activity Elos.
AI.result: Demonstrated on a point-in-time public snapshot of 288 models across 25 organizations as of June 2026. The paper describes the methodology, taxonomy, design decisions, limitations, and provides a reproducible framework for institutions facing model selection and governance challenges.
AI.conclusion: The meta-benchmarking framework addresses governance and domain-relevance gaps in model evaluation by organizing diverse benchmarks into work activities and domains, leveraging Elo-based cross-benchmark comparability and a rolling window to adapt to evolving benchmarks; it offers a reproducible approach while acknowledging limitations such as data heterogeneity and potential biases in benchmark mapping.

title: ICDepth: Taming Video Diffusion Models for Video Depth Estimation via In-Context Conditioning
comment: Accepted to ECCV 2026. Project page: https://xuanhuahe.github.io/ICDepth/
summary: Monocular video depth estimation requires temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization across diverse scenarios, yet existing methods struggle to achieve all three simultaneously. Discriminative models excel at per-frame accuracy but suffer from temporal drift due to limited context windows, while generative methods improve consistency and generalization at the cost of extensive training data (10M+ samples) and lack of geometric precision. In response to these issues, we introduce \textbf{ICDepth}, a framework that adapts pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation via In-Context Conditioning (ICC), leveraging their rich spatial-temporal priors. To address key challenges in transferring ICC from generation to dense prediction, we propose: (1)~\textbf{SAND-Attention}, which ensures precise spatial-temporal alignment via shared RoPE and enforces unidirectional attention to prevent noise contamination; (2)~\textbf{SRFM}, which injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. ICDepth achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple benchmarks with remarkable data efficiency, trained on only 0.8M frames ($6$--$13\times$ less than competing generative methods), while demonstrating strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.

AI.tldr: ICDepth adapts text-to-video diffusion transformers for video depth estimation using In-Context Conditioning, introducing SAND-Attention and SRFM; achieves SOTA with 0.8M training frames and strong zero-shot generalization.
AI.motivation: Need to reconcile temporal consistency, geometric accuracy, and generalization in monocular video depth estimation. Discriminative methods offer per-frame accuracy but drift with limited context; generative methods improve consistency and generalization but require massive data and often lack geometric precision. ICC leverages rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained diffusion models to address these gaps.
AI.method: ICDepth applies In-Context Conditioning (ICC) to pre-trained text-to-video diffusion transformers for dense video depth estimation. Key components: (1) SAND-Attention — shared RoPE and unidirectional attention to ensure precise spatial-temporal alignment and prevent noise contamination; (2) SRFM — injects DINOv2 semantic and resolution priors to enhance geometric precision. Trained on ~0.8M frames, significantly data-efficient relative to competing generative methods.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple depth-estimation benchmarks, with high data efficiency (0.8M frames, ~6–13x less data than competing generative methods) and strong zero-shot generalization to diverse domains.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that transferring In-Context Conditioning from generative to dense prediction is viable when supported by alignment-specific mechanisms (SAND-Attention) and semantic/resolution priors (SRFM). Indicates potential for data-efficient, temporally coherent, and geometrically precise depth estimation across varied scenarios.

title: SINA: A Fully Automated Circuit Schematic Image to Netlist Generator Using Artificial Intelligence
summary: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized Electronic Design Automation (EDA), particularly through Large Language Models (LLMs) for circuit design tasks. However, their application to analog and mixed-signal domains remains limited by the lack of machine-readable representations of existing circuit design knowledge. Circuit schematic images found in research manuscripts, textbooks, and websites constitute a vast repository of validated designs; however, these visual representations cannot be directly processed by EDA tools. Converting them into machine-readable netlists is essential for enabling simulation, verification, and building comprehensive databases for AI-based models. Current conversion methods lack generalization across both Integrated Circuit (IC) and Printed Circuit Board (PCB) level schematics. Moreover, they struggle with component recognition and connectivity inference, and fail to distinguish between connected junctions and crossing wires. In this paper, we propose SINA, an open-source circuit schematic image-to-netlist generator. SINA is a fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning for robust component detection, connected-component labeling for accurate connectivity inference, Optical Character Recognition (OCR) for component reference designator extraction, and a Vision-Language Model (VLM) for reliable reference designator assignment. SINA handles both IC- and PCB-level schematics and incorporates dedicated crossing-wires detection to differentiate wire intersections from connections. We validate the correctness of the generated netlists using graph isomorphism techniques. Our experiments demonstrate an overall netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, which is 2.72x higher compared to state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: SINA: an automated open-source pipeline that converts circuit schematic images into machine-readable netlists for IC and PCB schematics, using DL-based component detection, connected-component labeling for connectivity, OCR for reference designators, and a vision-language model for designator assignment, with dedicated crossing-wire detection. Validated by graph isomorphism; netlist accuracy 96.67%, 2.72x improvement over prior work.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of machine-readable representations of schematic knowledge and enable simulation, verification, and AI-driven modeling by converting visuals to netlists; ensure generalization across IC and PCB domains and robust connectivity inference.
AI.method: An end-to-end pipeline integrating (1) deep learning-based component detection, (2) connected-component labeling for connectivity inference, (3) OCR for component reference designator extraction, (4) a Vision-Language Model for assigning reference designators to components, and (5) dedicated crossing-wire detection to differentiate intersections from connections; verification uses graph isomorphism against ground-truth netlists; open-source.
AI.result: Netlist generation accuracy of 96.67%, outperforming state-of-the-art by 2.72x.
AI.conclusion: SINA enables robust, generalizable schematic-to-netlist conversion across IC- and PCB-level schematics, facilitating AI-driven EDA workflows and data-driven modeling.

title: Controllable Sim Agents with Behavior Latents
summary: Realistic traffic simulation requires agents that imitate logged behavior and can also be steered along interpretable axes. Such controllability enables engineers to isolate variables, reproduce specific edge cases, and test autonomous systems without real-world risk. We introduce Controllable Neural Variational Agents (CNeVA), a controllable simulated-agent framework that learns to infer a per-agent Gaussian behavior latent from per-channel discounted returns via a closed-form conjugate variational update, conditioning a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. To tackle scarcity in reward signals, we propose soft eligibility gates that replace hard binary thresholds with smooth exponential decay, preserving the gradient signal for near-threshold agents. On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA attains competitive realism on the benchmark while exposing per-channel controllability that the higher-ranked imitation models lack. Speed- and acceleration-based steering produces monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with the introduction of soft eligibility. We manage to achieve steerable map compliance under a context-residual return measure. Furthermore, our experiment demonstrates that steering metrics must be read alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.

AI.tldr: CNeVA provides a controllable neural variational agent framework for traffic simulation, enabling per-channel behavior control via a latent Gaussian inferred from rewards, combined with a rectified-flow trajectory generator and soft eligibility gates. It achieves competitive realism on Waymo while offering per-channel controllability and mitigating reward hacking through smooth thresholds and multi-metric safeguards.
AI.motivation: Realistic simulators must imitate logged behavior and be steerable along interpretable axes to isolate variables, reproduce edge cases, and safely test autonomous systems. Existing models often lack per-channel controllability and are prone to reward hacking due to sparse, binary rewards.
AI.method: Infer per-agent Gaussian latent from per-channel discounted returns using a closed-form conjugate variational update. Condition a rectified-flow trajectory generator trained on a mixed channel-mask curriculum for classifier-free guidance. Introduce soft eligibility gates (exponential decay) to replace hard thresholds, preserving gradient signals for near-threshold agents.
AI.result: On Waymo Open Motion Dataset, CNeVA achieves competitive realism and exposes per-channel controllability lacking in higher-ranked imitators. Steering via speed/acceleration yields monotone responses without stall-induced reward hacking. Safety controllability is monotone and substantial with soft eligibility. Demonstrates steerable map compliance under a context-residual return measure. Highlights that steering metrics should be read alongside physical-plausibility guardrails to avoid reward-hacking confounds.
AI.conclusion: CNeVA enables controllable, realistic, and safer traffic simulation by learning per-agent behavior latent factors and guiding trajectory generation with soft eligibility; per-channel controllability and context-residual evaluation are essential to prevent reward hacking, and multi-metric assessment is recommended when evaluating steering and safety.

title: Path-level Hindsight Instructions for Semantic Exploration in Vision-Language Navigation
summary: On-policy exploration is a crucial component for training robust Vision-Language Navigation agents, as it exposes the policy to a broader state distribution. However, such exploration inevitably leads to trajectories that deviate from expert demonstrations, resulting in a semantic mismatch between the executed visual stream and the original language instruction. In this work, we address this challenge by introducing Phi-Nav, a unified on-policy framework that leverages hindsight reasoning to align instructions with the agent's actual exploratory journey. Specifically, Phi-Nav operates through a three-stage dual-supervision cycle: 1) the agent performs oracle-guided on-policy exploration, sampling a trajectory while learning from expert action feedback, 2) a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level hindsight instruction grounded in the collected visual observations, and 3) the agent conducts a second imitation pass, treating the synthesized trajectory-instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration. Through this process, Phi-Nav bridges the critical semantic supervision gap inherent in on-policy methods, transforming semantically unlabeled movement into dense training signals. Evaluations on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks show that Phi-Nav yields competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations used by current baselines. These results underscore the necessity of semantic exploration in VLN, positioning Phi-Nav as an effective solution for training embodied agents with limited data.

AI.tldr: Phi-Nav introduces a three-stage on-policy framework that uses hindsight reasoning to align agent-driven trajectories with instructions, achieving competitive VLN performance while using substantially fewer expert demonstrations.
AI.motivation: On-policy exploration creates semantic drift between the executed visual stream and the original instruction, leaving a gap in semantic supervision that limit data efficiency.
AI.method: Stage 1: oracle-guided on-policy exploration with expert action feedback. Stage 2: a hindsight speaker synthesizes a path-level instruction from collected visuals. Stage 3: a second imitation pass treats the synthesized trajectory–instruction pair as an additional expert demonstration to refine the policy.
AI.result: On R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks, Phi-Nav achieves competitive performance while requiring only a fraction of the expert demonstrations compared with strong baselines.
AI.conclusion: Semantic supervision via hindsight alignment is crucial for data-efficient on-policy VLN training; Phi-Nav demonstrates an effective and unified framework for aligning exploratory trajectories with language instructions.

title: Structure-Aware Gaussian Splatting for Large-Scale Scene Reconstruction
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting has demonstrated remarkable potential in novel view synthesis. In contrast to small-scale scenes, large-scale scenes inevitably contain sparsely observed regions with excessively sparse initial points. In this case, supervising Gaussians initialized from low-frequency sparse points with high-frequency images often induces uncontrolled densification and redundant primitives, degrading both efficiency and quality. Intuitively, this issue can be mitigated with scheduling strategies, which can be categorized into two paradigms: modulating target signal frequency via densification and modulating sampling frequency via image resolution. However, previous scheduling strategies are primarily hardcoded, failing to perceive the convergence behavior of scene frequency. To address this, we reframe the scene reconstruction problem from the perspective of signal structure recovery and propose SIG, a novel scheduler that synchronizes image supervision with Gaussian frequencies. Specifically, we derive the average sampling frequency and bandwidth of 3D representations, and then regulate the training image resolution and the Gaussian densification process based on scene frequency convergence. Furthermore, we introduce Sphere-Constrained Gaussians, which leverage the spatial prior of initialized point clouds to control Gaussian optimization. Our framework enables frequency-consistent, geometry-aware, and floater-free training, achieving state-of-the-art performance by a substantial margin in both efficiency and rendering quality in large-scale scenes.
