AI.result: Experiments show that MMIR-TCM significantly outperforms leading models, including GPT-4o and Gemini 2.5 Flash, on the evaluated tasks.
AI.conclusion: MMIR-TCM demonstrates effective integration of multimodal LLMs with memory-augmented segmentation and retrieval-augmented generation for TCM diagnosis, introduces a new dataset and evaluation metric, and advances AI-assisted clinical decision support in traditional Chinese medicine.

title: MedStreamBench: A Time-Aware Benchmark for Streaming and Proactive Medical Video Understanding
summary: Existing medical video benchmarks primarily evaluate whether a model produces the correct answer, but rarely assess whether it answers at the right time. In real clinical settings, AI systems must decide not only what to predict, but also when to answer, defer judgment, or proactively raise alerts. This creates a critical gap between benchmark evaluation and deployment requirements. We present MedStreamBench, a benchmark for time-aware medical video understanding. MedStreamBench integrates 22 medical datasets and 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings: retrospective, present, future, and proactive. Unlike conventional benchmarks that assume full-video access, MedStreamBench restricts models to temporally bounded evidence windows and supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation. We further introduce a proactive monitoring setting that requires models to determine whether and when clinically relevant alerts should be triggered. Beyond answer correctness, MedStreamBench evaluates temporal behavior through responsiveness and post-evidence stability. Experiments on leading general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal a substantial gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping markedly in streaming and proactive settings. Our benchmark is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Venn2024/MedStreamBench.

AI.tldr: MedStreamBench is a time-aware benchmark for medical video understanding that evaluates not only accuracy but also when to answer, using bounded evidence windows, multiple temporal settings, and proactive alerting; it reveals a gap between offline recognition and temporally grounded decision-making.
AI.motivation: Current medical video benchmarks focus on correctness without temporal grounding, risking misaligned clinical decision timing in real deployments. There is a need to evaluate when models should answer, defer, or trigger alerts.
AI.method: Integrates 22 medical datasets with 5,419 QA instances across four temporal settings (retrospective, present, future, proactive); supports both single-turn and streaming evaluation; introduces a proactive monitoring setting; measures responsiveness and post-evidence stability in addition to accuracy; evaluates models under temporally bounded evidence windows.
AI.result: Experiments on general-purpose and medical vision-language models reveal substantial degradation from offline recognition to temporally grounded decision-making, with performance dropping notably in streaming and proactive settings; benchmark is accessible on HuggingFace.
AI.conclusion: Time-aware evaluation is essential for clinically deployable medical video systems; MedStreamBench provides a comprehensive framework to assess not only what to predict but when to predict, and offers a platform to drive improvements toward temporally aligned decision-making.

title: WARP: Weight-Space Analysis for Recovering Training Data Portfolios
comment: This work appears in the ICML 2026 Workshop on Weight-Space Symmetries (WSS): from Foundations to Practical Applications. Our source code is available at github.com/SprocketLab/WARP
summary: Foundation models are routinely released to the public, yet the data recipes used to train them -- such as domain mixture weights that determine how different sources are sampled -- are rarely disclosed. This creates an access asymmetry: researchers study the resulting models but lack visibility into the training distribution that produces them. Prior works for inferring training data, such as membership inference, detect at the level of individual samples and thus cannot characterize the global composition of the training corpus. We introduce WARP, a framework that recovers a fine-tuned model's training mixtures directly from its released weights. WARP interpolates between the base and fine-tuned models using model merging, generating pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the missing training trajectory and expose a geometric footprint of the training data in the weight space. From these simulated footprints, WARP extracts geometric features and maps them to domain proportions using either a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP projector trained on synthetic mixtures. In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with an average MAE as low as 0.046 and 0.104 respectively, outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.

AI.tldr: WARP reconstructs a model's training data mix by merging base and fine-tuned weights to create pseudo-checkpoints, then mapping geometric features to domain proportions. It recovers mixtures with low MAE on BERT and GPT-2, outperforming membership inference and baselines that use true trajectories.
AI.motivation: Address the lack of visibility into training data composition (domain mixtures) of foundation models. Prior methods infer individual samples but cannot capture global training data composition.
AI.method: WARP uses model merging to interpolate between base and fine-tuned models to generate pseudo-checkpoints that approximate the training trajectory. It then extracts geometric features from these footprints and maps them to domain proportions via a parameter-free softmax readout or an MLP trained on synthetic mixtures.
AI.result: In controlled experiments with BERT and GPT-2, WARP recovers domain mixtures with average MAE as low as 0.046 (BERT) and 0.104 (GPT-2), outperforming membership inference and a variant with access to the true training trajectory.
AI.conclusion: WARP provides a practical method to audit and understand the global training data composition of foundation models by revealing a geometric footprint in weight space, enabling quantitative estimation of domain mixtures.

title: Episodic-to-Semantic Consolidation Without Identity Drift
summary: Long-running adaptive intelligent agents face a structural tension between knowledge consolidation and information integrity. Memory consolidation is conventionally treated as an agent-changing operation: a model is fine-tuned, a prompt rewritten, a policy distilled, or a reflection appended to the context that governs future behaviour. In regulated autonomic deployment this is a liability because the agent operates under commitments and audit contracts that bind to a specific, cryptographically certified identity. We propose to treat consolidation not as a mutation of the planner or the identity manifest, but as a deterministic function f: M^ep -> M^sem over episodic memory whose output is a separately addressable semantic knowledge layer; the identity hash does not read M^sem, so consolidation updates knowledge without changing the agent's certified identity. We give a formal account of the agent representation, prove identity invariance through a structural lemma on the manifest's hash-input set, specify a deterministic aggregation algorithm whose outputs are auditable database rows with explicit confidence and supporting-event provenance, and validate the construction with synthetic experiments demonstrating per-field correctness, byte-equal identity across consolidation passes, and a mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%] across 10 seeds) against a calibrated Bayesian-shrunk baseline. The construction is a knowledge-update discipline for autonomic agents in which lessons accumulate as queryable facts while the agent's certified identity remains byte-equal across its operational lifetime, with an embodied service agent as the running case study.

AI.tldr: Deterministic, identity-preserving consolidation for long-running agents: separate semantic knowledge layer from the certified identity; formal invariants; auditable provenance; empirical validation showing reduced unproductive planner attempts.
AI.motivation: In regulated deployments, conventional memory updates mutate identity and violate audit constraints; need a knowledge-update discipline that preserves a cryptographically certified identity.
AI.method: Define f: M^ep -> M^sem; formalize agent representation; prove identity invariance via a lemma on manifest input hash set; design deterministic aggregation producing auditable rows with provenance; validate via synthetic experiments across seeds; measure per-field correctness, byte-equality of identity, planner efficiency.
AI.result: Outcome is a knowledge-update discipline with queryable facts while identity remains byte-equal; empirical mean 79.82% reduction in unproductive planner attempts (95% BCa CI [78.02%, 81.49%]) across 10 seeds against calibrated baseline.
AI.conclusion: Consolidation updates knowledge without altering certified identity; suitable for autonomic agents with regulated deployment; demonstrated with embodied service agent case study.

title: Pre-Flight: A Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models on Aviation Operational Knowledge
comment: 9 pages, 1 figure, 2 tables. Benchmark available in inspect_evals (UKGovernmentBEIS/inspect_evals)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for aviation business operations, from documentation and training generation to customer facing assistants. General purpose benchmarks do not measure whether a model reasons safely and correctly about aviation specific operational knowledge, and the high stakes, regulated nature of the domain makes that gap consequential. We present Pre-Flight, an open source benchmark of 300 multiple choice questions drawn from international standards and airport ground operations material, covering international airport ground operations, ICAO and US FAA regulations, aviation general knowledge and complex operational scenarios. Questions were authored and reviewed by practitioners with experience in air traffic management, ground operations and commercial flying. We evaluate a range of contemporary commercial and open weight models using the Inspect evaluation framework, scoring by accuracy under a standard multiple choice protocol, and we maintain the leaderboard on a rolling basis as new models are released. Against an informal expert reference of around 95%, obtained from a low sample quiz of aviation professionals at a conference, even the strongest model evaluated (released in 2026) reaches 82.7%, having improved only gradually from roughly 75% in early 2025. A substantial and persistent gap below expert level reliability therefore remains. We release the dataset, the evaluation harness and the results, and the benchmark is available within the community evaluations package distributed with inspect_evals. We argue that domain specific evaluation of this kind is a necessary precondition for responsible deployment of generative AI in non safety critical aviation operations.

AI.tldr: Open-source aviation-domain benchmark Pre-Flight with 300 MCQs; evaluated via Inspect; best model ~82.7% vs informal expert ~95%; dataset and harness released; underscores need for domain-specific evaluation for safe deployment.
AI.motivation: General benchmarks do not measure aviation-specific reasoning and regulatory knowledge; creating a standard, community-curated test to assess and improve model reliability in high-stakes aviation operations.
AI.method: Dataset: 300 MCQs drawn from ICAO, FAA regulations, and ground ops; questions authored/reviewed by air traffic management and pilots; Evaluation: Inspect framework with standard MCQ protocol; rolling leaderboard; multiple models tested; performance reported as accuracy.
AI.result: Strongest model (2026) achieves 82.7% accuracy; improvement from ~75% in early 2025; informal expert baseline ~95%; notable gap to expert reliability persists; dataset/harness released within inspect_evals package.
AI.conclusion: Domain-specific evaluation is essential for responsible deployment in safety-critical domains; Pre-Flight provides a reusable benchmark and resources to drive progress; calls for ongoing development to close the gap and broaden coverage.

title: The Turning Point of 3D Plant Phenotyping: 3D Foundation Models Enable Minute-to-Second Cross-Crop Reconstruction and Beyond
summary: 3D plant phenotyping is notoriously known to be procedure-complicated and of low throughput due to the extensive multi-view imaging, the fragile 3D reconstruction pipeline, and the additional cost from reconstructed geometry to phenotypic extraction. These limitations are further amplified in low-cost data acquisition, where smartphone videos or sparsely sampled multi-view images provide limited view overlap and self-occlusion. In this work, we show that the conventional 3D plant phenotyping pipeline could be streamlined and significantly accelerated with 3D Foundation Models (3DFMs), and particularly, present one of the first cross-crop 3D phenotyping frameworks powered by 3DFMs. The framework replaces COLMAP-style sparse initialization with 3DFM-based feed-forward geometric recovery, combines geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense reconstruction, enables few-view reconstruction through iterative view synthesis and refinement, and converts reconstructed geometry into measurable organs through 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation. We further construct a cross-crop dataset with smartphone-based image acquisition, diverse plant morphologies, and manual annotations for segmentation and phenotypic evaluation. Experiments across 26 plant sequences show that 3D Foundation Models reduce the average reconstruction time from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds while maintaining high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy. These results suggest a fresh technical route for high-throughput 3D plant phenotyping, from low-cost image acquisition to fast reconstruction, perception, scale recovery, and phenotypic measurement.

AI.tldr: 3D plant phenotyping boosted by 3D foundation models (3DFMs): fast, cross-crop, low-cost pipeline replacing COLMAP with feed-forward geometry, dense Gaussian splatting, few-view refinement, and 2D-3D semantic transfer, achieving massive speedups with maintained accuracy on smartphone-based data.
AI.motivation: High-throughput, low-cost 3D plant phenotyping is hampered by multi-view capture, fragile reconstruction, and expensive geometry-to-phenotype pipelines; smartphone acquisition exacerbates view gaps and self-occlusions.
AI.method: Replace COLMAP initialization with 3DFM-based geometry recovery; use geometry-constrained 3D Gaussian Splatting for dense 3D reconstruction; enable few-view reconstruction via iterative view synthesis/refinement; perform 2D-to-3D semantic transfer, metric scale recovery, and organ instance separation; build a cross-crop smartphone-based dataset with manual annotations for segmentation and phenotyping; evaluate across 26 plant sequences.
AI.result: Average reconstruction time reduced from 6.52 minutes to 1.58 seconds; maintains high reconstruction quality and phenotyping accuracy; cross-crop generalization demonstrated; dataset supports segmentation/phenotypic evaluation.
AI.conclusion: 3DFMs enable a fast, low-cost, cross-crop 3D phenotyping pipeline from image acquisition to geometry-to-phenotype measurement, offering a new route for high-throughput plant phenotyping.

title: Model Merging as Probabilistic Inference in Fine-Tuning Parameter Space
comment: Accepted for Publication at the 42nd Conference on Uncertainty in Artificial Intelligence (UAI), 2026
summary: Model merging aims to combine existing single-task solutions into a multi-task solution without additional data-driven fine-tuning.~Most existing approaches achieve this using geometric properties of local solution spaces. However, such geometric views provide limited guidance for scoring how statistically useful each task-specific update direction is across tasks during merging. To address this, we formulate model merging from a new perspective of probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) scenario where each single-task solution defines an energy-based expert model (EBM) over the merged parameters. We show that several existing model merging methods arise as special cases of our framework under energy designs that impose implicit Gaussian assumptions on directional residuals between merged and task-specific models. Empirically, we find that these residuals are often heavy-tailed which exposes a mismatch with the imposed light-tailed Gaussian structures. We address this with a heavy-tailed PoE design based on Cauchy experts, which better captures the observed residual behavior while admitting a provably convergent inference procedure. Experiments across multiple tasks and architectures show significant improvements over state-of-the-arts baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/MinhLong210/PoE-EBM-Merging.git.

AI.tldr: Proposes a probabilistic PoE-EBM framework for model merging, addressing heavy-tailed residuals with Cauchy experts, yielding state-of-the-art results.
AI.motivation: Geometric model merging lacks statistical guidance on how useful each task-specific update is across tasks; observed residuals between merged and task-specific models are often heavy-tailed, making Gaussian assumptions inadequate.
AI.method: Formulates model merging as probabilistic inference under a product-of-experts (PoE) where each single-task solution defines an energy-based model (EBM) over the merged parameters. Shows existing merging methods are special cases under Gaussian residuals. Introduces a heavy-tailed PoE design using Cauchy experts, with provable convergence. Experimental validation across tasks/architectures.
AI.result: Significant improvements over state-of-the-art baselines across multiple tasks and architectures; code released at the provided URL.
AI.conclusion: A heavy-tailed PoE-EBM framework provides a statistically principled, convergent, and more accurate approach to model merging, aligning with observed residual behavior and outperforming prior methods.

title: Actual causality in fault trees
summary: Fault trees are a widely used as effective risk models for complex systems, answering the question "what can go wrong?", especially through minimal cut set analysis. We study fault trees from the perspective of Halpern & Pearl's theory of actual causality. This allows us to use fault trees to answer the question "why has it gone wrong?", which is fundamental to failure diagnostics. We give a complete classification of each of the different notions of actual causality in terms of the fault tree's graph structure and logical structure, and show how minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.

AI.tldr: Fault trees analyzed under Halpern–Pearl actual causality; complete classification of causality notions via fault-tree structure; minimal cut sets correspond to actual causes.
AI.motivation: to extend fault-tree analysis from predicting what can go wrong to explaining why it happened using formal causality theory, enabling diagnostic insight.
AI.method: theoretical integration of Halpern & Pearl's actual causality with fault-tree graphs and logic; systematic classification across definitions of actual causality; analysis of how minimal cut sets instantiate causes.
AI.result: a complete classification of the various notions of actual causality in the fault-tree setting; evidence that minimal cut sets give rise to actual causes.
AI.conclusion: fault trees can support explanatory diagnostics by grounding explanations in Halpern–Pearl causality, enriching risk analysis with 'why' explanations.

title: ProSAC-CT: Progressive Spectral-Anatomical Co-Guided Multi-Stage Diffusion Model for Low-Dose CT Denoising
summary: Low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces radiation exposure but introduces stronger quantum noise, streak artifacts, and local texture degradation, which can obscure anatomical boundaries and weaken low-contrast structures. Diffusion models are promising for LDCT denoising by progressively recovering normal-dose CT (NDCT) images from degraded LDCT inputs, but existing methods often suffer from insufficient anatomical guidance, uncertain frequency-dependent recovery, and uniform reverse-process modeling. We propose ProSAC-CT, a progressive spectral-anatomical co-guided multi-stage diffusion model for image-domain LDCT denoising. ProSAC-CT integrates an anatomical-prior-guided conditioning (APGC) module, a residual frequency-domain decoupling stage (RFDDS), and a time-step-decoupling denoising decoder (TD3). APGC extracts LDCT-derived structural guidance, RFDDS enhances frequency-aware representations, and TD3 assigns them to different reverse-diffusion stages for anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery. Experiments on four LDCT degradation benchmarks show that ProSAC-CT improves image fidelity, structural similarity, perceptual quality, and information preservation over representative methods while better preserving boundary-sensitive anatomical details. Downstream anatomical-region classification on Mayo-2020 further indicates that ProSAC-CT retains task-relevant anatomical information, supporting its practical use for low-dose CT denoising.

AI.tldr: ProSAC-CT is a multi-stage diffusion framework for LDCT denoising that uses anatomical-prior guidance, frequency-aware decoupling, and stage-wise denoising to improve fidelity and preserve anatomy, validated on four LDCT datasets and Mayo-2020 classification.
AI.motivation: LDCT reduces radiation but exacerbates quantum noise, artifacts, and texture degradation, which hinder boundary delineation and diagnosis. Existing diffusion-denoising methods often lack strong anatomical guidance and effective frequency-aware recovery, leading to blurred boundaries and loss of task-relevant information.
AI.method: ProSAC-CT comprises (1) APGC: anatomical-prior-guided conditioning to leverage LDCT-derived structural cues; (2) RFDDS: residual frequency-domain decoupling to enhance frequency-aware representations; (3) TD3: time-step-decoupled denoising decoder that assigns reverse-diffusion stages to anatomical stabilization, boundary refinement, and fine-detail recovery.
AI.result: On four LDCT degradation benchmarks, ProSAC-CT yields higher image fidelity, SSIM, perceptual quality, and information preservation vs representative methods, with better boundary preservation. Mayo-2020 downstream anatomical-region classification confirms retention of task-relevant information.
AI.conclusion: Integrating anatomical priors with frequency-aware, stage-decoupled diffusion improves LDCT denoising, offering stronger anatomical fidelity and potential clinical utility.

title: A Mathematical Introduction to Diffusion Models
comment: Lecture notes for the John Tukey Summer Graduate School on Mathematics of Generative Models at SLMath (June 22nd, 2026 -- July 2nd, 2026)
summary: These notes give a proof-oriented introduction to diffusion models from the viewpoint of sampling, tracing a single arc from classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers, their error analysis, and inference-time control. Throughout, the material is layered into core definitions and identities proved in full, representative estimates proved under simplifying assumptions, and research-level theorems stated with a proof roadmap. The intended audience is beginning graduate students with a background in probability but no prior exposure to stochastic differential equations, stochastic numerics, or diffusion models.

AI.tldr: A structured, proof-oriented pedagogical introduction to diffusion models from a sampling perspective, linking classical sampling dynamics to modern diffusion samplers with layered rigor.
AI.motivation: To equip beginning graduate students with a solid, first-principles understanding of diffusion models via sampling dynamics, bridging theory and practical inference.
AI.method: Expository notes arranged in three layers: fully-proven core definitions/identities; representative estimates under simplifying assumptions; and research-level theorems with proof roadmaps; tracing an arc from classical sampling to diffusion-based samplers.
AI.result: A coherent, accessible walkway for learners to understand diffusion samplers, error analysis, and inference-time control; includes explicit proofs for foundational material and clear outlines for advanced results.
AI.conclusion: A valuable pedagogical primer that clarifies fundamental connections, and serves as a springboard for further study and research; potential extensions include numerical demonstrations and broader topics.

title: CLAP: Closed-Loop Training, Evaluation, and Release Control for Domain Agent Post-training
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to CRAE 2026; to appear in SPIE Proceedings. Best Poster Award
summary: Domain agents often face noisy business data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and adapter-release risk. This paper presents CLAP (Closed-Loop Agent Post-training), a closed-loop method that converts business data into structured SFT samples, decision-preference samples, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records. CLAP combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and application-chain replay to decide whether an adapter is suitable for the target application chain. On five anonymized manufacturing-scenario batches, QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score increases by 0.0098, pass rate by 0.0240, and evidence accuracy by 0.0280, while hallucination and wrong facts decrease. Yet only 3 of 5 batches improve, some batches regress, and GRPO exposes high KL risks. Application-chain replay further shows that RAG is necessary for factual extraction; under the same 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG-oriented LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but increases latency. These results support managing domain-agent post-training through an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop rather than relying on training completion or a single offline score.

AI.tldr: CLAP provides a closed-loop post-training framework that converts domain data into structured SFT, decision-preference, holdout sets, risk diagnostics, and release-gate records to guide adapter suitability for a target application chain. It integrates data validation, normalization, reward/KL diagnosis, offline gates, and replay; results show modest gains in some batches with reduced hallucinations but variance across batches, and RAG-based retrieval improves factual extraction at latency cost. Overall, an integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop outperforms relying on a single offline score.
AI.motivation: Domain agents face noisy data, uncertain post-training gains, offline/application mismatch, and release risk. A closed-loop, data-driven evaluation and gating mechanism is needed to reliably decide adapter deployment for a target application chain.
AI.method: CLAP constructs structured samples from business data (SFT), decision-preference data, holdout evaluation sets, and release-gate records. It combines data validation, target/evidence normalization, reward and KL-divergence diagnosis, offline gating, and application-chain replay to assess whether an adapter is suitable for the target chain. It uses QLoRA-style LoRA-SFT and app-chain replay with retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in some configurations.
AI.result: Across five anonymized manufacturing batches, LoRA-SFT yields modest average gains: overall score +0.0098, pass rate +0.0240, evidence accuracy +0.0280; hallucinations and wrong facts decrease. However, only 3/5 batches improve; some regress. GRPO reveals high KL risks. Application-chain replay shows RAG is necessary for factual extraction; with a 3B backbone and 100 replay cases, an application-RAG LoRA-SFT adapter improves value, core fields, and answer-evidence doc/page matching over base+RAG, but at increased latency.
AI.conclusion: An integrated data-training-evaluation-release loop is preferable to relying on training completion or a single offline score when deploying domain adapters; governance gates and risk diagnostics are essential to manage post-training risk.

title: Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine for Solving High-Frequency Partial Differential Equations
summary: Solving partial differential equations (PDEs) with high-frequency solutions remains a central challenge in physics-informed machine learning due to spectral bias -- the tendency of neural networks to learn low-frequency components preferentially. This paper proposes a Frequency Shift Physics-Informed Extreme Learning Machine (FS-PIELM) framework that addresses this limitation through an additive mechanism for weight initialization. Rather than multiplying random weights by a scaling factor, the method translates the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping the variance fixed at unity, thereby avoiding the variance amplification inherent in scaling-based methods. Two variants are developed: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons, while FS-PIELM-G groups neurons for improved robustness. Theoretical analysis shows that the frequency variance under the proposed framework remains bounded and approaches unity regardless of target frequency, in contrast to the quadratic growth of conventional approaches. The method preserves the computational efficiency of extreme learning machines, requiring only a single linear solve. Experiments on seven benchmark problems spanning six equation types -- Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, and advection-diffusion -- on both regular and complex geometries show that the linear variant achieves the best accuracy in six of seven cases, with improvements of one to nearly five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. The code and data accompanying this manuscript will be made publicly available at https://github.com/xgxgnpu/Physics-informed-vibe-coding/tree/main/FS-PIELM.

AI.tldr: FS-PIELM introduces a frequency-shift initialization for extreme learning machines to overcome spectral bias in physics-informed PDE solvers. By translating the Gaussian weight mean (not scaling variance), it maintains bounded frequency variance and enables high-frequency content representation. Two variants (L: independent frequencies per neuron, G: grouped) show strong empirical gains across seven PDEs with a single linear solve; six of seven cases achieve best accuracy, with up to ~5 orders of magnitude improvements over prior PIELM methods.
AI.motivation: Neural networks trained for PDEs exhibit spectral bias, prioritizing low-frequency components and underrepresenting high-frequency solutions. PIELM-based methods typically rely on random weight scaling, which can inflate variance and degrade high-frequency representation. A lightweight, computationally efficient fix is needed that preserves the ELM's single-solve advantage while improving high-frequency accuracy.
AI.method: Replace multiplicative random weight scaling with an additive frequency shift: translate the mean of the Gaussian weight distribution while keeping variance fixed at one. Develop two variants: FS-PIELM-L assigns independent frequency magnitudes to individual neurons; FS-PIELM-G groups neurons to improve robustness. Provide theoretical analysis showing bounded frequency variance under this scheme, approaching unity regardless of target frequency. Maintain the ELM’s computational efficiency (one linear solve). Evaluate on seven PDE benchmarks (Helmholtz, wave, Poisson, Klein-Gordon, heat, advection-diffusion) across regular and complex geometries.
AI.result: The linear variant (FS-PIELM-L/G) achieves best accuracy in six of seven problems, with substantial improvements: from one to almost five orders of magnitude over existing PIELM variants. FS-PIELM preserves computational efficiency and demonstrates robustness across geometries. Code and data to be released publicly.
AI.conclusion: A simple, efficient weight-initialization modification—frequency shift rather than scaling—substantially mitigates spectral bias in PIELM-based physics-informed learning. The approach yields accurate, high-frequency PDE solutions with a single linear solve and shows strong empirical performance across diverse equations and geometries.

title: Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement
summary: Safety training for large language models (LLMs) is conducted predominantly in English, leaving uncertain how well safety mechanisms generalize to low-resource languages and mixed-language code-switching. We show that this creates an epistemic gap in which models confidently generate harmful responses for inputs that fall outside the distribution of their safety training. To study this phenomenon, we introduce STEER (Safety Targeted Embedding Exploit via Refinement), a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing most strongly to the model's refusal behavior and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Across six open-source 8B-parameter models, STEER achieves attack success rates of up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench, outperforming random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG). The resulting prompts also transfer to GPT-4o-mini, achieving a 35.5% attack success rate without requiring access to the target model, suggesting that the underlying weakness is not specific to a single architecture. These findings demonstrate that safety mechanisms aligned primarily on English cannot be assumed to generalize across multilingual inputs. We argue that improving multilingual safety requires broader coverage during alignment and mechanisms that explicitly detect and abstain on out-of-distribution inputs.

AI.tldr: Multilingual safety gaps exist in LLMs trained predominantly on English; a gradient-guided code-switching attack (STEER) can suppress refusals in low-resource languages, achieving high success across multiple 8B-parameter models and transferring to GPT-4o-mini, indicating the need for broader multilingual safety alignment and out-of-distribution detection.
AI.motivation: Address the epistemic risk that safety mechanisms trained primarily on English fail to generalize to low-resource languages and code-switched inputs, potentially enabling harmful outputs outside the safety training distribution.
AI.method: Introduce STEER, a gradient-guided attack that identifies words contributing to refusal and iteratively translates them into low-resource languages to suppress refusal while preserving harmful intent. Evaluate on six open-source 8B-parameter models against JailbreakBench and AdvBench, compare to random code-switching and Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), and test transferability to GPT-4o-mini without model access.
AI.result: STEER achieves high attack success: up to 93.0% on JailbreakBench and 96.7% on AdvBench. Attacks transfer to GPT-4o-mini with 35.5% success without access to target model, suggesting a cross-architecture vulnerability rather than a model-specific weakness.
AI.conclusion: Safety alignment focused on English is insufficient for multilingual inputs. Improving multilingual safety requires broader alignment coverage and mechanisms to detect abstention on out-of-distribution inputs.

title: ProCal: Inference-Time Proposal Calibration for Open-Vocabulary Object Detection
summary: Open-vocabulary object detection aims to localize and classify objects beyond the fixed set of categories seen dur ing training. Recent open-vocabulary object detection methods improve localization and classification for unseen categories by leveraging a frozen VLM as a detector backbone. However, VLM classification score lacks recognizing position and scale of the object in an image. We observe that pretrained VLMs en able to classify foreground and background regions. According to this observation, we propose a simple inference-time Pro posal Calibration (ProCal) that improves localization quality of the classification score. ProCal computes a proposal prior by combining two scores: localization-aware foreground score and background-aware suppression score. Localization-aware foreground score captures whether a proposal contains an object area. Background-aware suppression score measures the extent to which the proposal resembles background. We analyze that ProCal suppresses false novel activation on background proposals and consistently ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel proposals. Applied to CLIPSelf ViT-L/14, ProCal improves APr +2.5 on OV-LVIS. The analyses show that proposal-level localization-aware reranking effects to mitigate ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

AI.tldr: ProCal is a simple inference-time proposal calibration for open-vocabulary object detection that re-ranks proposals using a localization-aware foreground score and a background-aware suppression score, improving localization and novelty detection; tested with CLIP-ViT-L/14 and yields +2.5 AP_r on OV-LVIS.
AI.motivation: VLM-based detectors struggle with localization since classification scores alone do not capture object location or background similarity; pretrained VLMs can distinguish foreground vs background, suggesting a calibration at the proposal level to improve localization of novel classes.
AI.method: Compute two proposal-level scores: (1) localization-aware foreground score indicating object content within a proposal, and (2) background-aware suppression score indicating similarity to background. Combine these to form a proposal prior and re-rank proposals at inference time, mitigating background activations and enhancing ranking of true novel proposals. Applied to a frozen VLM backbone (e.g., CLIP-Self ViT-L/14).
AI.result: ProCal consistently suppresses false activations on background proposals and ranks true novel proposals above background and partial novel ones, achieving an improvement of +2.5 AP_r on OV-LVIS for CLIP-Self ViT-L/14.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time proposal calibration is an effective, lightweight approach to improve open-vocabulary detection by aligning localization with VLM-based classification, reducing ranking miscalibration for novel objects.

title: Predicting Closed-Loop Performance of Latent World Models: Offline Checkpoint Selection for MPC and Model-Based RL Under Non-Markovian Rewards in LunarLander
comment: Preprint, 19 pages (16 main text + 3 pages appendix), 7 figures, 4 tables. Video: https://youtu.be/4PxHFW_TYUw , Code: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM
summary: We study how to predict the downstream closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model from validation-time diagnostics alone. Choosing the right checkpoint from a world-model training run is difficult: validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE keep improving long after closed-loop performance has collapsed. We present a suite of structural validation-time diagnostics drawn from optimal-control theory and apply them to Gymnasium's LunarLander v3, which features shaped rewards. We train an RSSM [5, 4] world model on it and treat per checkpoint CEM-MPC return as the oracle for closed-loop quality. By evaluating 40 metrics against this oracle, we find that the strongest single predictor is the Reward Observability Fraction (ROF), which measures the reward predictor's dependence on the observable subspace. We combine ROF with three structural regularizers into a single-number offline checkpoint selection score, the Composite Reward Observability Fraction (CROF). The CROF-selected world model trains a model-based A2C policy that beats a fairly evaluated model-free A2C baseline by ~24.5 return points while using ~65x fewer real-environment interactions, and the same world model also drives a strong zero-shot CEM-MPC policy. Code and data: https://github.com/nsmoly/LunarLander_RSSM.

AI.tldr: CROF (Composite Reward Observability Fraction) is an offline checkpoint-selection score combining Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) with structural regularizers to predict closed-loop performance of a learned latent world model, enabling sample-efficient model-based RL and zero-shot MPC on LunarLander v3.
AI.motivation: Offline diagnostics at validation-time often fail to predict online closed-loop performance; validation loss and multi-step prediction RMSE can improve even after the real policy performance collapses. The work seeks a metric that better forecasts post-deployment performance to guide checkpoint selection for learned world models.
AI.method: Train an RSSM world model on LunarLander v3. Compute 40 validation-time metrics; use an oracle based on CEM-MPC return to assess closed-loop quality. Identify Reward Observability Fraction (ROF) as the strongest predictor of the oracle. Combine ROF with three structural regularizers into CROF. Use CROF to select checkpoints and train a model-based A2C policy; compare to a model-free A2C baseline; also demonstrate zero-shot CEM-MPC performance using the same world model.
AI.result: The CROF-selected world model yields ~24.5 points higher return than the evaluated model-free A2C baseline, while requiring ~65x fewer real-environment interactions. The same world model also enables strong zero-shot CEM-MPC performance.
AI.conclusion: ROF is a robust predictor of closed-loop performance when combined with structural regularizers in CROF. CROF effectively guides offline checkpoint selection for latent-world models, delivering substantial sample efficiency for model-based RL and enabling strong zero-shot MPC performance on a shaped-reward task.

title: CamoNAS: Neural Architecture Search for Enhanced Camouflaged Object Detection
comment: Published in The Visual Computer. Author manuscript version
summary: Camouflaged Object Detection (COD) aims to locate and segment objects that blend into their surroundings, presenting challenges due to weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries. Traditional COD models rely on hand-designed architectures and multi-scale feature fusion, which are often guided by intuition rather than systematic search. This paper introduces CamoNAS, a frequency-aware multi-resolution Neural Architecture Search (NAS) framework for COD. CamoNAS automatically searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths, forming a hierarchical search space tailored to detect camouflaged objects. Additionally, it adopts an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture, where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream. CamoNAS achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON), highlighting the effectiveness of NAS for COD. Our code is available at https://github.com/rendaweiSIMIT/CamoNAS.

AI.tldr: CamoNAS proposes a frequency-aware, NAS-based framework for camouflaged object detection (COD) that jointly searches cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths within a hierarchical space and uses a dual-stream RGB-frequency architecture with a learnable wavelet transform, achieving state-of-the-art results on four COD benchmarks.
AI.motivation: COD presents weak edge cues and ill-defined boundaries, making traditional hand-crafted architectures and intuition-driven designs suboptimal. There is a need for systematic, data-driven architectural search that can exploit multi-scale and frequency information to improve camouflaged object localization and segmentation.
AI.method: Auto-searches both cell-level operations and network-level downsampling paths within a hierarchical search space tailored for COD. Introduces an RGB frequency dual-stream architecture where a learnable wavelet transform complements the RGB spatial stream, providing frequency-domain cues to aid detection.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance on four COD benchmarks (CAMO, COD10K, NC4K, CHAMELEON). Code is released at the provided GitHub URL.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates that NAS can effectively design COD architectures when augmented with frequency-aware, multi-resolution features and a dual-stream RGB-frequency design; this combination outperforms prior hand-crafted COD models.

title: JointHOI: Jointly Generating Contact Maps Enhances Hand Object Interaction Generation
summary: Text driven hand object interaction (HOI) generation is gaining attention for immersive applications and robotics, yet producing physically plausible interactions remains challenging. Even when individual motions appear natural, small contact errors can cause conspicuous artifacts such as floating and interpenetration. Prior methods mitigate these issues using explicit contact cues or implicit grasp priors, but typically rely on multi stage pipelines and fail to model temporally evolving contact. We present JointHOI, a single stage diffusion framework that jointly generates 3D hand object motion and dynamic, distance based contact maps from text. By treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality, joint generation enables the model to learn contact motion coupling during training. At inference, contact guided sampling enforces consistency between generated contact maps and motion implied geometry, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration and floating. Experiments on GRAB and ARCTIC demonstrate consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility over prior methods.

AI.tldr: JointHOI introduces a single-stage diffusion model that jointly generates 3D hand-object motion and dynamic, distance-based contact maps from text, improving temporal consistency and physical plausibility over prior multi-stage approaches.
AI.motivation: Text-driven hand-object interaction (HOI) generation often suffers from artifacts like floating and interpenetration due to weakly modeled contact; existing methods rely on multi-stage pipelines and fail to capture temporally evolving contact.
AI.method: A diffusion framework that jointly generates hand motion and distance-based contact maps, treating contact as an auxiliary inner modality; during inference, contact-guided sampling enforces consistency between motion and contact, improving temporal stability and reducing penetration/floating.
AI.result: On GRAB and ARCTIC benchmarks, the method achieves consistent improvements in text adherence and physical plausibility compared to prior methods.
AI.conclusion: JointHOI provides a single-stage, temporally coherent solution to text-driven HOI generation by coupling motion with dynamic contact, reducing artifacts and improving realism.

title: Finite-Lag Operator Geometry of Recurrent Representations
summary: Recurrent representations are trajectories, but representation geometry is often measured from static snapshots. We develop finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states from observed source-successor pairs $(X_t,X_{t+Δ})$. The primitive is the conditional transport law $Q_Δ(dy\mid x)$, estimated by a dense Gaussian source-smoothing operator. From this directed finite-lag law we derive a source-centered transport tensor $G_Δ$, which decomposes exactly into conditional spread and coherent displacement, and an antisymmetric coordinate circulation $W_Δ^ρ$, which summarizes directed lagged flow. We prove affine covariance with explicit metric dependence of scalar summaries, dense estimator stability on bounded trajectory clouds, and a finite-lag separation result showing that source-centered transport detects deterministic recurrent motion not recorded by infinitesimal carre-du-champ geometry. A linear-Gaussian closed form calibrates the quantities in terms of the update $A_Δ$, source covariance, and innovation covariance. Controlled experiments validate the decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions. In performance matched repeat-copy networks, the framework reveals architecture dependent differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, while coherent displacement fraction is metric and resolution dependent.

AI.tldr: Finite-lag operator geometry for recurrent hidden states: defines Q_Δ, G_Δ, W_Δ^ρ, proves affine covariance and stability, provides linear-Gaussian calibration, and validates with experiments showing architecture-dependent transport characteristics.
AI.motivation: Static representations of recurrent dynamics are insufficient; a finite-lag, transport-based geometry is needed to quantify how information flows and disperses over time in trajectories.
AI.method: Estimate conditional transport law Q_Δ(dy|x) from observed source–successor pairs via dense Gaussian smoothing; derive a source-centered transport tensor G_Δ with exact decomposition into conditional spread and coherent displacement; define antisymmetric coordinate circulation W_Δ^ρ; prove affine covariance and metric-dependent summaries; show estimator stability for bounded trajectory clouds; establish finite-lag separation from infinitesimal carré-du-champ geometry; provide a linear-Gaussian closed form calibrating quantities to update A_Δ and covariance terms; validate via controlled experiments and analyses on performance-matched repeat-copy networks.
AI.result: G_Δ decomposes into conditional spread and coherent displacement; W_Δ^ρ captures directed lagged flow (circulation); scalar summaries are affine-covariant with explicit metric dependence; dense estimators are stable on bounded trajectories; finite-lag separation detects deterministic recurrent motion not captured by infinitesimal geometry; linear-Gaussian calibration relates metrics to A_Δ and covariances; experiments confirm decomposition, circulation, covariance, and stability predictions; architecture comparisons reveal differences in total transport scale and coherent displacement trace, with coherent displacement fraction depending on metric and resolution.
AI.conclusion: The finite-lag operator geometry provides a principled, metric-aware framework to quantify recurrent dynamics, offering decomposition and circulation diagnostics, stability guarantees, and practical calibration, while complementing infinitesimal geometric approaches and informing network design.

title: SkillCoach: Self-Evolving Rubrics for Evaluating and Enhancing Agentic Skill-Use
summary: Skills are becoming a reusable operational layer for LLM agents, encoding SOPs, domain rules, tool workflows, scripts, and validation routines. In realistic skill repositories, overlapping skills make reliable skill-use difficult. Final verifier success is too coarse for both evaluation and training, since an agent may pass through trial and error while selecting distractor skills, skipping required steps, composing workflows incorrectly or omitting final checks. We introduce SkillCoach, a self-evolving rubric framework for evaluating and enhancing agentic skill-use. SkillCoach derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts and evaluates trajectories along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection. It keeps the external verifier as a separate outcome signal, allowing process quality to be distinguished from accidental task success. The evolved rubrics further serve as process supervision for selecting high-quality training trajectories. Experiments show that evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, expose failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for enhancing agentic skill-use.

AI.tldr: SkillCoach is a self-evolving rubric framework that derives skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts to evaluate and improve agentic skill-use along four dimensions: skill selection, skill following, skill composition, and skill-grounded reflection, while keeping an external verifier separate from the process outcome.
AI.motivation: Overlapping and noisy skill repositories make reliable skill-use difficult and coarse final success signals fail to reveal process errors; there is a need for fine-grained, process-level evaluation and training signals.
AI.method: Derive skill-grounded process rubrics from real rollouts; evaluate trajectories along four dimensions (selection, following, composition, reflection); keep an external verifier as a separate outcome signal; use evolved rubrics to supervise training data and select high-quality trajectories.
AI.result: Evolved rubrics substantially improve evaluation quality, uncover failures hidden by final accuracy, and provide stronger supervision signals than outcome-only filtering for improving agentic skill-use.
AI.conclusion: Process-based rubrics enable more reliable evaluation and training of skill-use in LLM agents, facilitating better error detection, supervision, and iterative improvement of skill repositories.

title: LLM-Empowered Multimodal Fusion Framework for Autonomous Driving: Semantic Enhancement and Channel-Adaptive Design
comment: 6 pages, 4 figures. Accepted by 2026 IEEE 37th International Symposium on Personal, Indoor and Mobile Radio Communications (PIMRC)
summary: Vision-radar fusion is central to robust autonomous driving, combining dense visual semantics with precise range and velocity measurements from radar. However, real-world fusion quality is fundamentally challenged by dynamically varying input quality, stemming from occlusion, adverse weather, and channel noise. To address this, we re-frame the problem from static data fusion to channel-aware semantic reasoning and propose a Large Language Model-centric Semantic-layer Channel-aware Integrated Perception (LM-SCIP) framework. It places a Large Language Model (LLM) as a central reasoning core to fuse a local visual stream with a quality-varying external radar stream used to cover perception-blind spots. Concretely, LM-SCIP couples a hierarchical radar-vision encoder with a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) that maps link indicators into a "Channel Prompt" to dynamically gate external radar features. A parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM, in conjunction with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE), then arbitrates between local visual cues and the channel-conditioned radar context. Finally, a decoupled multi-task decoder outputs localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Experiments on nuScenes and VIRAT validate our approach. On nuScenes, under a controlled toggle of radar input, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, the model attains a 0.214m localization RMSE and 0.179m minFDE (k=1). These results reveal that the proposed LM-SCIP enables a robust vision-dominant fallback at low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.

AI.tldr: LM-SCIP introduces an LLM-centered, channel-aware fusion framework for vision–radar perception in autonomous driving. It uses a Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module to gate external radar features via a Channel Prompt, a LoRA-tuned LLM with a heterogeneous MoE to arbitrate between local visual cues and radar context, and a decoupled multi-task decoder for localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction. Demonstrates robust localization improvements under varying radar quality on nuScenes and VIRAT datasets.
AI.motivation: Real-world fusion quality degrades with occlusions, adverse weather, and channel noise. Static fusion cannot adapt to input quality variations; there is a need for dynamic, semantic, channel-aware reasoning that can reweight sensor modalities using external radar cues.
AI.method: Proposes LM-SCIP: (1) a hierarchical radar–vision encoder; (2) Channel-Adaptive Semantic Module (CASM) mapping link indicators to a 'Channel Prompt' to gate external radar features; (3) a parameter-efficient, LoRA-tuned LLM coupled with a heterogeneous Mixture-of-Experts (H-MoE) to arbitrate between local visual cues and channel-conditioned radar context; (4) a decoupled multi-task decoder for localization, trajectory forecasting, and image reconstruction.
AI.result: On nuScenes, with controlled radar input toggling, LM-SCIP reduces localization RMSE by 40.0% versus a vision-only baseline. On VIRAT, it achieves 0.214 m localization RMSE and 0.179 m minFDE (k=1). These results indicate robust performance under low SNR and synergistic fusion at high SNR.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework demonstrates that an LLM-centric, channel-aware reasoning layer can robustly fuse vision and radar, adaptively leveraging radar context when visual cues are degraded and maximizing fusion gains when radar quality is high.

title: Efficient Temporal Point Processes via Monotone Alternating Splines
summary: Temporal point processes (TPPs) have widespread applications across various domains. Compared to modeling the conditional intensity of a TPP, modeling its cumulative conditional intensity function (CCIF) improves computational efficiency and eliminates numerical approximation errors. However, current CCIF parameterizations uniformly rely on Monotone Neural Networks (MNNs), which we identify as suffering from three structural deadlocks--convexity restrictions, saturation limits, and violations of CCIF modeling requirements--that fundamentally restrict their representational capacity for complex temporal dynamics. To resolve these bottlenecks, this paper proposes a novel framework called Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS). By leveraging distinct interpolation and extrapolation components, MAS provides a flexible and efficient framework for modeling CCIFs. Theoretically, MAS's interpolation provides strong fitting accuracy, while its extrapolation supports robust generalization, reducing the irreducible approximation gaps of MNNs. Extensive experiments show that MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.

AI.tldr: MAS: a Monotone Alternating Splines framework for CCIF in temporal point processes that overcomes MNNs' convexity, saturation, and modeling constraints, offering flexible interpolation/extrapolation, improved accuracy and generalization, with superior results on synthetic and real data.
AI.motivation: Current CCIF modeling relies on Monotone Neural Networks which impose convexity, saturation, and CCIF modeling constraints that limit expressiveness for complex temporal dynamics; modeling CCIF instead of intensity improves computational efficiency and reduces numerical errors.
AI.method: Propose Monotone Alternating Splines (MAS) with separate interpolation and extrapolation components to flexibly model CCIFs; theoretical analysis attributes interpolation to fitting accuracy and extrapolation to generalization; designed to avoid MNN deadlocks.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show MAS achieves superior performance on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: MAS overcomes the structural limitations of MNNs, offering enhanced expressiveness and robustness for CCIF modeling in TPPs, with better accuracy and generalization.

title: Spec-AUF: Accept-Until-Fail Training under Train-Inference Misalignment for Masked Block Drafters
summary: Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by drafting a block of tokens that the target model verifies left-to-right, committing only the longest accepted prefix. Block (DLM-style) drafters predict the whole block in parallel, which is fast but trained with a full-block cross-entropy that supervises every position against the gold continuation -- even though inference discards every token after the first rejection. Recent acceptance-aware objectives patch this by reweighting the full-block loss; we instead use teacher-forced learning as a motivation for how supervision should concentrate on the accepted prefix. A mask-only block drafter has no input-side channel for gold-prefix conditioning, so AUF approximates that prefix-sensitive supervision on the loss side by keeping the cross-entropy support only through the drafter's first predicted failure. AUF is a single, detached change to the CE support -- no auxiliary objective, no verifier rollouts, and no change to the inference pipeline or the exactness contract. Within fixed drafter backbones and serving settings on Qwen3-8B, AUF raises the DFlash drafter's average emitted length $τ$, averaged over six benchmarks, from 2.40 to 2.61, with a gain on every benchmark, and transfers to Domino's two-branch head (2.56 to 2.68). Two findings sharpen the picture: the decay-only baseline reaches higher token accuracy on the shared block mask yet decodes worse, and on DFlash, once AUF truncates the support, the standard exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.

AI.tldr: AUF is a minimal training-loss modification for block-drafter autoregressive models that concentrates supervision on the accepted prefix, yielding longer emitted blocks and consistent gains without changing inference.
AI.motivation: Speculative/block-drafting accelerates generation by drafting entire blocks and verifying left-to-right; traditional full-block CE supervises all positions against the gold continuation, which mismatches inference where tokens after the first rejection are discarded. AUF aims to align supervision with the actual, accepted prefix using a prefix-focused CE support.
AI.method: Introduce a loss-side change to cross-entropy support that concentrates on the drafter's first predicted failure, using a mask-only block drafter without input-side gold-prefix conditioning. No auxiliary objectives, verifier rollouts, or inference changes. Evaluate within fixed backbones (Qwen3-8B, DFlash) and Domino head across six benchmarks, tracking average emitted length τ.
AI.result: AUF increases the average emitted length τ for the DFlash drafter from 2.40 to 2.61 and for Domino head from 2.56 to 2.68, with gains on all six benchmarks. It suggests that truncating loss-coverage after the first failure is effective. Two additional findings: (1) a decay-only baseline yields higher token-accuracy on the shared block mask but decodes worse; (2) for DFlash, once AUF truncates support, the exponential position-decay weighting becomes empirically inert.
AI.conclusion: AUF is a single, detached CE-support modification that improves draft-length and cross-benchmark performance without altering the inference pipeline, objective, or exactness guarantees. It highlights the importance of prefix-focused supervision and provides a simple, robust way to extend effective draft length across heterogeneous backbones.

title: SpaceEra++: A Unified Framework Towards 3D Spatial Reasoning in Video
summary: Visual-spatial understanding, defined as the ability to infer object relationships and scene layouts from visual inputs, is fundamental to downstream tasks such as robotic navigation and embodied interaction. However, pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) remain constrained by spatial uncertainty stemming from inherently 2D observations and by the scarcity of data for 3D spatial understanding. To address these limitations, we proposed a novel framework, SpaceEra, in the NeurIPS 2025 Spotlight paper. Although it achieved significant performance gains, we further observed that its effectiveness is hindered by insufficient input from scanning videos and weak reasoning constraints. To tackle these newly emerged challenges, we extend the original framework into a comprehensive system, termed SpaceEra++, which spans data construction, model design, training optimization, and prompting inference. Specifically, to alleviate input insufficiency, we introduce ScenePick, a frame sampling strategy that balances spatial coverage with object semantics to produce compact yet comprehensive scene representations. In addition, to enhance spatial reasoning, we develop SpaceAlign, which enforces pairwise object constraints by jointly exploiting absolute coordinates and relative spatial relations, thereby aligning optimization with spatial accuracy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, while ablation studies validate both the individual and joint contributions of each component, and further analyses provide guidance for future research.

AI.tldr: SpaceEra++ extends SpaceEra to tackle input insufficiency and weak spatial reasoning in visual-spatial understanding for vision-language models, via ScenePick frame sampling and SpaceAlign pairwise spatial constraints, yielding consistent gains and validated by ablations.
AI.motivation: Overcome 2D spatial uncertainties and data scarcity for 3D spatial understanding in VLMs; enhance input coverage and reasoning for better robotic navigation and embodied interaction.
AI.method: Data construction, model design, training optimization, and prompting inference; ScenePick frame sampling balancing spatial coverage with object semantics; SpaceAlign enforcing absolute and relative spatial constraints to align optimization with spatial accuracy.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong baselines across multiple benchmarks; ablation studies confirm the contributions of ScenePick and SpaceAlign; joint usage provides further gains; analyses guide future research.
AI.conclusion: SpaceEra++ effectively advances visual-spatial understanding in VLMs by addressing input insufficiency and reasoning constraints; components are complementary and scalable; suggests directions for future work and broader applicability.

title: Role-Aware Neural Convex Divergence Heads for Asymmetric Representation Learning
summary: Many representation learning problems involve directed relations, such as lexical entailment, sentence entailment, ontology hierarchy, and citation links. Standard Euclidean, cosine, and Mahalanobis heads are symmetric, while generic neural scorers can model directionality but provide limited geometric structure. This paper proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning. The head applies source- and target-role projections before evaluating an input-convex neural Bregman divergence, yielding a nonnegative structured score in the role-projected space. We characterize its projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based local curvature. Experiments on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed graph benchmarks compare symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant. Across ten random seeds on the main semantic and ontology benchmarks, role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads while preserving zero observed negative divergence rate. The results also identify a boundary case: on large fixed-feature citation prediction, specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines remain stronger in ranking accuracy. Overall, the proposed head is best understood as a structured and interpretable plug-in distance module for tasks where directional relations matter.

AI.tldr: Proposes a role-aware neural convex divergence head for asymmetric representation learning using source/target projections and an input-convex neural Bregman divergence to yield a nonnegative directional score. Demonstrates improved directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads across lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed-graph benchmarks with zero observed negative divergence rate; notes a boundary case where large fixed-feature citation tasks favor specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines; frames the approach as a structured, interpretable plug-in distance for directional relations.
AI.motivation: Address the limitation of symmetric similarity measures and unstructured asymmetrical scorers in capturing directed relations (e.g., entailment, ontology edges) by introducing a projection-enhanced, convex-divergence-based distance with interpretable geometry.
AI.method: Introduce source- and target-role projections that feed an input-convex neural network (ICNN) to compute a Bregman divergence in the projected space. Analyze properties including projected-space identity, source-role convexity, directional-gap decomposition, and Hessian-based curvature. Empirically evaluate on lexical, sentence, ontology, and directed-graph benchmarks, comparing against symmetric distances, unstructured asymmetric scorers, order/hyperbolic baselines, plain ICNN-Bregman heads, and the proposed role-aware variant.
AI.result: Role-aware projections consistently improve directional accuracy over plain ICNN-Bregman heads across ten random seeds on main semantic and ontology benchmarks, while preserving zero negative divergence rate. A boundary case appears in large fixed-feature citation prediction where specialized symmetric or hyperbolic baselines exceed in ranking accuracy.
AI.conclusion: The role-aware ICNN-Bregman head provides a structured, interpretable plug-in distance for tasks with directional relations, offering robust directional performance across diverse benchmarks, though not universally superior (certain large-citation tasks favor alternative baselines).

title: Rethinking Complexity Metrics for LLM-Integrated Applications: Beyond Source Code
summary: LLM-integrated applications blend natural language prompts with program code, and much of their runtime behavior originates in the prompt layer rather than in the code itself. Existing complexity metrics, however, operate solely at the code level and therefore overlook this behavioral logic entirely. We present HECATE, the first tool designed to assess complexity in both the prompt and code layers of such applications. Central to HECATE is Prompt-as-Specification, a Hoare-logic-inspired formalism that interprets every prompt as a specification of intended behavior. Grounded in 25 complexity dimensions identified across published taxonomies, the tool generates 52 candidate metrics. We assess each metric against 118 components collected from 18 open-source repositories, relying on maintenance activity derived from version history as an empirical proxy for complexity, and discard any metric that loses significance once code size is accounted for. Only ten metrics withstand this test. Seven belong to our newly introduced set; rather than measuring sheer volume, each tallies structurally distinct elements, such as LLM call sites, memory attributes, and prompt templates, an attribute we call structural breadth. Of the three surviving conventional metrics, RFC exhibits a similar breadth-oriented character, while Halstead N and V survive only as a residual effect of size; our top-performing metrics exceed all three. Crucially, the prompt-layer metrics retain significance even when the strongest code-level metric is added as a covariate, establishing prompt complexity as a dimension in its own right. A final validation on 20 components spanning six held-out repositories shows that the two best-performing metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting their generalizability beyond the training set.

AI.tldr: HECATE introduces Prompt-as-Specification to measure complexity across both prompt and code layers in LLM-integrated apps, deriving 52 metrics from 25 dimensions and validating them against 118 components from 18 repos; only 10 metrics survive after accounting for code size, with seven new structural-breadth metrics and strong prompt-layer predictive power for maintenance, generalizing to held-out data.
AI.motivation: Existing complexity metrics focus on code and miss prompt-driven behavior in LLM-integrated apps; there is a need for quantitative, generalizable complexity measures that capture both layers.
AI.method: Define Prompt-as-Specification inspired by Hoare logic; derive 25 complexity dimensions from published taxonomies; generate 52 candidate metrics; empirically assess on 118 components from 18 open-source repos; use version-history maintenance activity as an empirical proxy for complexity; discard metrics that lose significance after controlling for code size; identify top metrics; validate on held-out repos.
AI.result: Ten metrics survive size-adjusted tests; seven are newly introduced structural-breadth metrics (counting LLM call sites, memory attributes, prompt templates, etc.). Among conventional metrics, RFC shows a breadth-like character, while Halstead N and V mostly reflect size. The top-performing metrics exceed these. Prompt-layer metrics remain significant even when a strong code-level metric is included, indicating prompt complexity is a distinct dimension. On 20 components from six held-out repositories, the two best metrics continue to predict maintenance effort, supporting generalizability.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-layer complexity is a distinct, generalizable dimension in LLM-enabled software; HECATE provides a dual-layer, structure-focused metric framework that can guide maintenance planning and future research.

title: Denser $\neq$ Better: Limits of On-Policy Self-Distillation for Continual Post-Training
summary: Continual post-training enables foundation models to acquire new knowledge while preserving existing capabilities. Recent work suggests that on-policy learning can mitigate forgetting, with on-policy self-distillation emerging as a particularly attractive approach. In this work, we revisit this optimistic view through self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO). Our experiments show that SDPO can accelerate in-domain specialization when teacher signals are stable and well aligned, but it struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution scenarios. In continual post-training, SDPO exhibits stronger forgetting and can even collapse, whereas on-policy reinforcement learning methods such as GRPO adapt more conservatively and better preserve prior capabilities. Further analyses reveal that denser self-distillation induces larger drift in both parameter space and response space, and can amplify high-frequency formatting artifacts through a self-reinforcing teacher--student loop. These findings suggest that on-policy data alone is insufficient for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can accelerate specialization when teacher targets are stable and token-level supervision is reliable, but it should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Moenupa/SDPO-CL.

AI.tldr: SDPO accelerates in-domain specialization with stable teacher signals but generalizes poorly out-of-distribution and can cause stronger forgetting and collapse; dense self-distillation introduces drift and artifacts, making on-policy data alone insufficient for continual learning; GRPO preserves prior capabilities more reliably; dense SDPO should not be a default stabilizer.
AI.motivation: To evaluate the viability and limitations of self-distillation-based on-policy methods (SDPO) for continual post-training of foundation models, particularly in balancing new knowledge with retention across in-domain and out-of-domain settings.
AI.method: Empirical study comparing SDPO with on-policy GRPO across continual post-training scenarios, varying teacher signal stability, and analyzing parameter- and response-space drift, as well as formatting artifact amplification from self-distillation loops.
AI.result: SDPO boosts in-domain specialization when teacher targets are stable and aligned but fails to generalize out-of-distribution; in continual post-training, SDPO shows stronger forgetting and even collapse, while GRPO adapts conservatively and preserves prior abilities better; increasing distillation density increases drift and high-frequency formatting artifacts; on-policy data alone is insufficient for robust continual learning.
AI.conclusion: On-policy data by itself is not enough for continual learning. Dense self-distillation can aid specialization only under stable, reliable targets and token-level supervision, and should not be treated as a default stabilizer for continual post-training. Prefer conservative on-policy methods (e.g., GRPO) for retention, and use SDPO with caution under stable conditions.

title: ContextSniper: AntTrail's Token-Efficient Code Memory for Repository-Level Program Repair
summary: Large language model agents can repair real repository issues, but they often spend large context budgets on whole-file reads, broad searches, and long terminal outputs where useful evidence is mixed with irrelevant code and logs. This paper presents ContextSniper, AntTrail's token-efficient code memory layer for repository-level program repair. As the coding specialization of AntTrail's broader agent memory engine, ContextSniper implements the Sniper feature for precision evidence selection: it retrieves candidate code and runtime evidence, ranks it with hybrid retrieval signals, filters long outputs through an intention-aware context gate, and returns compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt. We evaluate ContextSniper on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code, using 50 task runs per host-agent condition. ContextSniper reduces total token use by 51.5% and logged cost by 36.4% for OpenClaw, and reduces total token use by 38.9% and estimated cost by 27.3% for Claude Code. Submitted-resolution rates decrease slightly, from 26.0% to 24.0% for OpenClaw and from 32.0% to 30.0% for Claude Code. ContextSniper's pilot testing scripts are open-sourced at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper

AI.tldr: ContextSniper is a token-efficient memory layer for repository-level program repair that reduces token usage and cost while preserving evidence, evaluated on SWE-bench Lite with OpenClaw and Claude Code; slight drop in submission-resolution rates; open-sourced.
AI.motivation: LLM agents repair repository issues but incur large token usage due to whole-file reads, broad searches, and long outputs; a precision evidence retrieval mechanism can reduce context size and latency.
AI.method: Sniper feature: retrieve candidate code and runtime evidence; rank with hybrid retrieval signals; filter long outputs through an intention-aware context gate; return compact evidence packets while preserving recoverable source context outside the prompt.
AI.result: Token use reduced by 51.5% (OpenClaw) and 38.9% (Claude Code); logged/estimated costs reduced by 36.4% and 27.3% respectively; submitted-resolution rates declined from 26.0% to 24.0% (OpenClaw) and 32.0% to 30.0% (Claude Code). Open-source pilot scripts at https://github.com/Calluking/ContextSniper.
AI.conclusion: ContextSniper demonstrates a practical, token-efficient memory-layer approach for repository-level program repair, achieving substantial prompt-efficiency gains with a small decrease in effectiveness; open-source availability supports reproducibility.

title: MMBench-Live: A Continuously Evolving Benchmark for Multimodal Models
summary: Evaluation benchmarks are essential for assessing vision-language models (VLMs), but most multimodal benchmarks are static, making them vulnerable to temporal staleness, data contamination, and costly maintenance.
