AI.tldr: The work identifies two structural issues in post-hoc calibration for semantic segmentation—translation-dependence of calibrators and misalignment with segmentation metrics—and proposes TI calibrators and class-conditional affine calibrators to balance calibration quality with decision preservation, with empirical gains across datasets and under covariate shift.
AI.motivation: Reliable confidence estimates in semantic segmentation are essential for safety-critical applications. Post-hoc calibration must align with the dense prediction setting and won’t trivially degrade segmentation maps. The paper isolates two issues: (i) translation invariance of calibration despite logit shifts, and (ii) alignment between calibration objectives (likelihood) and segmentation metrics (e.g., Dice).
AI.method: Define translation-invariant (TI) calibrators and characterize which common calibrators are TI; construct TI versions of shift-sensitive calibrators to isolate representation dependence. Analyze decision-preserving calibration under argmax- and order-preserving constraints; show that enforcing these constraints collapses affine calibrators to temperature scaling, and propose class-conditional affine calibrators to maintain expressivity while preserving decisions. Empirically evaluate on natural-image and medical segmentation benchmarks under corruption-based covariate shift, comparing TI vs non-TI and decision-preserving vs not.
AI.result: TI calibrators generally yield better calibration metrics; decision-preserving calibrators prevent degradation of segmentation maps while retaining calibration performance; under covariate shift, matched comparisons show the proposed methods outperform baselines in both calibration and segmentation quality.
AI.conclusion: The paper offers practical design principles for post-hoc calibration in semantic segmentation. Translation-invariant calibrators are preferable for robust confidence estimates, and when decision preservation is required, class-conditional affine calibrators provide a flexible, more expressive alternative to temperature scaling. The study highlights a calibration-segmentation trade-off and guides practitioners in building well-defined calibration pipelines for dense prediction.

title: Decomposer: Learning to Decompile Symbolic Music to Programs
summary: Musical performance involves executing a set of high-level musical instructions, yet recovering those instructions from the performance is a challenging inverse problem. We present Decomposer, a post-training framework for symbolic music decompilation: the task of recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic music. We instantiate the task as MIDI-to-Strudel decompilation, where the model takes symbolic MIDI as input and produces a program in Strudel, a music programming language, that reconstructs the input when executed. The task poses two challenges: Strudel is a low-resource language with little naturally paired MIDI-code data, and optimizing faithful reconstruction of MIDI alone can collapse to unreadable note-by-note transliteration. We address these challenges in two stages. First, we construct Strudel-Synth, a synthetic corpus of paired Strudel programs and rendered MIDI, and use it for supervised fine-tuning. Second, we refine the model with reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI, optimizing rewards for both MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability. Our evaluation across synthetic and real-world MIDI benchmarks shows that Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs while producing more readable and diverse code than the heuristic converter.

AI.tldr: Decomposer is a post-training framework to decompile MIDI into executable Strudel programs, enhancing reconstruction faithfulness and code readability through synthetic data and reinforcement learning.
AI.motivation: Recovering executable, editable music programs from symbolic scores is an ill-posed inverse problem, worsened by Strudel's low-resource status and the risk of unreadable transliteration.
AI.method: Two-stage approach: (1) create Strudel-Synth, a synthetic paired corpus of Strudel programs and rendered MIDI for supervised fine-tuning; (2) apply reinforcement learning on unpaired MIDI to optimize a reward for MIDI reconstruction faithfulness and code readability/diversity.
AI.result: Decomposer achieves substantially higher MIDI reconstruction faithfulness than closed-source LLMs and yields more readable and diverse code than a heuristic converter across synthetic and real MIDI benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates effective post-training decompilation from MIDI to executable Strudel programs, highlighting the value of synthetic data plus RL for low-resource languages and opening avenues for improving symbolic-to-code mappings in music.

title: PACE: A Proxy for Agentic Capability Evaluation
summary: Evaluating LLM agents on benchmarks like SWE-Bench and GAIA can be expensive, time-consuming, and requires complex infrastructure. A single evaluation can cost thousands of dollars and take days to complete. In contrast, non-agentic LLM benchmarks that test individual capabilities (e.g., reasoning, code generation) are fast and cheap to run. In this paper, we investigate whether performance on expensive agentic benchmarks can be accurately predicted by the performance on a small, carefully selected subset of atomic evaluation instances. We introduce PACE, a framework that constructs proxy benchmarks by selecting instances from existing non-agentic evaluations whose aggregate scores most reliably predict model performances on agentic benchmarks. Given a pool of candidate instances spanning atomic capabilities, PACE fits a regression that maps a model's scores on a compact subset of source instances to its score on the target agentic benchmark. The subset itself is curated by combining two complementary instance-selection strategies, target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection. We apply PACE to the 4 target agentic benchmarks in this paper, which yields PACE-Bench, the concrete proxy benchmark that we evaluate in the paper. Experiments across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks show that PACE-Bench predicts agentic scores with leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) mean absolute error (MAE) under 4%, Spearman correlation above 0.80, and pairwise model-ranking accuracy around 85%, all at much less than 1% of the full agentic evaluation cost. We further analyze the selected proxy instances, revealing which skills each agentic benchmark uniquely demands. PACE enables practitioners to obtain reliable estimates of agentic performance during model development, selection, and routing, without the overhead of full agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: PACE creates proxy benchmarks from existing non-agentic evaluations to predict expensive agentic benchmark scores, yielding accurate estimates at a tiny fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: Agentic benchmarks are expensive and slow to run; a cheaper, reliable predictor is needed to guide model development, selection, and routing.
AI.method: PACE selects a compact subset of non-agentic evaluation instances via target-relevance local selection and globally informative global selection, fits a regression mapping scores on this subset to the target agentic benchmark score, and composes a concrete proxy benchmark (PACE-Bench).
AI.result: Across 14 models, 4 agentic benchmarks, and 19 non-agentic benchmarks, PACE-Bench achieves LOOCV MAE < 4%, Spearman > 0.80, and pairwise ranking accuracy ~85%, at <1% of full agentic evaluation cost.
AI.conclusion: PACE enables reliable, low-cost estimation of agentic performance during model development and selection, with interpretable proxy instances that reveal the skills each agentic benchmark demands.

title: SFKD: Spatial--Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation via Multi-Level Wavelet Spectral Interaction
summary: Most existing knowledge distillation methods focus on homogeneous models (e.g., CNN-to-CNN), thereby overlooking the flexibility and potential of knowledge transfer across heterogeneous models. Due to intrinsic inductive bias discrepancies between heterogeneous models that cause spatial distribution inconsistencies, prior heterogeneous distillation methods often weaken or discard spatial information in heterogeneous representations. However, the spatial information in representations often encodes transferable global structural semantics as well as architecture-specific local details, and therefore should not be directly ignored. To better leverage the spatial information encoded in heterogeneous representations, we propose a Spatial-Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation framework (SFKD). By leveraging the complementary properties of wavelet transform spatial locality and Fourier representations in characterizing global energy distributions, we first apply multi-level discrete wavelet transform to explicitly decouple spatial information. The resulting wavelet sub-bands are further refined by a dual-stream dual-stage refinement module, and finally combined with a Gaussian-filtered frequency loss to selectively capture informative global information. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets under both homogeneous and heterogeneous models demonstrate the superiority of our method.

AI.tldr: Proposes Spatial-Frequency Joint-Aware Heterogeneous Knowledge Distillation (SFKD) to transfer knowledge across heterogeneous models by decoupling spatial information with multi-level wavelet transforms, refining via a dual-stream module, and using a Gaussian-filtered frequency loss, yielding superior results on benchmark datasets.
AI.motivation: Heterogeneous distillation faces spatial distribution mismatch due to inductive bias differences, causing loss of spatial information. Spatial cues carry transferable global structure and architecture-specific local details, which should be exploited rather than discarded.
AI.method: Apply multi-level discrete wavelet transform to decouple spatial information into sub-bands. Refine sub-bands with a dual-stream, dual-stage refinement module. Combine with a Gaussian-filtered frequency loss to selectively capture informative global information.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple benchmarks demonstrate superiority of SFKD under both homogeneous and heterogeneous model settings.
AI.conclusion: SFKD effectively leverages spatial-frequency representations to improve knowledge transfer across heterogeneous architectures by explicitly decoupling and refining spatial information and incorporating a frequency-domain loss.

title: Learning the Supports for Categorical Critic in Reinforcement Learning
summary: Value functions are an essential component in actor-critic based deep reinforcement learning (RL). Conventionally, these functions are trained as a regression task by minimising the mean squared error (MSE) relative to bootstrapped target values. Meanwhile, in distributional RL, a distribution of returns is modelled based on the distributional Bellman operator. This work investigates the Gaussian Histogram Loss (HL-Gauss), a recent approach that reframes value estimation as classification by encoding each scalar Bellman target as a Gaussian-smoothed categorical target. Despite its potential, applying histogram-based losses to RL presents inherent challenges, most notably the requirement to pre-define a fixed support interval, which is often complicated by the non-stationary and stochastic nature of target values typically found in RL tasks. In this work, we propose an approach that dynamically learns the lower and upper bounds of the support instead of assigning them beforehand. We derive an objective that jointly learns these bounds whilst learning the categorical representation of the scalar values, and we show that this objective forms an upper bound on the mean-squared Bellman error. Our theoretical analysis further shows that this bound is tighter than that of non-learned supports of HL-Gauss. Empirically, the proposed objective enables stable adaptation of the support interval and matches HL-Gauss-based actor-critic algorithms on most continuous-control tasks whilst improving on a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.

AI.tldr: Dynamic learning of HL-Gauss support bounds for value estimation in distributional RL. The proposed objective jointly learns lower/upper bounds and the Gaussian-smoothed categorical representation, yielding an upper bound on MSE that is tighter than fixed-support HL-Gauss. Empirically, it matches HL-Gauss on most continuous-control tasks and improves on some, without predefining the support interval.
AI.motivation: Address the challenge of fixed histogram supports in HL-Gauss under non-stationary RL targets. Learnable bounds aim to stabilize and improve value estimation by adapting the support to the data.
AI.method: Introduce an objective that jointly optimizes the lower and upper bound of the support along with the categorical distribution over values. Prove that this objective upper-bounds the MSE (Bellman error) and is tighter than using a fixed, non-learned support. Integrate into actor-critic with distributional RL.
AI.result: The learned-bound objective enables stable adaptation of the support. Empirically, it yields performance comparable to HL-Gauss-based actor-critics on most continuous-control tasks and outperforms in a subset, without requiring a pre-specified support interval.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic, learnable support bounds for HL-Gauss improve stability and performance in distributional RL and remove the need for fixed pre-specified supports while providing a theoretical tightening over non-learned supports.

title: Algebraic Model Counting for Global Analysis of Optimal Decision Trees
comment: Proc. Joint European Conference on Machine Learning and Principles and Practice of Knowledge Discovery in Databases (ECML-PKDD 2026), LNCS, Naples, Italy, 7-11 September 2026
summary: Ensuring model reliability in Explainable AI requires a global assessment of the hypothesis space. We propose a formal framework for the exhaustive analysis of optimal and near-optimal decision trees, called Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC). Inspired by Algebraic Model Counting (AMC) in knowledge representation, ADTC reformulates diverse analytical tasks, such as optimization, counting, and sampling, into a unified sum-of-products computation over a semiring $R$. While the hypothesis space of decision trees is doubly exponential with respect to the maximum depth $Δ$, our dynamic programming algorithm achieves $O^*(n^{O(Δ)})$ time complexity in the number of features $n$, where $O^*$ suppresses polynomial factors. To handle complex constraints consisting of multiple tree metrics, we introduce model behavior tensors that aggregate semiring values via convolution products over a tensor semiring. This algebraic approach efficiently constructs a model profile that captures the global landscape and trade-offs between criteria such as accuracy, size, and fairness. We demonstrate the utility of our software, emtrees, on real-world datasets, illustrating how ADTC facilitates evidence-based model selection in sensitive domains.

AI.tldr: Algebraic Decision Tree Counting (ADTC) reframes optimal/near-optimal decision-tree analysis as a semiring-based sum-of-products computation, enabling exhaustive global assessment of the hypothesis space with efficient DP, and extends to multi-metric model profiles via tensor semirings; software emtrees demonstrates practical utility on real data.
AI.motivation: Address the need for global reliability assessment in Explainable AI by analyzing the entire hypothesis space of decision trees, which is doubly exponential in depth, rather than relying on local or heuristic evaluations.
AI.method: Reformulate optimization, counting, and sampling tasks as semiringed sum-of-products (AMC-inspired). Use dynamic programming to attain O*(n^{O(Δ)}) time, with O*(...) suppressing poly factors. Introduce model behavior tensors to combine multiple tree metrics via tensor semiring convolutions, enabling unified aggregation into a model profile.
AI.result: The framework provides a scalable approach to exhaustive or near-exhaustive analysis of decision trees under multiple criteria, and the authors implement emtrees to illustrate practical utility and evidence-based model selection on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: ADTC offers a principled, algebraic pathway to quantify and compare global trade-offs (accuracy, size, fairness) across the decision-tree hypothesis space, enabling reliable model selection in sensitive domains through a unified, extensible software framework.

title: Towards Real-World Ultrasound Understanding: Large Vision-Language Models from Multi-Image Examinations with Long-Form Reports
summary: Large vision-language models (LVLMs) have achieved strong performance across many medical imaging tasks, yet their application to ultrasound remains limited due to its inherent complexity and variability. In this work, we revisit what is truly needed to enable real-world ultrasound understanding. Instead of introducing complex architectures or elaborate training strategies, we show that data scale and clinically faithful data alignment are the key factors. We construct a large-scale dataset of 1.5M real-world ultrasound examinations, containing 17.7M images, multi-organ coverage, and paired uncurated clinical reports. Crucially, we organize the data at the examination level, aligning multiple images with their corresponding reports to reflect real clinical workflows. We then fine-tune a standard LVLM using low-rank adaptation (LoRA) on this dataset without task-specific modifications. Surprisingly, this simple recipe already leads to strong performance across diverse ultrasound understanding tasks, outperforming prior methods designed with more complex pipelines. Beyond these results, we present model and data scaling analyses that provide insights into the role of scale in ultrasound LVLMs.

AI.tldr: Scale data and faithful exam-level alignment enable ultrasound LVLMs with LoRA, achieving strong results without complex architectures.
AI.motivation: Ultrasound exhibits high variability and complexity; scalable, clinically faithful data and workflow-aligned supervision are needed to unlock real-world understanding.
AI.method: Assemble a large-scale dataset of 1.5M ultrasound examinations (17.7M images) with multi-organ coverage and paired uncurated reports; organize data at the examination level with image-report alignment reflecting clinical workflows; fine-tune a standard LVLM using LoRA without task-specific modifications.
AI.result: Achieves strong performance across diverse ultrasound understanding tasks, outperforming prior methods designed with more complex pipelines; data and scale analyses provide insights into their role.
AI.conclusion: Data scale and clinically faithful data alignment are the primary drivers for ultrasound LVLM success; a simple, scalable approach with LoRA suffices to achieve strong results.

title: Regularized Variational and Spectral Log-Density-Ratio Estimation in the Gaussian Location Model
summary: We study ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in the Gaussian location model with a common covariance matrix. By affine invariance, the model is written as q $\sim$ N(0, I), p $\sim$ N($Δ$, I), with linear features, where $Δ$ is a mean vector. The variational estimator is the empirical Kullback-Leibler (KL) log-normalized fit with a squared L2-penalty on its nonconstant coefficient, and the spectral estimator recently introduced in [1] replaces a single variational problem by a continuum of ridge-regularized least-squares problems. We derive high-dimensional deterministic asymptotic equivalents when the numbers of observations and dimension tend to infinity with fixed ratios. The regularized variational limit is characterized by a scalar entropy minimization problem derived from the convex-Gaussian-min-max theorem (CGMT), while the regularized spectral limit follows from deterministic equivalents for resolvents of weighted sums of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices. We use these formulas to compare population risks, with experiments focused on fixed-signal aspect-ratio sweeps and optimized regularization. Our conclusion is that with many observations, under the criteria and asymptotic regimes analyzed here, the well-specified variational estimator has the smaller risk, while with fewer observations, the spectral estimator is favored because its covariance-based construction has lower variance. We also study how a nuclear penalty can be used and partially analyzed to perform feature learning.

AI.tldr: High-dimensional ridge-regularized log-density-ratio estimation in a Gaussian location model; compares variational (KL-based) and spectral (ridge-regularized least squares) estimators via CGMT and resolvent analysis; shows variational estimator prevails with many samples, while the spectral estimator excels in small-sample, high-variance settings; discusses nuclear penalties for feature learning.
AI.motivation: Understand performance trade-offs between two regularized density-ratio estimators in high dimensions and guide regularization choice through deterministic equivalents derived from CGMT and random matrix theory.
AI.method: Derive high-dimensional deterministic equivalents: a scalar entropy minimization (CGMT) for the regularized variational limit; resolvent-based equivalents for the weighted sum of two independent Gaussian sample covariance matrices for the spectral limit; analyze population risks under fixed-signal aspect ratios; conduct aspect-ratio sweeps and optimize regularization; extend with a nuclear penalty for feature learning.
AI.result: Asymptotically, the well-specified variational estimator has lower risk in regimes with many observations, while the spectral estimator is advantageous in data-sparse regimes due to lower variance; provides guidance on regulator choices and demonstrates feasibility of nuclear-penalized feature learning.
AI.conclusion: Regime-dependent preference: use variational, well-specified, high-sample settings; use spectral, low-sample/high-variance settings. The framework enables principled regularization and extension to feature learning via nuclear penalties.

title: Evidence-State Rewards for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Long-context reasoning requires models to locate, revise, and synthesize evidence distributed across lengthy inputs. Existing long-context RL methods usually reward final answers or static evidence extraction, offering little feedback on how intermediate actions change the model's evidence state. We propose Maven, a reinforcement learning framework with an editable evidence memory. Maven defines an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and rewards action-level state transitions: add actions are credited by marginal gain and hindsight contribution, link actions by evidence synergy, and drop actions by improved answer support after removing misleading evidence. These rewards are assigned to the corresponding action spans in GRPO. Across Llama and Qwen models on LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER, Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, producing more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention. Our results show that long-context RL benefits from optimizing stateful evidence navigation rather than one-shot evidence extraction.

AI.tldr: Maven is an RL framework for long-context reasoning that maintains an editable evidence memory and uses action-level rewards to guide evidence addition, linking, and dropping, improving evidence quality and reducing distractors compared to baselines across multiple models and datasets.
AI.motivation: Long-context reasoning requires iterative evidence navigation and state-aware feedback. Existing RL approaches often optimize only final answers or static evidence extraction, neglecting how intermediate actions reshape the evidence state.
AI.method: Propose Maven with an answer-conditioned evidence-state value and action-level rewards. Add actions gain marginal/ hindsight-based credit, link actions reward evidence synergy, and drop actions reward improved answer support after pruning misleading evidence. Apply rewards to action spans in GRPO. Evaluate on Llama and Qwen across LongBench v2, LongReason, and RULER datasets.
AI.result: Maven outperforms outcome-only RL and evidence-identification baselines, yielding more sufficient evidence sets and lower distractor retention across tested models and datasets.
AI.conclusion: Optimizing stateful evidence navigation is beneficial for long-context RL, demonstrating gains beyond one-shot evidence extraction and generalizing across models and benchmarks.

title: Rank-Then-Act: Reward-Free Control from Frame-Order Progress
summary: We introduce Rank-Then-Act (RTA), a framework for learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards. RTA trains a Vision-Language Model (VLM) offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer, using a Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) objective over shuffled frame sequences, which forces the model to recover temporal ordering from visual semantics rather than trivial time cues. Importantly, instead of using the scorer directly as a scalar reward model, we propose a correlation-based reward function for reinforcement learning: at each interaction window, we compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices, yielding a bounded, scale-invariant learning signal. This design decouples reward learning from absolute calibration and enables stable transfer across tasks and environments. We evaluate RTA on discrete control benchmarks (PyBoy: Catrap, Kirby) and continuous control tasks (PointMaze, MetaWorld). RTA consistently matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning methods and rank-based baselines, while demonstrating strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer. Our results suggest that correlation-structured supervision over video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for policy learning, offering a scalable alternative to explicit reward design.

AI.tldr: Introduces Rank-Then-Act (RTA): learning control policies from expert video demonstrations without environment rewards via a progress-based ordinal scorer trained offline and a correlation-based reward for RL.
AI.motivation: Reward specification from video demonstrations is challenging; need a scalable, transfer-friendly signal that captures temporal progression from visual data without relying on exact timing or environment rewards.
AI.method: Train a Vision-Language Model offline as a progress-based ordinal scorer using a Group Relative Policy Optimization objective on shuffled frame sequences to force learning of temporal semantics. During RL, compute the Spearman rank correlation between predicted progress rankings and true temporal indices within each window to generate a bounded, scale-invariant reward.
AI.result: RTA matches or outperforms prior video-based reward learning and rank-based baselines across discrete (PyBoy Catrap, Kirby) and continuous (PointMaze, MetaWorld) tasks, with strong cross-task reuse of a single pretrained progress scorer.
AI.conclusion: Correlation-structured supervision on video-derived ordinal signals is sufficient for effective policy learning and provides a scalable alternative to explicit reward design, enabling robust cross-task transfer.

title: SUNTA: Hierarchical Video Prediction with Surprise-based Chunking
summary: Hierarchical state-space models (HSSMs) offer a promising approach to long-horizon prediction by segmenting sequences into temporal chunks. However, their performance hinges on how chunk boundaries are determined. While prior HSSMs typically rely on fixed-length chunking or similarity-based boundary detection, these methods often misalign with the intrinsic temporal structure of the data. We argue that chunking should instead be driven by prediction errors, which more directly indicate when longer-range context becomes necessary. Nevertheless, integrating surprise-based chunking into HSSMs introduces critical challenges, including hierarchical collapse during end-to-end training and the absence of surprise signals during open-loop prediction. To address these issues, we propose Surprise-based Nested Temporal Abstraction (SUNTA), a method that employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric to determine chunk boundaries within imagined rollouts. Experiments on video prediction tasks in 2D and 3D environments demonstrate that SUNTA outperforms baselines, uniquely maintaining accurate predictions over 250 timesteps, whereas all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.

AI.tldr: SUNTA introduces surprise-based chunking for hierarchical state-space models, using decoupled training and internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise signal to determine chunk boundaries in imagined rollouts. It outperforms baselines on long-horizon video prediction, maintaining accuracy up to 250 timesteps where others fail early.
AI.motivation: HSSMs struggle with chunk boundaries that misalign with data’s temporal structure. Fixed-length or similarity-based chunking often fails to capture when longer-range context is needed. Surprisal-driven chunking aims to align chunk boundaries with predictive needs, but end-to-end training risks hierarchical collapse and open-loop predictions lack surprise signals.
AI.method: SUNTA employs a decoupled training strategy to preserve surprise signals and uses internal inconsistency as a top-down surprise metric. Chunk boundaries are determined within imagined rollouts based on this internal signal, enabling adaptive, prediction-error-driven subdivision of sequences.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation on 2D and 3D video prediction tasks shows SUNTA outperforms baselines, achieving accurate predictions up to 250 timesteps, while all baselines degrade within the first 10 timesteps.
AI.conclusion: Prediction-error-driven, surprise-based chunking with decoupled training improves long-horizon forecasting in HSSMs. Internal inconsistency serves as an effective top-down surprise signal for adaptive chunking in imagined rollouts.

title: Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization for Bandwidth-Efficient Collaborative 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction
summary: Collaborative perception extends single-agent perception by enabling multiple vehicles to exchange complementary perceptual information. However, it introduces an inherent trade-off between perception gain and communication overhead, which is particularly severe for 3D semantic occupancy prediction that relies on fine-grained spatial structures. Existing methods typically compress 3D features into 2D, causing severe spatial information loss, or transmit dense 3D representations, hindering real-world deployment. To overcome these limitations, we propose a bandwidth-efficient collaborative Vector Quantization Semantic Occupancy Prediction (VQSOP) framework. VQSOP employs a Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization (SAVQ) mechanism that exploits 3D scene sparsity to compactly encode informative regions, drastically reducing communication overhead while preserving complete geometric context. Furthermore, to enhance structural consistency and feature continuity, we design a Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement (ASR) module that dynamically fuses local high-frequency details with broad contextual semantics. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing communication volume by up to 82x.

AI.tldr: A bandwidth-efficient framework (VQSOP) for collaborative 3D semantic occupancy prediction using Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization to exploit scene sparsity and a Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement module to preserve detail, achieving up to 82x reduction in communication while maintaining state-of-the-art accuracy.
AI.motivation: Address the trade-off between perception gains and communication overhead in collaborative 3D perception; existing approaches either compress 3D data to 2D, losing spatial detail, or transmit dense 3D representations, hindering deployment.
AI.method: Propose Sparse-Aware Vector Quantization (SAVQ) that leverages 3D scene sparsity to compactly encode informative regions and preserve geometric context, plus a Dual-Branch Adaptive Spatial Refinement (ASR) that fuses local high-frequency details with broad contextual semantics through a two-branch architecture.
AI.result: Achieves state-of-the-art performance while reducing communication volume by up to 82x across evaluated scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The VQSOP framework delivers substantial bandwidth savings without sacrificing 3D occupancy prediction accuracy, indicating strong potential for practical, scalable collaborative perception in multi-vehicle systems.

title: SABER: A Semantic-Aligned Brain Network Analysis Framework via Multi-scale Hypergraphs
comment: Accepted to IEEE International Conference on Multimedia and Expo (ICME) 2026;
summary: Effective brain disease diagnosis requires the synergy of brain connectivity patterns and high-level semantic knowledge. Existing methods, however, largely treat semantics from large language models (LLMs) as auxiliary features or supervision, limiting their direct role in decision-making and constraining classification stability and robustness. To overcome this, we propose a semantic-aligned brain network framework that actively integrates LLM-derived semantics into the prediction process. Specifically, ROI-level semantics are first incorporated via global self-attention to enrich node representations and provide whole-brain context. Multi-scale hypergraphs are then constructed to explicitly model functional subnetworks and multi-ROI interactions, addressing the locality limitations of traditional GNNs and capturing high-order dependencies. Finally, a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism selectively injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations, enabling semantics to directly guide predictions without perturbing the underlying network structure. Experiments on public brain network datasets ABIDE and ADHD-200 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance, enhanced stability, and improved interpretability, particularly in small-sample settings.

AI.tldr: A semantic-aligned brain network framework integrates LLM-derived semantics into graph-based brain connectivity analysis via ROI-level global attention, multi-scale hypergraphs for higher-order subnetworks, and a decision-level semantic alignment that injects patient-specific textual embeddings into predictions, achieving state-of-the-art results on ABIDE and ADHD-200 with improved stability and interpretability, especially in small-sample settings.
AI.motivation: To move beyond treating semantics as auxiliary features or supervision, and enable direct, robust, and interpretable use of semantic knowledge in brain disease diagnosis by tightly coupling LLM-derived semantics with brain-network representations.
AI.method: 1) Apply global self-attention to ROI-level semantics to enrich node representations with whole-brain context. 2) Construct multi-scale hypergraphs to model functional subnetworks and high-order ROI interactions, addressing locality limits of traditional GNNs. 3) Implement a decision-level semantic alignment mechanism that injects patient-specific textual embeddings into graph representations during prediction, without perturbing the underlying network structure.
AI.result: The approach achieves state-of-the-art performance on ABIDE and ADHD-200 datasets, with enhanced stability and interpretability, notably in small-sample settings.
AI.conclusion: Semantic alignment of LLM-derived semantics with brain network representations enables direct semantics-guided decision-making while preserving network structure, offering improved performance, robustness, and interpretability in neuroimaging classification.

title: ContextNest: Verifiable Context Governance for Autonomous AI Agent
summary:
Autonomous AI agents increasingly depend on external knowledge stores, yet most retrieval pipelines provide relevance without durable guarantees of provenance, version identity, integrity, traceability, or point-in-time reconstruction. We formalize this as context governance and present ContextNext, an open specification and reference implementation for governed AI-consumable knowledge vaults. ContextNext does not replace Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG); it supplies the governance layer beneath retrieval, determining which artifacts are approved, current, attributable, and integrity-verified before retrieval systems operate over them.
  The specification combines typed Markdown documents with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URI references, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, source nodes for live data through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and audit traces of agent context consumption. These mechanisms let organizations reconstruct which knowledge versions informed an agent output and whether those versions were AI-eligible when consumed.
  We report first empirical results from two controlled experiments. In a stale-version attack isolating the governance-versus-retrieval failure mode, governed selection strictly Pareto-dominates BM25 sparse retrieval, with higher answer-quality pass rate (97% versus 93-90%) at about one-third the input-token cost. In a retrieval-determinism experiment over a 1,060-document corpus, deterministic selectors and BM25 return stable document sets across repeated identical queries (Jaccard 1.0), while a dense+HNSW baseline is non-deterministic on 80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst case 0.210). These results suggest that context governance addresses failure modes retrieval quality alone is not designed to resolve. We release a core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.

AI.tldr: ContextNext offers an open governance layer for AI knowledge vaults that enforces provenance, versioning, and integrity prior to retrieval; empirically improves retrieval quality and determinism against baseline retrieval, and open-sources core tooling.
AI.motivation: The lack of durable provenance, version identity, and traceability in retrieval-augmented systems undermines auditability and reproducibility of AI outputs.
AI.method: Proposes ContextNext as a formal specification combining typed Markdown with metadata, deterministic set-algebraic selectors, contextnest:// URIs, SHA-256 hash-chained version histories, graph-level checkpoints, Model Context Protocol (MCP) for live data sources, and audit traces. Evaluation includes two controlled experiments: a stale-version governance-vs-retrieval attack and a retrieval-determinism study on a 1,060-document corpus, comparing deterministic selectors and BM25 against dense+HNSW baselines. Also releases core engine, CLI, and MCP server under open licenses.
AI.result: Governed selection outperforms BM25 in the stale-version test (97% vs 93-90% answer-quality; ~1/3 token cost). Determinism: deterministic selectors + BM25 yield stable document sets (Jaccard 1.0); dense+HNSW is non-deterministic for ~80% of queries (mean Jaccard 0.611, worst 0.210). Core tooling released.
AI.conclusion: Context governance fills a gap in retrieval systems by enabling reconstruction of which knowledge versions informed outputs and ensuring eligibility and integrity of sources. The results indicate governance can improve answer quality and consistency beyond retrieval alone, with practical open-source tooling to adopt it.

title: LiZAD: A Lightweight Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection Framework for Industrial Manufacturing
comment: Accepted at the IEEE International Conference on Omni-Layer Intelligent Systems (COINS) 2026
summary: In modern high-throughput industrial production lines, product configurations and visual characteristics frequently change, making it impractical to collect and annotate data for every new scenario. This dynamic setting makes Zero-Shot Anomaly Detection (ZSAD) particularly suitable, as it enables defect detection without requiring training on target-specific samples. Although recent ZSAD approaches show promising results, they are computationally intensive and thus unsuitable for deployment on resource-constrained devices. We propose LiZAD: a lightweight framework designed for real-time ZSAD specifically tailored for use on edge devices. The proposed approach pairs the dense and spatially aware visual features of DINOv3, crucial for precise pixel-level localization, with the highly computationally efficient text embeddings of MobileCLIP2. These features are then mapped into a shared latent space via low-memory trainable projection heads. Compared to six state-of-the-art ZSAD models, LiZAD achieves an average memory reduction of 61.5%, a parameter reduction of 74.6%, and a speedup of 3.02x in terms of latency. Despite substantial reductions in computational and memory costs, our approach maintains competitive anomaly detection performance, dropping the average P-AUROC by just 6.4% relative to the best state-of-the-art model across the VisA, BTAD, MPDD, and MVTec-AD datasets. Finally, it is successfully deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson NX and Jetson AGX edge devices and tested on the real production line of the Industrial Computer Engineering Laboratory (ICE Lab) at the University of Verona. The code is available at https://github.com/intelligolabs/LiZAD.

AI.tldr: LiZAD is a lightweight real-time zero-shot anomaly detection framework for edge devices that fuses DINOv3 visual features with MobileCLIP2 embeddings into a shared latent space via low-memory projection heads. It achieves large reductions in memory (61.5%), parameters (74.6%), and latency (3.02x) while incurring a modest 6.4% drop in average P-AUROC across standard datasets; it runs on NVIDIA Jetson devices and on ICE Lab production line, with code available publicly.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot anomaly detection in industrial settings must generalize to changing product configurations without costly per-sample data collection, while edge deployments require highly memory- and compute-efficient models.
AI.method: Use dense, spatial DINOv3 features for precise pixel-level localization and combine them with efficient MobileCLIP2 text embeddings. Project both modalities into a common latent space using low-memory trainable projection heads to enable efficient anomaly scoring suitable for edge devices.
AI.result: Compared with six state-of-the-art ZSAD models, LiZAD reduces memory by 61.5%, parameters by 74.6%, and latency by 3.02x. It maintains competitive detection performance with only a 6.4% average decrease in P-AUROC across VisA, BTAD, MPDD, and MVTec-AD datasets. It is demonstrated on NVIDIA Jetson NX/AGX hardware and tested on an industrial production line (ICE Lab).
AI.conclusion: LiZAD delivers substantial efficiency gains for real-time edge ZSAD with minimal loss in anomaly detection accuracy, enabling deployment in constrained environments, with public code availability.

title: Population-Based Multi-Objective Training of Discriminators for Semi-Supervised GANs
comment: The 2nd International Conference on Federated Learning and Intelligent Computing Systems (FLICS2026)
summary: Semi-supervised generative adversarial networks (SSL-GANs) can exploit large unlabeled datasets while retaining a classifier in the discriminator, but their training is often unstable. This paper proposes a population-based evolutionary training strategy in which discriminator learning is formulated as a multi-objective optimization problem. Instead of aggregating the supervised and unsupervised components of the SSL objective into a single scalar loss, the method maintains a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance, enabling the exploration of different trade-offs between classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination. This formulation aims to improve both roles of SSL-GANs: learning accurate classifiers and training generators capable of producing realistic samples. We analyze several variants, including an elitist strategy and a mono-objective ablation, to assess the role of multi-objective selection. Experiments on MNIST with limited labels show improved training robustness compared to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN state-of-the-art baselines, while the elitist variant consistently achieves the highest classification accuracy.

AI.tldr: A population-based multi-objective training method for SSL-GANs using Pareto-ranked discriminators improves robustness and accuracy on MNIST with limited labels, with elitist selection delivering the best classifier performance.
AI.motivation: SSL-GANs are powerful but training is unstable; combining supervised and unsupervised objectives into a single loss can hamper exploration of trade-offs; a Pareto-based, population-level optimization can better balance classification and realism objectives.
AI.method: Maintain a population of discriminators ranked by Pareto dominance with respect to two objectives: supervised classification accuracy and real/fake discrimination; evolve discriminators over training, enabling exploration of trade-offs; analyze variants including elitist strategy and mono-objective ablation; evaluate on MNIST with limited labels; compare to SSL-GAN and CE-SSL-GAN baselines.
AI.result: Improved training robustness relative to state-of-the-art SSL-GAN baselines; elitist variant consistently yields the highest classification accuracy on MNIST with limited labels.
AI.conclusion: Pareto-based population dynamics for SSL-GANs can improve both classifier performance and generator realism by better navigating objective trade-offs; elitist selection is particularly effective; the approach offers a robust alternative to single-objective SSL loss design.

title: Enhancing Fitness Intelligence through Domain-Specific LLM Post-Training
comment: 8 pages, 6 tables, 2 figures. Accepted by the 12th International Conference on Big Data Computing and Communications (BigCom 2026)
summary: Scientific Fitness Coaching (SFC) is typically delivered by human professionals, making it costly and inaccessible to many. While recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) show considerable promise for more inclusive fitness coaching, directly deploying prevailing general-purpose LLMs in SFC reveals critical limitations. These models often lack sufficient domain-specific knowledge integration, leading to weak performance on complex SFC scenarios. In this paper, we introduce FitOne, a series of fitness LLMs (with 8B and 32B parameters) designed to improve reliability and domain specialization for SFC applications. Built upon the Qwen3 foundation models, FitOne is developed through a three-stage post-training pipeline consisting of continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning, using large-scale, high-quality datasets derived from rigorous knowledge engineering. We conduct comprehensive evaluations of FitOne on professional fitness certification exams, including ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS, as well as general capabilities such as knowledge reasoning and instruction following. Experimental results show that, while retaining strong general capabilities, FitOne-8B/32B achieves average improvements of up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. Furthermore, in-depth ablation studies confirm the necessity of each training stage, highlighting the pipeline's effectiveness in balancing domain expertise enhancement with general ability retention. We believe this research advances LLM systems toward more reliable fitness intelligence and will inspire future research on developing domain-specific LLMs.

AI.tldr: FitOne: domain-specific fitness LLMs (8B/32B) built on Qwen3 using a three-stage post-training pipeline to improve SFC reliability and domain knowledge; achieves notable exam-score gains on ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS and preserves general abilities; ablation supports each training stage.
AI.motivation: General-purpose LLMs struggle with domain-specific SFC scenarios; professional fitness certification requires reliable knowledge integration; need accessible, capable SFC agents.
AI.method: Three-stage post-training: continual pre-training, supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning; data from rigorous knowledge engineering; base on Qwen3; evaluate on ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS; ablation studies.
AI.result: FitOne-8B/32B yield average improvements up to 10.09%/9.29% and 12.73%/7.01% on the ACSM-EP and NSCA-CSCS exams, respectively, compared with the Qwen3 base models. In-depth ablation confirms necessity of each training stage and balance between domain expertise and general ability.
AI.conclusion: This work advances domain-specific LLMs for fitness coaching and establishes a pathway for future domain-focused LLM development.

title: Personalized 4D Whole-Heart Mesh Reconstruction from Cine MRI via Multi-Scale Temporal Modeling and Differentiable Contour Rendering
summary: Accurate 4D whole-heart mesh reconstruction from sparse cine MRI is critical for creating cardiac digital twins, but remains challenging due to limited 2D slice coverage and the complex coupling between cardiac shape and motion. Existing methods often rely on intermediate contour fitting and typically reconstruct static, single-phase, or partial cardiac geometries, limiting their ability to capture full-chamber dynamics. We propose a novel end-to-end framework for reconstructing temporally resolved whole-heart meshes from multi-view 2D cine MRI sequences by learning an image-to-mesh mapping. The framework incorporates a differentiable contour renderer inspired by the Beer-Lambert attenuation principle, enabling anatomy-aware supervision of 3D+t mesh deformation through contour-based projection losses. To improve temporal consistency across the cardiac cycle, we further introduce a multi-scale temporal modeling module that integrates global cycle-level dynamics with local inter-frame coherence to generate smooth and physiologically plausible mesh trajectories. The proposed method achieved a whole-heart mean absolute error of 1.68 $\pm$ 0.31 mm and a motion jitter of 0.77 $\pm$ 0.17 $\mathrm{mm}/\mathrm{frame}^{3}$, outperforming existing methods with lower reconstruction error and substantially improved motion smoothness. It also improved 2D contour alignment across multiple cine MRI views and supported downstream proof-of-concept electrophysiological simulation. The code will be released publicly upon acceptance of the manuscript for publication.

AI.tldr: An end-to-end image-to-mesh framework reconstructs temporally resolved whole-heart meshes from sparse cine MRI using a differentiable contour renderer and multi-scale temporal modeling, achieving high accuracy and smooth motion, with potential downstream simulations.
AI.motivation: Addresses the challenge of 4D whole-heart reconstruction from limited 2D cine data due to sparse coverage and complex shape-motion coupling; overcomes limitations of contour fitting and static/partial geometries.
AI.method: Learned image-to-mesh mapping with a differentiable contour renderer inspired by Beer-Lambert attenuation; contour-based projection losses for anatomy-aware supervision; multi-scale temporal modeling combining global cycle dynamics with local inter-frame coherence.
AI.result: MAE 1.68 ± 0.31 mm; motion jitter 0.77 ± 0.17 mm/frame^3; outperforms baselines, improved 2D contour alignment across views; demonstrated viability for electrophysiological simulation; code to be released.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework enables accurate, temporally consistent 4D whole-heart reconstructions from sparse cine MRI, with improved smoothness and potential for downstream simulations.

title: Zeus: Towards Tuning-Free Foundation Model for Time Series Analysis
summary: We present Zeus, a unified tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that delivers superior performance across diverse analysis tasks without any task-specific fine-tuning. Unlike prior studies that primarily focus on zero-shot forecasting but require task-specific tuning for other tasks, Zeus bridges this gap by addressing two fundamental challenges in multi-task generalization. First, to reconcile point-level granularity with long-sequence scalability, Zeus incorporates a multi-scale Transformer featuring point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, effectively balancing fine-grained fidelity with computational efficiency. Second, to accommodate varying inductive biases across different tasks, Zeus introduces Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM), a unified strategy that supports heterogeneous tasks (e.g., extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction) within a single framework. Extensive experiments across five representative tasks demonstrate that Zeus consistently achieves competitive results in tuning-free settings, underscoring its potential as a general-purpose TSFM.

AI.tldr: Zeus is a tuning-free Time Series Foundation Model (TSFM) that unifies multiple tasks without task-specific fine-tuning, combining a multi-scale Transformer with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchy, plus Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM) to handle extrapolation, interpolation, and global abstraction within a single framework.
AI.motivation: The field requires a single model capable of diverse time-series analysis without task-specific tuning, addressing (i) balancing point-level fidelity with long-sequence scalability and (ii) accommodating different inductive biases across tasks.
AI.method: Introduce a multi-scale Transformer with point-wise tokenization and a U-shaped hierarchical design to reconcile granularity and efficiency. Propose Multi-Objective Temporal Masking (MOTM) to support heterogeneous tasks (extrapolation, interpolation, global abstraction) in one framework. Train and evaluate in a tuning-free regime across five representative tasks.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation across five tasks shows Zeus achieves competitive performance in tuning-free settings, indicating strong multi-task generalization without task-specific fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: Zeus demonstrates strong potential as a general-purpose Time Series Foundation Model, effectively bridging zero-shot forecasting with other analyses via its multi-scale architecture and MOTM strategy.

title: Coding-agents can replicate scientific machine learning papers
summary: Scientific machine learning papers typically make computational claims, e.g., that the relative mean square error is less than 5% or that the 95% predictive credible interval covers the test data. A coding agent can be prompted to replicate those claims from paper materials alone, but the prompt does not by itself reliably preserve progress or check whether generated evidence supports the paper's claims. We introduce Paper-replication, a workflow that makes each selected paper claim a target with recorded evidence, and implement it as a coding-agent skill. The workflow makes the agent record those targets, reconstruct the paper's method, run computational experiments, link generated outputs to provenance and comparisons with the paper's claims, record where matched evidence appears in the replication report, and pass validation checks before completion. We evaluate Paper-replication on twelve independent runs across four scientific machine learning papers. All twelve workspaces pass the completion gate, and all 158 recorded targets are matched with report coverage. Even in this completed workspace state, repeated runs differ in how papers are divided into targets, in numerical fidelity to the source papers, in elapsed replication time, in the number of intermediate executions replaced before final evidence is accepted, and in the rules used to accept evidence. Paper-replication makes completion depend on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than on the agent's final message.

AI.tldr: A coding-agent workflow, Paper-replication, converts paper claims into verifiable, provenance-tied targets and validates evidence via replication runs.
AI.motivation: To make computational ML claims verifiable and reproducible by anchoring progress to recorded evidence and automated checks.
AI.method: Identify targets from claims; reconstruct methods; run experiments; link outputs to provenance; compare results to claims; enforce completion gates; accumulate report coverage.
AI.result: Twelve independent runs across four papers; 158 targets matched; all workspaces passed; observed variability in partitioning, fidelity, time, intermediate steps, and evidence rules; completion is evidence-driven.
AI.conclusion: Reproducibility becomes dependent on workspace evidence and validation checks rather than the final agent message.

title: Conditional Co-Ablation: Recovering Self-Repair Backups in Transformer Circuits
summary: Mechanistic interpretability often relies on component-level interventions to discover how a model produces a behavior. This guides attribution, capability knockout, and model pruning downstream to operate by scoring each unit by the effect of ablation in isolation. Such first-order scoring is natural when component importance is additive, but becomes misleading when a transformer self-repairs: after a primary component is removed, a dormant backup can take over, muting the primary's measured effect while the backup itself appears irrelevant on the intact model. We recast this failure as a recovery task, conditional circuit completion, and introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free, output-grounded score that asks how much each remaining unit's ablation effect grows once a primary set has been removed. This conditional growth exposes the second-order interaction that single-unit scores discard. On the GPT-2-small IOI circuit, CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC, outperforming all baselines, including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82); counterfactual patching verifies that the recovered heads causally carry the repair. The same label-free procedure transfers to induction across eight models. Beyond discovery, the recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution, identify the components required for capability knockout, and yield repair-aware structured pruning scaling from 124M to 7B. Component importance is therefore not merely an isolated-unit property: in robust circuits, the components that matter can become visible only under the interventions that make them necessary.

AI.tldr: CoAx (Conditional Co-Ablation) is a label-free, output-grounded scoring method for mechanistic interpretability that reveals second-order interactions by measuring how ablation effects of remaining units grow after removing a primary set; it exposes dormant backups, improves recovery metrics, and enables repair-aware pruning across multiple models.
AI.motivation: First-order ablation scores fail in the presence of self-repair through dormant backups, misidentifying component importance. A second-order, conditionally grown ablation score can reveal these backups and guide interventions such as knockout and pruning.
AI.method: Introduce Conditional Co-Ablation (CoAx), a label-free score that assesses the growth of ablation effects on remaining units after removing a primary set (conditional growth). The score is output-grounded and does not require ground-truth intervention labels. Validate on GPT-2-small IOI circuit, compare to self-repair-aware gradient scores and baselines, use counterfactual patching to verify causal repair, and transfer to eight models for induction tasks.
AI.result: CoAx raises backup-head recovery from 0.33 to 0.91 ROC-AUC on GPT-2-small IOI circuit, outperforming baselines including self-repair-aware gradient scores (best 0.82). Counterfactual patching confirms causal repair by the recovered heads. The procedure transfers to induction across eight models and supports repair-aware structured pruning, scaling from 124M to 7B. Recovered backups correct self-repair-masked attribution and identify components needed for capability knockout.
AI.conclusion: In robust circuits, component importance is revealed only under specific interventions; second-order interactions matter and can be uncovered via conditional growth scoring, enabling better discovery, knockout design, and pruning across models.

title: A$^{2}$utoLPBench: An Auto-Generated, Agent-Friendly LP Benchmark via Inverse-KKT Construction
summary: Most LP-from-text benchmarks are static datasets of word problems written and labeled by hand. Once such a dataset is released, its size is fixed, its difficulty is fixed, and every problem can leak into the training data of future LLMs. We present \textbf{A$^{2}$utoLPBench}, a benchmark for testing LLM-driven agents on linear programming problems written in plain text. We first pick a feasible point and dual, then write down a problem for which that point is optimal and the objective value is known. The answer is known by construction, with no solver call and no human annotator. The evaluation environment bundles a reference solver-critic baseline and a Docker image whose usage instructions are written for an LLM-driven agent to read. With these in place, any agent can run the benchmark and get a calibrated score with one command. Because the benchmark is a generator rather than a fixed dataset, it has properties no fixed dataset can match: an unlimited supply of fresh problems, a difficulty knob set by $(n,m)$, ground-truth answers correct by construction, low LLM-side cost per problem relative to human authoring, repeatable scores across independent batches, and resistance to training-data leakage when fresh post-cutoff seed ranges are used.

AI.tldr: A2utoLPBench is a generator-based benchmark for LP-from-text that constructs problems with known optima, enabling solver-free ground-truth and calibrated scoring. It provides a Docker-based evaluation environment, unbounded problem generation, and resistance to data leakage, with difficulty controlled by problem dimensions (n, m).
AI.motivation: Current LP-from-text benchmarks are static, leak-prone, and annotator-dependent. A generator-based benchmark with provable ground-truth and reproducible scoring offers scalable, leakage-resistant evaluation for LLM-driven agents.
AI.method: For each instance, pick a feasible point and a dual, then construct a linear program in which that point is optimal and the objective value is known; no solver or human annotation is required. The environment includes a reference solver-critic baseline and Docker usage instructions so an LLM-driven agent can run with one command. Difficulty is adjustable via problem dimensions (n, m).
AI.result: A scalable, fresh, calibration-friendly benchmark that yields ground-truth answers by construction, enables low per-problem human cost, supports repeatable scores across batches, and resists training-data leakage via seed-based problem generation.
AI.conclusion: A2utoLPBench offers advantages over fixed datasets by providing unlimited, difficulty-controllable, leakage-resistant LP-from-text benchmarks with readily runnable evaluation setup and calibrated scoring for LLM-driven agents.

title: Assessing VLM Reliability for Medical Image Quality Evaluation Under Corruption and Bias
summary: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are increasingly applied in medical tasks such as pathology description, report generation, and visual question answering. Medical Image Quality Assessment (MIQA) supports diagnostic accuracy and patient safety by determining whether images meet the standards required for clinical decision-making. Automating MIQA with VLMs may reduce workload, but their behavior under real-world conditions, where images may be degraded or textual context may affect judgments, should be further explored before deployment. We benchmark VLMs on medical image quality using the MediMeta-C dataset zero-shot across seven corruption types and five severity levels. We evaluate sensitivity to degradation patterns, the effect of corruptions on embedding geometry, and whether textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution) alter scores. Across 16 VLMs and seven modalities, pixelation produced the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%, up to -34.4% for OCT), whereas brightness had limited effect (-0.81%). Embedding displacement was associated with score changes. Same-family models showed correlations of 0.67-0.83; some produced increases up to +31% for corrupted mammography. Textual attributes affected scores: institutional prestige raised them +17.15%, and equipment age lowered them -14.7%. The largest changes were +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma). Current VLMs show limitations for medical image quality assessment. Pixelation, a privacy-preserving transformation, reduces performance, indicating a trade-off between patient privacy and reliability. Sensitivity to contextual metadata indicates limited objectivity and marks metadata as a privacy and bias source. Privacy protection and objective quality assessment are related requirements for use.

AI.tldr: VLMs are not reliably objective for medical image quality assessment under degradation or contextual metadata; pixelation harms performance; text attributes can bias scores; privacy vs. objective QA is a key trade-off.
AI.motivation: MIQA supports diagnostic safety; automating with VLMs could reduce workload but requires robustness to real-world degradation and contextual cues.
AI.method: Zero-shot evaluation on MediMeta-C across 7 corruption types and 5 severities; 16 VLMs, 7 modalities; analyze sensitivity to degradations, embedding geometry shifts, and influence of textual attributes (demographics, expertise, infrastructure, institution).
AI.result: Pixelation yielded the largest score reductions (mean -20.58%; up to -34.4% for OCT); brightness effects minimal (-0.81%). Embedding displacement associated with score changes. Same-family models showed correlations (0.67–0.83); some increased up to +31% for corrupted mammography. Textual attributes affected scores: institutional prestige +17.15%, equipment age -14.7%. Largest changes: +95.62% (InternVL-8B) and -37.7% (MedGemma). Pixelation, a privacy-preserving transform, reduces performance; context metadata can bias scores, signaling limited objectivity.
AI.conclusion: Current VLMs show limitations for MIQA; privacy-preserving transformations trade off reliability; metadata introduces bias; need privacy-protective yet objective MIQA approaches and careful handling of contextual attributes.

title: Hybrid quantum-classical neural network for sentiment analysis
summary: Quantum machine learning has recently emerged as a promising paradigm that leverages the expressive power of quantum circuits to address complex learning tasks. In this work, we investigate the applicability of hybrid quantum-classical neural networks to sentiment analysis, a central problem in natural language processing. We focus on a dataset of tweets related to COVID-19, where the textual content is vectorized using TF-IDF and fed into both classical feedforward networks and hybrid architectures incorporating parameterized quantum circuits. Our results show that hybrid models can achieve accuracy comparable to the classical baseline, while exhibiting distinct learning dynamics, especially in terms of validation loss and accuracy, that suggest a richer representational capacity. Moreover, when applying transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task, the hybrid models consistently outperform the classical counterpart, achieving an accuracy increase of 15 percentage points (from 66% to 81%) on the spam class, demonstrating enhanced generalization. These findings highlight the feasibility of employing QML for natural language processing and point toward the potential advantages of hybrid models as quantum hardware continues to advance.

AI.tldr: Hybrid quantum-classical neural networks for NLP show comparable sentiment-analysis accuracy to classical models and improved generalization on SMS spam with transfer learning, indicating potential representational advantages of QML as hardware advances.
AI.motivation: Assess whether hybrid quantum-classical architectures can enhance NLP tasks by enriching feature representations via parameterized quantum circuits.
AI.method: Vectorize text with TF-IDF; compare classical feedforward networks to hybrid models incorporating parameterized quantum circuits; evaluate on COVID-19 tweet sentiment analysis; apply transfer learning to an SMS spam classification task.
AI.result: Hybrid models achieve accuracy comparable to classical baselines in sentiment analysis, with distinct learning dynamics in validation metrics suggesting richer representations; on SMS spam, hybrids outperform classical models, improving spam-class accuracy from 66% to 81% (a 15-point gain).
AI.conclusion: The results indicate the feasibility of quantum-assisted machine learning for NLP and potential generalization benefits of hybrid models as quantum hardware advances.

title: A rubric-based controlled comparison of frontier language models on expert-authored clinical reasoning tasks
summary: Multiple-choice medical benchmarks are increasingly saturated, and recent rubric-based evaluations such as HealthBench have shown that open-ended clinical performance is far from solved - its "Hard" subset top score remains 32%. We present a small, deliberately difficult evaluation dataset of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios spanning four specialties (anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, and obstetrics), each accompanied by an atomic, weighted, MECE rubric (25-62 criteria per task; 184 criteria total) authored from a clinician-drafted golden answer. We evaluate three frontier models: GPT 5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, and Gemini 3.1 Pro. Mean rubric pass rates were 0.47 (Claude), 0.39 (GPT), and 0.37 (Gemini). The central finding is an inversion of clinical priority: the highest-weighted (weight-5, critical) criteria passed at only 32.4-41.7%, while low-stakes weight-1 criteria passed at 80-90%. 56 of 108 critical (weight-5) criteria (52%) were satisfied by no model. Three LLM autoraters reproduced expert met/not-met labels on 92.8-94.7% of 552 graded criteria. We position this as a methods-and-preliminary-findings contribution: the five tasks demonstrate a scalable, defensible pipeline ready to develop into a large-scale benchmark.

AI.tldr: Small, deliberate benchmark of five clinician-authored clinical scenarios with a weighted MECE rubric to assess open-ended clinical reasoning; three frontier LLMs show limited coverage on high-weight criteria, enabling a scalable pipeline for larger benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Address saturation of MCQ benchmarks and gaps in open-ended clinical reasoning evaluation; establish a defensible, granular, clinician-authored dataset and rubric to probe critical decision criteria.
AI.method: Five clinician-authored tasks across anaesthesia, internal/family medicine, emergency medicine, obstetrics; each task annotated with an atomic, weighted MECE rubric (total 184 criteria, 25-62 per task). Evaluated GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3.1 Pro; three LLM autoraters labeled criteria; compute pass rates.
AI.result: Mean rubric pass rates: Claude 0.47, GPT 0.39, Gemini 0.37. High-weight criteria (weight-5) pass rate 32.4-41.7%; weight-1 criteria pass 80-90%. 56 of 108 weight-5 criteria (52%) unmet by all models. Autoraters replicated expert labels with 92.8-94.7% agreement across 552 graded criteria.
AI.conclusion: Demonstrates a scalable, defensible pipeline for small-scale benchmarking that can be expanded; highlights strong performance gaps on critical criteria and the value of clinician-authored rubrics for evaluating open-ended clinical reasoning.

title: MolSight: A Graph-Aware Vision-Language Model for Unified Chemical Image Understanding
summary: Using molecular large language models (LLMs) as a unified framework for understanding molecular structures and functions is emerging as a new trend in tasks such as molecular design and drug discovery. However, these models struggle to fully capture the visual representation of molecular structures, limiting their potential. While existing molecular vision-language models (VLMs) show promise, they still face challenges in structural alignment and lack the necessary topological modeling for accurate molecular understanding. To address this, we propose MolSight, a graph-aware vision-language model framework designed to enhance the understanding of molecular images by VLMs. MolSight integrates a Molecular Topology Module to inject chemical-bond adjacency information into vision tokens, and a Molecular Grounding Module to align visual features with chemical symbolic semantics. Our experiments demonstrate that MolSight significantly outperforms existing VLMs, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving a new level of molecular image reasoning.

AI.tldr: MolSight is a graph-aware vision-language framework for molecules that injects bond topology into vision tokens and grounds visual features to chemical semantics, achieving state-of-the-art performance on chemical visual understanding tasks.
AI.motivation: Current molecular LLMs underperform in visually understanding molecular structures due to inadequate visual representations; vision-only and VLM approaches lack explicit topology and reliable alignment between visuals and chemical semantics, hindering molecular design and discovery.
AI.method: MolSight comprises two key modules: (1) Molecular Topology Module, which injects chemical-bond adjacency information into vision tokens to encode molecular graph structure; (2) Molecular Grounding Module, which aligns visual features with chemical symbolic semantics to improve cross-modal understanding. It is a graph-aware vision-language framework designed to enhance molecular image understanding.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows MolSight significantly outperforms existing vision-language models, molecular LLMs, and specialized tools across multiple chemical visual understanding tasks, achieving a new level of molecular image reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating topology-aware tokenization and semantic grounding into a VLM enables more accurate molecular image understanding and reasoning, suggesting a path forward for unified molecular perception and design tools.

title: A More Accurate Algorithm Comparison through A/B Testing using Offline Evaluation Methods
summary: A/B testing is the gold standard for selecting the better algorithm in online services. While offline evaluation has attracted attention as a safer alternative due to the high experimental costs and the potential risk of degrading user experience and revenue in A/B testing, it is widely recognized that the estimation accuracy of offline evaluation is substantially lower. As a result, final selection decisions are typically made through A/B testing. Contrary to this conventional view, we reveal a counterintuitive phenomenon in which A/B testing can produce a higher algorithm selection error rate than offline evaluation. This occurs because the sample mean estimator used in A/B testing does not induce positive correlation, which is crucial for reducing critical selection errors, namely underestimating the truly superior algorithm and overestimating the truly inferior one. In contrast, offline evaluation methods unintentionally generate this beneficial correlation by relying on shared offline data when estimating and comparing the performance of multiple algorithms. Building on this insight, we propose an estimator that intentionally induces positive correlation to improve algorithm selection in A/B testing. The key idea is to introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm and to estimate the performance difference between algorithms A, M, and B in a stepwise manner using shared data at each step. This approach enables the application of offline evaluation techniques in each step, thereby inducing positive correlation and reducing critical selection errors. Furthermore, we derive the optimal middle algorithm regarding the resulting variance and analyze its advantages over existing methods through bias-variance analysis. Experiments on real-world data demonstrate that our estimator achieves the same selection error rate as existing approaches while using only one half of the A/B testing data.

AI.tldr: Correlation-aware A/B testing estimator using a hypothetical middle algorithm to enable stepwise offline-like evaluation, achieving comparable selection error with half the A/B data.
AI.motivation: A/B testing is costly and risky; offline evaluation is safer but tends to be less accurate. A surprising finding: A/B can incur higher algorithm-selection error due to lack of positive correlation between estimates. Inducing positive correlation can reduce critical errors in selection.
AI.method: Introduce a hypothetical middle algorithm M and estimate performance differences among A, M, B in a stepwise manner using shared data. Apply offline-evaluation techniques at each step to induce positive correlation. Derive the optimal M by minimizing variance and perform a bias-variance analysis.
AI.result: The proposed estimator attains the same algorithm-selection error rate as existing methods but uses only half of the A/B testing data, as demonstrated on real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: Intentionally inducing positive correlation between evaluations improves algorithm selection; the approach bridges offline and online evaluation, reducing data requirements and offering a practical path to safer, cheaper model selection. Future work includes extending to more than three algorithms and dynamic settings.

title: UA-ChatDev: Uncertainty-Aware Multi-Agent Collaboration for Reliable Software Development
summary: Software development is a complex task that demands cooperation among agents with diverse roles. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled autonomous multi-agent software development frameworks that leverage role-based collaboration to automate requirements analysis, coding, testing, and refinement. However, existing approaches typically assume that intermediate agent outputs are equally reliable, leaving them vulnerable to hallucination propagation, where incorrect decisions generated in early development phases are transferred to downstream agents and negatively impact final software quality. To address this challenge, we propose UA-ChatDev, an uncertainty-aware multi-agent software development framework that integrates uncertainty quantification into agent interactions. It introduces a lightweight uncertainty estimation mechanism based on token-level log probabilities to assess the confidence of agent responses and employs phase-aware threshold calibration to selectively trigger retrieval-based verification when uncertainty exceeds acceptable levels.
