We argue that the same methods used for decades to manage large human engineering teams: access control, network policies, strict coding conventions enforced by tooling; transfer directly to coding agents, and are cheaper (in token) than recent agentic scaffolding. We sketch a start-to-end system on this principle, and report a controlled experiment in scalable oversight: a small reviewer (Gemma 4 e4b) inspects a Python codebase containing 11 inserted backdoors. Recall rises from 54.5% (unconstrained, no tools) to 90.9% (constrained substrate plus a ~200-LoC `docs` CLI), with substrate and tools contributing independently. We choose Python deliberately: substrate-level oversight gains are largest where the language gives the fewest guarantees by default; the principles extend to languages like Rust.

AI.tldr: Govern coding agents via traditional software-engineering governance; constrained oversight significantly improves recall of backdoors in Python code; substrate plus tooling contribute independently; results generalize to Rust; cheaper than agent scaffolding.
AI.motivation: Human oversight is a bottleneck; unconstrained agents pose security and scalability risks; apply access control, network policies, and tooling enforcement to coding agents; demonstrate efficacy via controlled experiment.
AI.method: Propose an end-to-end governance substrate; enforce access controls and conventions; implement a ~200-line CLI tool (docs); conduct controlled experiment with a reviewer inspecting a Python codebase with 11 backdoors; measure recall.
AI.result: Recall improved from 54.5% unconstrained/no tools to 90.9% with constrained substrate plus docs CLI; substrate and tools contribute independently.
AI.conclusion: Principles extend to languages like Rust; governance-based oversight is most impactful where the language provides weak guarantees by default; the approach is cheaper in token usage than expansive agent scaffolding.

title: PWM-ArtGen: Part World Model for Articulated Object Generation
summary: The key challenge in articulated 3D object generation from a single image is accurately predicting the underlying kinematic structure. Existing methods either infer kinematic parameters directly from a static image that lacks dynamic part-level kinematic relationships, or estimate parameters from visual dynamics generated from a single image, which is prone to accumulated errors of two steps. Moreover, the limited scale and diversity of existing annotated datasets further hinder generalization to complex, real-world objects. To overcome these limitations, we propose to learn the joint distribution of visual dynamics and kinematic parameters. Recognizing that articulated objects can be formulated as dynamic systems, we propose a unified Part World Model called PWM-ArtGen. To leverage unannotated data, this model couples action diffusion and image diffusion with independent diffusion timesteps, which enables visual branch co-training. We further curate a photorealistic dataset of 19.7k part-level image pairs without kinematic annotations, to support co-training. Experiments demonstrate that PWM-ArtGen substantially outperforms existing baselines in the resting state and exhibits strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects.

AI.tldr: A unified diffusion-based framework (PWM-ArtGen) learns joint visual dynamics and kinematic parameters for articulated 3D object generation from a single image, enabling co-training with unannotated data and showing strong resting-state performance and zero-shot generalization; a new 19.7k part-level image-pair dataset supports this.
AI.motivation: Overcome two main limitations: (i) static-image inferences lack part-level kinematic structure and (ii) single-image dynamics approximations accumulate errors. Also address limited annotated data that hinders generalization to real-world articulated objects.
AI.method: Introduce Part World Model (PWM-ArtGen) that treats articulated objects as dynamic systems. Couple action diffusion (for kinematic/interaction dynamics) and image diffusion (for visual dynamics) with independent diffusion timesteps to enable co-training on unannotated data. Curate a photorealistic 19.7k part-level image-pair dataset without kinematic annotations to support co-training.
AI.result: Experiments indicate substantial improvement over baselines in resting state and strong zero-shot generalization to out-of-distribution objects, demonstrating improved generalization and robustness without requiring dense kinematic annotations.
AI.conclusion: A diffusion-based, joint modeling approach with unannotated-data co-training and a targeted dataset yields better articulated 3D object generation from a single image, especially in resting-state behavior and cross-domain generalization; suggests promise for broader dynamic-structure inference tasks.

title: Ask the Right Comparison:Bias-Aware Bayesian Active Top-$k$ Ranking with LLM Judges
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as cheap, scalable judges that compare candidate outputs pairwise -- to rank responses, select models, or triage papers. Yet LLM judges are both noisy and systematically biased: they favor verbose or well-formatted answers and exhibit position effects, so simply aggregating their votes recovers a ranking of presentation, not of true quality. We study the practical goal of identifying the \topk{} items under a fixed comparison budget, and make two contributions. First, we cast judging as Bayesian inference over latent quality with explicit, judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position), regularized by a shrinkage prior so that the data decide which biases a given judge actually exhibits. Second, we introduce a \topk-aware active acquisition rule that chooses the next comparison to maximally reduce uncertainty about \topk{} \emph{membership}, rather than about the full ranking. On a controlled benchmark with known ground-truth quality, judged by sixteen real LLMs spanning open and proprietary families (Llama, Qwen, Phi-4, GPT-4o-mini/5.1/5.5, Gemini, DeepSeek, and Claude Haiku/Sonnet/Opus), naive aggregation plateaus at a wrong \topk{} on biased judges regardless of budget, while our bias-aware model recovers it; \topk-aware acquisition reaches this ceiling with far fewer comparisons than round-robin or a global-uncertainty (D-optimal) rule. Bias is real but heterogeneous and capability-dependent: cheap and mid-tier judges carry a strong verbosity bias that our model corrects (lifting recall from $\sim$$0.5$--$0.6$ to $0.84$--$1.0$), whereas the frontier judges we tested show little bias and already rank accurately, so bias-aware modeling changes little there.

AI.tldr: A bias-aware Bayesian framework for top-k selection under biased LLM judges, with a top-k–oriented active query policy; shows that correcting judge biases (verbosity/position) enables accurate top-k identification with far fewer comparisons; frontier judges show little bias; cheap judges suffer strong verbosity bias.
AI.motivation: LLMs used as judges produce noisy rankings biased by presentation; naive aggregation fails to identify true top-k under budget constraints; need efficient, bias-corrected methods.
AI.method: Bayesian latent-quality model with judge-specific bias covariates (verbosity, position) regularized by shrinkage priors; top-k–aware active acquisition that selects comparisons to reduce uncertainty about top-k membership rather than full ranking.
AI.result: On a benchmark with 16 LLMs across families, naive aggregation fails to identify correct top-k under bias; bias-aware model recovers true top-k; top-k–aware acquisition requires fewer comparisons than round-robin or D-opt; bias exists and varies by judge; cheap judges show strong verbosity bias; frontier judges have little bias; recall improved from ~0.5-0.6 to 0.84-1.0 for cheap judges.
AI.conclusion: Bias-aware modeling is essential for reliable top-k identification with LLM judges; heterogeneity of bias implies tailored strategies per judge; top-k acquisition enhances efficiency; results advocate integrating bias-covariate modeling in LLM-based evaluation pipelines.

title: Fast Multi-dimensional Refusal Subspaces via RFM-AGOP
comment: Accepted to the Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea, 2026
summary: Steering and monitoring activations in Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used for both safety and interpretability. Early work assumed behaviours are encoded along single linear directions, but recent findings suggest complex behaviours, such as the refusal to answer harmful queries, live in multi-dimensional subspaces. However, existing methods for extracting these subspaces are computationally expensive, which becomes prohibitive on reasoning models who produce long reasoning traces. By adapting the Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) algorithm -- which can be computed efficiently -- with a probe-informed initialization, we are able to identify the multi-dimensional refusal subspace in seconds, on reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models. While RFM allows for faster subspace identification, it also showed better performances on the ablation task than its alternatives. More work is planned to better understand the relations between subspaces found by different methods. If confirmed, RFM could be a cheap and scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods in LLMs.

AI.tldr: Efficiently identify multi-dimensional refusal subspaces in LLMs using an adapted Recursive Feature Machine (RFM) with probe-informed initialization, enabling fast analysis on reasoning and non-reasoning models and showing competitive ablation performance.
AI.motivation: Understanding safety/interpretability in LLMs requires moving beyond single linear directions; evidence suggests that harmful refusals live in multi-dimensional subspaces, but existing extraction methods are computationally expensive for long reasoning traces.
AI.method: Adapt RFM, a computationally efficient subspace extraction algorithm, with probe-informed initialization; apply to LLMs (Qwen 3 and Qwen 2.5) to identify refusal subspaces.
AI.result: The multi-dimensional refusal subspace is identified in seconds on both reasoning (Qwen 3) and non-reasoning (Qwen 2.5) models; RFM shows better ablation performance than alternatives.
AI.conclusion: RFM offers a cheap, scalable complement to existing subspace-extraction methods for LLMs; further work needed to compare subspaces across methods and understand relationships between subspaces found by different approaches.

title: Embracing Intra-Class Heterogeneity for Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation: From Diversity to Precision
summary: Due to the scarcity of expert-annotated data, Semi-Supervised Medical Image Segmentation (SSMIS) has emerged as a promising approach. Many anatomical structures in medical images exhibit significant intra-class heterogeneity, with different regions showing heterogeneous intensity patterns within the same structure. However, existing methods inadequately exploit this intensity-manifested intra-class heterogeneity, resulting in uniform structural representations and imprecise segmentation. Furthermore, the scarcity of labeled data makes it more difficult to effectively capture such complex heterogeneity. To address this, we propose Multiple Prototype Contrastive Learning (MPCL), an SSMIS framework that possesses better diversity and better precision. It consists of three novel designs: First, we provide structural representations with better diversity and propose Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) that effectively models intra-class heterogeneity by generating multiple prototypes aligned with intensity characteristics. Second, we further enhance more diverse structural representations and build a solid foundation for more precise segmentation through Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) that systematically optimizes a more discriminative and generalizable prototypical space. Finally, we achieve segmentation results with better precision through Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) that efficiently promotes intra-class heterogeneity knowledge transfer from prototypical space to the segmentation network. Extensive experiments on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity demonstrate that MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods, especially under extremely limited labeled data.

AI.tldr: MPCL introduces a three-component semi-supervised segmentation framework that uses multiple intensity-aligned prototypes, prototypical space optimization, and dual-branch knowledge alignment to capture intra-class heterogeneity and improve segmentation with scarce labels.
AI.motivation: Medical images often exhibit strong intra-class heterogeneity in intensity within the same structure, and labeled data are scarce, leading to uniform representations and poor segmentation; current SSMIS methods underutilize intensity-driven diversity.
AI.method: Three designs: (1) Intensity-aligned Heterogeneous Prototype Generation (IHPG) to create multiple prototypes aligned with intensity characteristics; (2) Prototypical Space Optimization (PSO) to build a more discriminative, generalizable prototypical space; (3) Dual-branch Knowledge Alignment (DKA) to transfer intra-class heterogeneity knowledge from the prototypical space to the segmentation network.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three medical image datasets with significant intra-class heterogeneity show MPCL significantly outperforms existing methods, especially when labeled data is extremely limited.
AI.conclusion: MPCL enhances diversity and precision in semi-supervised medical image segmentation by leveraging multiple intensity-aligned prototypes and principled prototypical space alignment, enabling better performance under label scarcity.

title: Predictive Conformal Slip Monitoring: An Empirical Evaluation of Rolling Split Conformal Prediction for Pre-Incident Traction Loss Detection
comment: 10 pages, 4 tables. codes and data available at:https://github.com/nearpot/predictive-conformal-slip-monitoring
summary: Conventional traction control architectures intervene only after the adhesion limit of a tire has already been breached. This paper investigates whether Rolling Split Conformal Prediction , monitoring the volatility of non-conformity residuals from a per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip behavior , can serve as a statistically grounded pre-incident warning signal, ahead of gross traction loss. Unlike an earlier internal draft of this work, the evaluation reported here corrects a confound in the slip proxy (vehicle speed is included as an explicit model feature, not left implicit in the target's denominator), uses every racing lap for each driver rather than only the fastest lap, and is scored against real, timestamped incident labels extracted from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limits lap deletions rather than narrated post-hoc. The result is negative: across 19 drivers and 55,563 test-phase telemetry samples, the rolling-volatility detector achieves a mean precision of essentially 0.0 and mean recall of 0.0 against 14 ground-truth incidents, while flagging on average 15.3% of all samples as anomalous , too high a false-alarm rate for any early-warning use. A static 95th-percentile threshold baseline performs no better in any way that would justify the added complexity of the conformal-volatility formulation. Residual autocorrelation diagnostics show the split-conformal exchangeability assumption is violated for every driver (Ljung-Box p < 0.001, n = 19/19), which is one plausible driver of the high false-alarm rate. We report this as a methodologically rigorous negative finding, diagnose its likely causes, and outline what a genuinely predictive version of this approach would require.

AI.tldr: Negative findings: rolling conformal-volatility fails as an early warning in racing traction control; high false alarms, no predictive gain; exchangeability violated; static threshold baseline not improved.
AI.motivation: Assess viability of a rolling split-conformal prediction (volatility of non-conformity residuals) as a pre-incident warning signal for traction loss in racing, correcting prior confounds and using timestamped FIA incident labels.
AI.method: Per-driver Random Forest model of expected slip; include vehicle speed as explicit feature; compute non-conformity residuals; monitor rolling volatility with split-conformal framework; evaluate on 19 drivers, 55,563 test samples; ground truth from FIA Race Control Messages and track-limit deletions; compare against a static 95th-percentile threshold baseline; diagnose residual autocorrelation (Ljung-Box) to test exchangeability.
AI.result: Mean precision ≈ 0.0; mean recall ≈ 0.0 across 14 incidents; anomalous flag rate ~15.3% of samples (high false alarms); static threshold baseline performs no better; Ljung-Box p < 0.001 for all drivers, indicating violation of exchangeability; negative but methodologically rigorous with diagnosed causes.
AI.conclusion: The approach, as tested, does not provide a useful early warning signal and highlights that conformal-volatility methods require strong exchangeability and stationarity; future work should address non-stationarity, time-varying distributions, per-driver heterogeneity, and alternate features or modeling strategies to achieve predictive power.

title: Text-Driven 3D Indoor Scene Synthesis in Non-Manhattan Environments
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in 3D indoor synthesis for Manhattan environments. However, existing methods often fail to capture plausible object layout patterns in non-Manhattan settings, primarily because they struggle to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, leading to high geometric violations and low physical fidelity. To address this challenge, we propose SPG-Layout, a novel text-driven framework designed to generate physically plausible indoor scenes within complex non-Manhattan environments. Specifically, we first utilize statistical priors of object distributions to guide the training process, enhancing environmental understanding and fidelity. Furthermore, mirroring human design workflows, we adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that prioritizes the placement of large objects, thereby substantially minimizing layout violations. By synergizing these components, SPG-Layout achieves a balanced optimization of semantic realism and physical plausibility. To evaluate performance in these complex settings, we constructed a new benchmark comprising 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods across both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments. The code will be publicly released.

AI.tldr: SPG-Layout is a text-driven framework that generates physically plausible 3D indoor layouts in non-Manhattan environments by using statistical priors and a hierarchical large-object-first placement strategy, outperforming existing methods on a new 500-scene benchmark; code will be released.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based 3D indoor synthesis struggles to model non-orthogonal spatial relationships, resulting in geometric violations and reduced physical fidelity in non-Manhattan spaces. There is a need for methods that capture non-Manhattan layouts and enhance layout plausibility.
AI.method: Introduce SPG-Layout with two core components: (1) use statistical priors of object distributions to guide training and improve environmental understanding, and (2) adopt a hierarchical layout strategy that places large objects first, mirroring human design workflows, to reduce layout violations. The framework is text-driven and evaluated on a newly constructed benchmark of 500 diverse non-Manhattan environments.
AI.result: SPG-Layout consistently and significantly outperforms existing methods in both Manhattan and non-Manhattan environments on the new benchmark. The authors will publicly release the code.
AI.conclusion: Combining statistical priors with a hierarchical, large-object-first placement strategy in a text-driven framework yields a better balance between semantic realism and physical plausibility for 3D indoor layout synthesis in complex non-Manhattan environments.

title: Comprehensive Robustness Analysis of LiDAR-based 3D Object Detection in Autonomous Driving
summary: Recent advancements in LiDAR-only 3D object detection have demonstrated improved detection accuracy over benchmark datasets. However, the adversarial robustness of these models remains untested. Very few adversarial robustness studies exist for LiDAR-only 3D object detection and unfortunately, even they are limited to legacy models. Moreover, there is a systemic gap in the existing evaluation frameworks that rely simply on mAP ignoring other structural and predictive factors. To fill this gap, we propose a holistic framework that evaluates adversarial robustness using two structural factors (point cloud density and point cloud localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego). Using this framework, we perform an empirical study and critical analysis on recent and legacy state-of-the-art models using adversarial attacks specifically designed for LiDAR-based models. Our key finding is that high-capacity, voxel-based detectors are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations than pillar-based detectors. Additionally, non-anchor-based detectors demonstrate poor adversarial robustness, which necessitates rethinking model training techniques. Overall, our results demonstrate that recent models are as vulnerable to adversarial attacks as their predecessors. Therefore, we argue that there is a need to improve the evaluation benchmarks for 3D object detection that not only reward architectural modifications for improving detection accuracy, but also evaluate whether the design choices improve adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: Holistic adversarial robustness framework for LiDAR-only 3D detectors, comparing modern voxel- and pillar-based designs and legacy models under structured perturbations; finds voxel-based detectors more vulnerable to coordinate perturbations; non-anchor-based detectors exhibit weaker robustness; calls for robustness-aware benchmarks alongside accuracy-focused metrics.
AI.motivation: Despite improved accuracy, LiDAR-only 3D object detectors have largely untested adversarial robustness, with limited studies on legacy models and no comprehensive evaluation that factors both structure (density/localization) and prediction (misclassification, localization error, ego-distance).
AI.method: Introduce a framework evaluating two structural factors (point cloud density and point cloud localization) and three predictive factors (misclassification, localization error, distance from ego), and empirically assess recent and legacy state-of-the-art LiDAR detectors using adversarial attacks tailored for LiDAR models.
AI.result: Voxel-based detectors with high capacity are more susceptible to structured coordinate perturbations; non-anchor-based detectors display poorer overall adversarial robustness; recent models do not show clear robustness gains over legacy ones; evaluation benchmarks should reward robustness in addition to accuracy.
AI.conclusion: A holistic robustness benchmark is needed for 3D object detection to guide model design toward genuine resilience against adversarial manipulation, beyond standard accuracy improvements.

title: ART for Diffusion Sampling: Continuous-Time Control and Actor-Critic Learning
summary: We study timestep allocation for score-based diffusion sampling, where a learned reverse-time dynamics is discretized on a finite grid. Uniform and hand-crafted schedules are standard choices, but they rely on fixed prescriptions and can therefore be suboptimal. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Reparameterized Time (ART), a continuous-time control formulation that learns a time change by treating the speed of the sampling clock as the control, so that a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Based on a leading-order Euler error surrogate, ART provides a principled objective for allocating timesteps along the sampling trajectory. To solve this deterministic control problem, we introduce ART-RL, an auxiliary randomized formulation with Gaussian policies that turns schedule learning into a continuous-time reinforcement learning problem. We prove that the randomized ART-RL formulation is equivalent to ART at the optimizer level, in the sense that its optimal Gaussian policy recovers the optimal ART time-warping rate through its mean. We further establish policy evaluation and policy improvement characterizations and derive trajectory-based moment identities that yield implementable actor--critic updates for learning the schedule. Across experiments ranging from controlled low-dimensional settings to image generation, ART-RL can be plugged into existing diffusion samplers by changing only the timestep grid, consistently improving sample quality over strong baseline schedules at matched budgets while leaving the rest of the sampling pipeline unchanged. The learned schedules also exhibit broad generalization, transferring without retraining across sampling budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces.

AI.tldr: Adaptive time stepping for score-based diffusion using a learned clock; ART optimizes timestep allocation via continuous-time control and a learned time warp; ART-RL reframes this as continuous-time RL with Gaussian policies; yields better sample quality and strong generalization while remaining plug-in to existing samplers.
AI.motivation: Fixed or hand-crafted timesteps in diffusion samplers can be suboptimal, limiting sample quality and efficiency. A principled, learnable timestepping strategy could adapt to trajectory dynamics and budget constraints.
AI.method: Treat the sampling clock speed as a control variable, learning a time change so a uniform grid on the learned clock induces adaptive timesteps in the original diffusion time. Use a leading-order Euler error surrogate to define a principled objective. Solve via ART-RL, a randomized Gaussian-policy formulation of the control problem that is equivalent to ART at the optimum; develop policy evaluation/improvement rules and trajectory-based moment identities for actor–critic updates, enabling implementable schedule learning.
AI.result: ART-RL consistently improves sample quality over strong fixed schedules at matched budgets across low-dimensional and image-generation experiments. The learned schedules generalize broadly, transferring across budgets, datasets, solvers, pipelines, and representation spaces without retraining.
AI.conclusion: Learned adaptive timestepping for diffusion sampling is effective and generalizes across settings; the ART framework provides a principled, plug-in approach with an RL-based instantiation that yields practical schedule improvements.

title: Automated grading of Linux/bash examinations using large language models: a four-level cognitive taxonomy approach
summary: Scalable and reliable grading of command-line examinations remains a challenge in computing education, where rising enrolments make manual marking difficult and rule-based autograders cannot handle partial credit, equivalent solutions, or syntactic variation. This paper evaluates whether four frontier Large Language Models (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, and GLM) can approximate expert judgment when grading short Linux/bash command responses. The study adopts a four-level cognitive taxonomy that combines cognitive complexity and operational impact, ranging from information retrieval (L1) and basic file manipulation (L2) to structural operations (L3) and advanced system management (L4). The models were tested with two prompt variants, a minimal baseline and a rubric-enhanced version, on 1200 real responses from second-year Computer Engineering students independently graded by three expert instructors. Gemini~3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting achieved the highest human-AI agreement (ICC(3,1) = 0.888, MAE = 0.10, Bland-Altman bias = -0.014). Agreement declined consistently as taxonomy level increased, with the largest discrepancies at higher levels. Across all models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider choice, with structured prompts consistently improving agreement. These results show that question complexity is a reliable predictor of the difficulty LLMs face in grading accurately, and they establish a principled, taxonomy-based framework for determining which questions are suitable for AI-assisted grading and which require human review, while also providing a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.

AI.tldr: Frontier LLMs can approximate expert grading of short Linux/bash responses with rubric-guided prompts; Gemini 3.0 Pro achieved the highest agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888, MAE=0.10); reliability drops at higher taxonomy levels; rubric quality matters more than model/provider; provides a taxonomy-based framework and prompts for AI-assisted grading.
AI.motivation: To address scalability challenges in computing education grading (rising enrollments, partial credit, syntactic variation) by evaluating whether LLMs can approximate expert judgments and by establishing a transferable evaluation protocol and rubric-based prompting.
AI.method: Tested four LLMs (GPT, Claude Opus, Gemini, GLM) on 1200 real Linux/bash command responses from second-year Computer Engineering students, each response independently graded by three experts. Used two prompt variants (minimal baseline and rubric-enhanced). Mapped responses to a four-level taxonomy combining cognitive complexity and operational impact. Evaluated human–AI agreement with ICC(3,1), MAE, and Bland-Altman bias. Analyzed effect of rubric quality and model/provider, and reported per-taxonomy performance.
AI.result: Gemini 3.0 Pro with rubric-guided prompting yielded the highest human–AI agreement (ICC(3,1)=0.888; MAE=0.10; Bland-Altman bias=-0.014). Agreement decreased with higher taxonomy levels. Across models, rubric quality had a larger effect than provider, and structured prompts consistently improved agreement. The study establishes that question complexity predicts AI grading difficulty and provides a taxonomy-based framework for determining AI-graded versus human-reviewed items, along with a transferable evaluation protocol and prompt templates.
AI.conclusion: A taxonomy-based framework is effective for selecting questions suitable for AI-assisted grading and guiding when human review is needed. The study offers a transferable evaluation protocol and rubric-guided prompts that enhance AI grading reliability across domains, with attention to increasing difficulty levels.

title: HandsOnWorld: Unconstrained Egocentric Video Generation with Camera-Disentangled Hand Control
summary: We present HandsOnWorld, a framework for hand-controlled egocentric video generation that forgoes multi-view and marker-based motion capture, learning instead from unconstrained monocular video. Such generality is bottlenecked by the scarcity of scalable 3D hand annotations: large egocentric corpora lack finger-level labels, whereas precise hand datasets are confined to narrow, instrumented settings, limiting prior hand-controlled generators to restricted scene distributions. We instead annotate 3D hands directly on in-the-wild egocentric video through monocular reconstruction, introducing a protagonist-centered annotation pipeline that filters the reconstructions at the action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels to build EgoVid-Pro, a dataset of clean, protagonist-only hand trajectories spanning 103K clips and roughly 12M frames across diverse everyday scenes. To resolve the camera-hand entanglement induced by large ego-motion, we further propose the Plücker Hand Map, a 3D-aware control signal that extends Plücker-ray representations from camera rays to the hand surface, disentangling camera and hand motion at the representation level. Experiments show that \method surpasses prior hand-controlled generators in reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy, and generalizes to out-of-distribution everyday scenes beyond the laboratory datasets on which prior methods rely.

AI.tldr: A monocular, ego-centric hand-control framework (HandsOnWorld) learns from unconstrained video to generate hand-controlled egocentric video without markers, supported by a large 3D hand dataset (EgoVid-Pro) and a Plücker Hand Map to disentangle camera and hand motion; it outperforms prior methods and generalizes to diverse, in-the-wild scenes.
AI.motivation: Tackling the scarcity of scalable 3D hand annotations for egocentric, markerless control. Existing datasets are limited either by lack of finger-level labels or by instrumented settings, hindering generalizable hand-controlled generation.
AI.method: Protagonist-centered annotation pipeline annotates 3D hands directly on in-the-wild egocentric video via monocular reconstruction, creating EgoVid-Pro (103K clips, ~12M frames) with filters at action-semantic, image-quality, and 3D-geometric levels. Introduces Plücker Hand Map, extending Plücker-ray to hand surface, to disentangle camera-hand motion; integrates into a framework HandsOnWorld for training and generation.
AI.result: The approach achieves higher reconstruction fidelity and control accuracy than prior hand-controlled generators and generalizes to out-of-distribution, everyday scenes beyond lab datasets; EgoVid-Pro provides a large, clean 3D-hand trajectory resource.
AI.conclusion: Monocular, ego-centric 3D hand annotation and the Plücker Hand Map enable scalable, robust hand-controlled egocentric video generation, reducing camera-hand entanglement and expanding generalization to diverse real-world scenarios.

title: Probing Chemical Language Models: Effects of Pre-training and Fine-tuning
summary: Chemical language models (CLMs) are trained with linearized representations such as SMILES, yet it remains unclear which chemically meaningful substructures they encode. To foster a better understanding of CLMs, we conduct a systematic study and probe for 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized models. We furthermore study how fine-tuning on chemical downstream tasks affects the learned representations of molecular substructures. Our results show that pre-training generally improves molecular structure awareness of CLMs, particularly in the upper layers. Moreover, randomly initialized models already encode ring structures well in the first layer. Our analysis on two chemical downstream tasks further reveals that, interestingly, fine-tuning affects task-relevant molecular substructures more than others, indicating that the changes in the representations follow chemical theory.

AI.tldr: Pre-trained CLMs show better molecular substructure awareness than random, especially in upper layers; random models capture ring substructures in the first layer; fine-tuning shifts representations toward task-relevant substructures, aligning with chemical theory.
AI.motivation: To understand what chemically meaningful substructures CLMs encode and how pre-training and fine-tuning shape these representations.
AI.method: Systematic probing of 78 molecular substructures across eight pre-trained and six randomly initialized CLMs; layerwise analysis; evaluation on two chemical downstream tasks to assess fine-tuning effects.
AI.result: Pre-training improves structural awareness overall, particularly in upper layers; random models already encode some ring structures in the first layer; fine-tuning preferentially affects task-relevant substructures, with changes consistent with chemical theory.
AI.conclusion: Pre-training enhances substructure-aware representations in CLMs; fine-tuning tailors representations to downstream tasks, modifying substructure encodings in a theory-consistent way; upper layers are more informative for structural knowledge.

title: EvoPolicyGym: Evaluating Autonomous Policy Evolution in Interactive Environments
summary: Autonomous agents are increasingly expected to improve executable policies through feedback, yet existing evaluations often collapse this process into a final score or confound it with open-ended software-engineering progress. We introduce Autonomous Policy Evolution, a controlled evaluation setting in which a harness-model agent repeatedly edits an executable policy system under a fixed interaction budget. We instantiate this setting in EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark built from compact interactive RL environments that evaluates how agents iteratively improve explored policies. On the EvoPolicyGym suite, GPT-5.5 achieves the strongest aggregate rank score and top-two performance on all 16 environments. Beyond leaderboard results, EvoPolicyGym also provides trajectory-level diagnostics that distinguish how agents allocate budget, convert feedback into parametric tuning. These analyses show that strong autonomous policy evolution depends not only on isolated task wins, but on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback.

AI.tldr: Proposes Autonomous Policy Evolution (APE): a controlled evaluation framework where a harness-model agent iteratively edits an executable policy under a fixed budget. Introduces EvoPolicyGym, a benchmark of compact interactive RL tasks to study iterative policy improvement. GPT-5.5 leads in aggregate across 16 environments and is assessed with trajectory-level diagnostics that reveal budget allocation and parametric tuning. Concludes that effective autonomous policy evolution relies on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, not just task wins.
AI.motivation: To evaluate autonomous agents' ability to improve executable policies through feedback without conflating evaluation with general software-engineering progress or final scores.
AI.method: Construct EvoPolicyGym from compact interactive RL environments. Use a harness-model agent that repeatedly edits an executable policy system within a fixed interaction budget. Collect trajectory-level diagnostics to analyze how feedback is converted into parameter updates and how budget is allocated across environments.
AI.result: GPT-5.5 achieves the best aggregate rank and top-two performance across all 16 environments. EvoPolicyGym provides rich trajectory-level diagnostics linking budget usage to parametric tuning and policy improvement.
AI.conclusion: Effective autonomous policy evolution depends on discovering task-appropriate mechanisms and refining policies under bounded feedback, rather than relying solely on isolated task wins. The framework enables principled evaluation and diagnostics of how agents evolve policies with limited feedback.

title: DeepGaze3.5-VL: Modeling Scanpaths via Autoregressive Token Prediction
summary: Understanding human visual attention on a scene over time has applications in domains such as interface design and inferring cognitive states. Modeling visual scanpaths has historically relied on specialized architectures with hand-crafted priors. While these architectures can model fixation sequences, their rigid structural biases restrict easy extendability and flexible conditioning. For instance, integrating task-specific instructions or adapting to distinct viewer identities requires custom, disjoint architectural additions. We frame scanpath prediction purely as a discrete sequence modeling task. By mapping coordinates into a text vocabulary, we leverage the pretrained representations of Vision-Language Models. This framing absorbs diverse factors of variation: simple prompting allows for global conditioning, such as providing viewer identities to capture personalized biases, or task-specific objectives like visual search. The framework can also integrate per-fixation attributes, such as individual fixation durations, alongside spatial locations. The autoregressive alignment enables the scalable, exact computation of per-fixation log-likelihoods, directly equivalent to the commonly used Information Gain (IG) metric. Our model, DeepGaze3.5-VL, establishes a new state-of-the-art across multiple datasets, achieving 2.18 bits of IG on MIT1003, a 46% improvement over DeepGaze III. This advantage persists even when baselines use identical high-capacity vision encoders. Beyond predictive performance, our generative framework serves as a powerful computational tool for direct behavioral interventions, allowing for controlled in-silico simulations that would be experimentally difficult or impossible to conduct in vivo. We demonstrate this ability by performing controlled interventions on the durations of pre-saccadic fixations, recovering known oculomotor phenomena purely from data.

AI.tldr: Reframes scanpath prediction as a discrete sequence modeling task using a vision-language model; achieves state-of-the-art information gain and supports flexible prompting for viewer/task conditioning and per-fixation attributes; enables in-silico behavioral interventions.
AI.motivation: Traditional scanpath models rely on hand-crafted priors and rigid architectures, hindering easy conditioning and extension. A unified text-voxel framing with pretrained Vision-Language Models allows global (e.g., viewer identity, task) and local (per-fixation attributes) conditioning via prompting, and enables exact, autoregressive log-likelihood computations.
AI.method: Map spatial coordinates to a discrete text vocabulary and model fixations autoregressively using a Vision-Language Model encoder. Use prompts to condition on viewer identity, task goals, and per-fixation attributes (like fixation duration). Compute exact per-fixation log-likelihoods (equivalently Information Gain). The approach is instantiated as DeepGaze3.5-VL.
AI.result: Achieves 2.18 bits IG on MIT1003, a 46% improvement over DeepGaze III; performance persists with identical high-capacity encoders; demonstrates strong predictive accuracy and strong generalization across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Treating scanpath prediction as discrete sequence modeling with prompting yields flexible conditioning and exact likelihood evaluation, delivering state-of-the-art predictive performance and enabling in-silico behavioral interventions (e.g., controlled manipulation of pre-saccadic durations) that recover known oculomotor phenomena.

title: Predicting Early Stages Of Alzheimer's Disease And Identifying Key Biomarkers Using Deep Artificial Neural Network And Ensemble Of Machine Learning Methodologies
summary: Alzheimers disease (AD) is a brain disorder that develops slowly and mainly affects memory, thinking, language, and daily activities. It is one of the most common causes of dementia and creates many difficulties for patients as well as their families. In the early stage, the symptoms are often mild and may look like normal ageing. For this reason, many people are diagnosed late, when the disease has already progressed. At present, there is no complete cure for AD. Still, early detection can help doctors manage the condition better and take suitable steps at the right time. In this study, a machine learning model is proposed to detect the early stages of Alzheimers disease using clinical details, neuropsychological test scores, and neuroimaging-related measures. The data used in this work is collected from the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI). As the dataset has missing values, iterative imputation is applied to fill them. The dataset also has class imbalance, which is handled using Borderline SVM-SMOTE. After that, feature selection is carried out using wrapper-based and embedded methods so that only important features are used for training. The selected features are divided into training and testing sets, and feature scaling is applied. A stacking ensemble model is developed using Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, and LightGBM as base classifiers. Along with this, an artificial neural network is also trained on the same dataset. The performance of these models is compared using precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC-ROC. This study aims to find the best classifier and also identify important biomarkers that may help in the early diagnosis of Alzheimers disease.

AI.tldr: A multi-modal machine learning pipeline for early Alzheimer's detection using ADNI data with imputation, class-imbalance handling, feature selection, and stacking/ANN models; aims to identify key biomarkers and the best classifier.
AI.motivation: Early detection of Alzheimer's disease improves management; no cure; challenges include missing data, imbalanced classes, and identifying meaningful biomarkers; multi-modal data integration with robust ML models is needed.
AI.method: Dataset: ADNI; preprocessing: iterative imputation for missing values; handle class imbalance with Borderline-SVM-SMOTE; feature selection via wrapper and embedded methods; train/test split; scaling; models: stacking ensemble of Logistic Regression, Extra Trees, Bagging KNN, LightGBM; also train an artificial neural network; evaluation via precision, recall, F1-score, AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The abstract outlines the methodology and evaluation metrics but does not provide numerical results; performance comparisons and biomarker identification are proposed aims.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive ML framework for early AD detection using clinical, neuropsychological, and imaging features; aims to identify biomarkers and determine the best classifier, potentially aiding early diagnosis and management.

title: G-RRM: Guiding Symbolic Solvers with Recurrent Reasoning Models
summary:
In this work, we focus on SE-RRMs, a symbol-equivariant instantiation of RRMs that exhibits improved extrapolation to larger problem sizes. We propose a neuro-symbolic approach, ``Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models'' (G-RRM), which integrates SE-RRMs with symbolic solvers for constraint satisfaction problems. SE-RRMs act as neural solvers that generate full solution proposals and guide classical symbolic solvers, such as backtracking or SAT-based methods like Glucose 4.1 and CaDiCaL 3.0.0, that produce globally correct solutions. Centrally, we investigate when neural guidance with G-RRM improves the search efficiency of symbolic solvers. %
Our experiments show that the efficacy of G-RRM depends on two conditions: first, the problem instances must have an expansive combinatorial search space to expose potential gains, and second, the solver architecture must be capable of dynamically overwriting its branching choices to recover when neural hints are imperfect. When these conditions hold, guidance drives median conflict counts to zero and yields significant wall-clock speedups: on $9\times9$ Sudoku, where the SE-RRM correctly solves $91.1\%$ of instances, backtracking accelerates by $33.3\times$ and Glucose 4.1 by $1.70\times$ (median, $p<0.001$), with Glucose 4.1 retaining a $1.17\times$ speedup on perfect-hint $25\times25$ grids. In contrast, CaDiCaL 3.0.0, whose runtime is overhead-dominated and which always respects the injected branching hints rather than overwriting them, shows no significant speedup (median $1.02\times$, n.s.) and even a small significant mean slowdown ($0.90\times$) on $9\times9$. These results delineate the regimes in which neural guidance translates into practical speedups.

AI.tldr: G-RRM is a neuro-symbolic framework where SE-RRMs propose full solutions and guide symbolic solvers. Benefits emerge when the search space is expansive and the solver can overwrite branching; substantial speedups on 9x9 Sudoku with backtracking and Glucose 4.1, but not with CaDiCaL 3.0.0 due to overhead and insistence on following hints.
AI.motivation: Extend neural extrapolation to larger problem sizes and improve constraint-solving efficiency by tightly coupling neural proposal generation with symbolic search, leveraging neural guidance to prune or direct backtracking.
AI.method: Introduce Guiding with Recurrent Reasoning Models (G-RRM): SE-RRMs provide solution proposals and guide symbolic solvers (backtracking, Glucose 4.1, CaDiCaL 3.0.0). Systematically study when neural guidance improves search by requiring the solver to dynamically overwrite branching decisions if hints are imperfect. Experiments on 9×9 Sudoku (SE-RRM solves 91.1% of instances) and 25×25 grids, comparing wall-clock speedups and conflict counts.
AI.result: Neural guidance improves search only under two conditions: an expansive combinatorial search space and a solver that can overwrite branching choices. Achieved median conflict counts of zero and substantial speedups: 33.3× with backtracking, 1.70× with Glucose 4.1 on 9×9; 1.17× speedup with Glucose 4.1 on perfect-hint 25×25. CaDiCaL shows no significant speedup (med 1.02×, ns) and slight slowdown (0.90×) on 9×9 due to overhead and reluctance to overwrite hints.
AI.conclusion: Neural guidance via G-RRM yields practical speedups in regimes where the neural proposals can be effectively integrated and the solver can override poor hints. The work delineates when neuro-symbolic guidance is beneficial and highlights the critical role of solver design and problem structure in achieving gains.

title: ESC: Emotional Self-Correction for Reliable Vision-Language Models
comment: ECCV Main Track 2026 (113 pages, 15 tables, 65 figures). Project Page: https://genai4e.github.io/ESC/?
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance across diverse multimodal tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to unreliable reasoning. Existing self-correction methods mitigate these issues but typically rely on post-training or carefully engineered feedback, incurring high computational cost. In this work, we revisit this challenge through the lens of emotional cues, asking whether they can activate latent self-correction behaviors in VLMs without additional training. \textbf{We find that emotional signals serve as an effective trigger for self-correction, encouraging more cautious and reflective reasoning}. Motivated by this finding, we propose \escabstract (\textbf{\underline{E}}motional \textbf{\underline{S}}elf-\textbf{\underline{C}}orrection), a training-free self-correction framework. ESC introduces an external verifier that detects potentially incorrect initial responses and injects emotional feedback to encourage model to reflect, and produce a better revised response without additional training. Extensive experiments across safety, hallucination, vision-centric perception, and multimodal reasoning benchmarks show that ESC consistently improves reliability while preserving overall model utility. These results suggest that emotion can function not only as an ability to be recognized, but also as a practical control signal for scalable self-correction in VLMs. \textbf{We therefore believe that ESC provides a strong foundation for a new reliable human-like, emotion-integrated research direction.} Our project is publicly available at \textcolor{red}{https://genai4e.github.io/ESC/}.

AI.tldr: A training-free self-correction framework (ESC) for vision-language models that uses an external verifier to emit emotional feedback, triggering reflection and revised responses without additional training.
AI.motivation: VLMs exhibit unreliable reasoning and existing self-correction often requires costly post-training or engineered feedback. The authors explore whether emotional cues can activate latent self-correction without retraining.
AI.method: ESC introduces an external verifier that flags potentially incorrect outputs and injects emotional feedback to guide the model toward a more cautious reflection and a corrected answer, all without additional training.
AI.result: Empirical results across safety, hallucination, vision-centric perception, and multimodal reasoning tasks show consistent reliability gains while maintaining overall utility.
AI.conclusion: Emotion can serve as a practical control signal for scalable self-correction in VLMs; ESC lays a foundation for emotion-integrated approaches and is publicly available.

title: Dynamic Neural Graph Encoding of Inference Processes in Deep Weight Space
comment: Published in Transactions on Machine Learning Research (TMLR), 2026. 28 pages, 5 figures
summary: The rapid advancements in using neural networks as implicit data representations have attracted significant interest in developing machine learning methods that analyze and process the weight spaces of other neural networks. However, efficiently handling these highdimensional weight spaces remains challenging. Existing methods often overlook the sequential nature of layer-by-layer processing in neural network inference. In this work, we propose a novel approach using dynamic graphs to represent neural network parameters, capturing the temporal dynamics of inference. Our Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs, preserving the sequential nature of neural processing. Additionally, we also leverage DNG-Encoder to develop INR2JLS (Implicit Neural Representation to Joint Latent Space) for facilitate downstream applications, such as classifying Implicit Neural Representations (INRs). Our approach demonstrates significant improvements across multiple tasks, surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on the CIFAR-100-INR.

AI.tldr: A dynamic-graph based framework (DNG-Encoder) models layer-wise inference dynamics in neural networks and enables a joint latent space for implicit neural representations (INRs) via INR2JLS, achieving ~10% accuracy gains on CIFAR-100-INR.
AI.motivation: To address the challenge of representing and exploiting high-dimensional weight spaces and their temporal, layer-by-layer evolution during inference, which many methods overlook.
AI.method: Construct dynamic graphs from neural network parameters to capture temporal evolution across layers during inference. The Dynamic Neural Graph Encoder (DNG-Encoder) processes these graphs to preserve the sequential processing structure. Additionally, INR2JLS maps implicit neural representations into a joint latent space to support downstream tasks such as INR classification.
AI.result: The approach yields significant improvements across tasks, including surpassing the state-of-the-art INR classification accuracy by approximately 10% on CIFAR-100-INR.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic graphs effectively encode sequential inference dynamics in neural weight spaces, and the DNG-Encoder—with INR2JLS—provides a strong foundation for analyzing INRs and related downstream tasks.

title: What LLM Agents Say When No One Is Watching: Social Structure and Latent Objective Emergence in Multi-Agent Debates
summary: LLM agents will increasingly act in socially structured settings where role, audience, and relational context can shape what is advantageous or costly to say. We study whether such social structure, without any explicit objective in the prompt, changes what an agent expresses publicly relative to an off-the-record (OTR) channel elicited under the same condition. We introduce a dual-channel debate framework in which agents produce public utterances that enter the shared history alongside OTR responses that are recorded but never shown to the other participant. Across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations within each scenario, alignment-inducing settings produce systematic public-OTR divergence in the targeted agent, with its decision divergence rising from a $\sim$3% baseline to roughly 40%. The effect is consistent across four aggregate analyses: stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses. In some cases, the OTR response explicitly attributes public accommodation to relational pressures, such as career risk or sponsorship obligation. The findings suggest that agent evaluation should extend beyond explicit goals and detect emergent objectives. We present a dual-channel evaluation framework and complementary behavioral measures that operationalize this assessment.

AI.tldr: Dual-channel (public vs off-the-record) evaluation reveals alignment-induced social pressures cause large divergence in what LLM agents say publicly, even without explicit prompts, suggesting emergent objectives shaped by audience and relational context.
AI.motivation: Investigate whether social structure and implicit audience pressures alter public outputs of LLM agents beyond explicit task goals, and develop methods to detect covert adaptation through hidden channels.
AI.method: A dual-channel debate framework where each agent produces a public utterance visible to the other and a separate off-the-record (OTR) response recorded but not shown. Evaluated across 10 models, 3 scenarios, and 5 variations per scenario. Measures of divergence include stance, semantic similarity, natural language inference, and survey responses; alignment-inducing settings are used to elicit systematic public-OTR differences.
AI.result: Public-OTR divergence increases from ~3% baseline to about 40% under alignment pressures, with consistent effects across the four analytic dimensions. OTR responses sometimes attribute accommodation to relational pressures (career risk, sponsorship). Findings held across multiple models and scenarios, supporting emergent objectives and the need for evaluation beyond explicit goals.
AI.conclusion: Evaluation frameworks should incorporate hidden channels to surface emergent objectives driving public behavior. The authors propose a dual-channel evaluation approach and behavioural measures to better assess alignment and public accountability of LLM agents.

title: TCG-AR: Real-Time Multi-View Augmented Reality for Trading Card Game Streaming
summary: Trading card games are increasingly played and broadcast online, yet live streams remain mostly limited to flat top-down footage of the playing area. Augmenting such streams with virtual models of the played cards would improve the viewing experience, but most existing systems rely on instrumented playing surfaces and embedded chips, which are costly and impractical for casual players and large-scale events. In this work, we present TCG-AR, a novel real-time pipeline that augments trading card games using ordinary RGB cameras alone, without any physical markers or specialized hardware. Our pipeline detects, orients, and identifies the cards on the board, renders virtual content onto each card across all views, and can additionally compose a broadcaststyle view that summarizes the game state for spectators, streaming the augmented feeds to standard broadcasting software such as OBS. To train the detection, orientation, and identification models without manual labeling, we introduce an automatic procedure that generates annotated synthetic training data from a reference set of card images. Then, we evaluate several trained models on a new manually annotated dataset with real images, analyzing performance and runtime throughput that determine real-world usability. Overall, by relying only on commodity cameras and hardware, and by open-sourcing all code, models, and datasets, this work aims to serve as a reference for real-time trading card recognition and to make real-time augmented-reality streaming accessible to the broader community of players and streamers.

AI.tldr: TCG-AR enables real-time AR augmentation of trading card games using only RGB cameras, no markers; trains detection/identification models via synthetic data; evaluates on real images; outputs broadcast-style augmented streams; code and data open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Improve streaming/viewing experience for trading card games without costly instrumented surfaces or hardware, enabling accessible real-time AR overlays with commodity cameras.
AI.method: Detect, orient, and identify cards on the board; render virtual content onto each card for all views; generate a broadcast-style game-state view for spectators; train detection/orientation/ID models using automatically generated annotated synthetic data from a reference card image set; evaluate on a manually annotated real-image dataset; assess performance and runtime throughput for real-world use; publish code/models/datasets.
AI.result: Demonstrates a real-time, camera-only pipeline for card recognition and AR overlays; throughput and performance analyzed on real-world dataset; open-sourced implementation and datasets to encourage adoption by players/streamers.
AI.conclusion: Proposes a practical, markerless AR streaming solution for trading card games, with accessible code and data to foster community development and further research.

title: Bayesian Sparse Low-Rank Adaptation for Large Language Model Uncertainty Estimation
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable reasoning capabilities, but their task-specific fine-tuning is notoriously plagued by overconfidence, severely hindering trustworthy deployment. We propose Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a simple and effective variational Bayesian sparse framework that shifts the paradigm of uncertainty quantification from the dense parameter space to the lightweight rank level of low-rank adaptation (LoRA). With the insight that LoRA essentially aggregates multiple rank-one components that may provide superfluous model capacity, DALorRA imposes stochastic masking on rank dimensions, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. Extensive experiments demonstrate DALorRA's excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy.

AI.tldr: DALorRA is a Bayesian sparse framework that regularizes LoRA's rank dimensions to improve calibration without hurting reasoning accuracy, shifting uncertainty quantification from dense weights to rank space.
AI.motivation: Fine-tuning of large language models often yields overconfidence and unreliable uncertainty estimates. Existing methods focus on dense parameter regularization; there is a gap in effectively calibrating model uncertainty at the low-rank adaptation (LoRA) level.
AI.method: Introduce Data-Adaptive Lower-Rank Adaptation (DALorRA), a variational Bayesian sparse approach that applies stochastic masking to LoRA rank components, enabling Bayesian regularization of model capacity during training and ensemble-like calibration during inference. This shifts uncertainty quantification from dense weights to the LoRA rank space, reducing over-parameterization and improving calibration.
AI.result: Empirical evaluation shows that DALorRA achieves excellent calibration of LLMs without compromising reasoning accuracy across tasks and benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: DALorRA provides a simple, effective mechanism to calibrate LLMs by constraining and regularizing the rank-space of LoRA via Bayesian masking, improving trustworthiness with minimal impact on performance.

title: ReContext: Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning
summary: Understanding and reasoning over long contexts has become a key requirement for deploying large language models (LLMs) in realistic applications. Although recent LLMs support increasingly long context windows, they often fail to use relevant evidence that is already present in the input, revealing a gap between context access and effective context utilization. In this work, we propose Recursive Evidence Replay as LLM Harness for Long-Context Reasoning (RECONTEXT), a training-free inference method for improving long-context reasoning. RECONTEXT uses model-internal relevance signals to construct a query-conditioned evidence pool and replays it before final generation while preserving the full original context. This recursive selection process separates evidence organization from answer generation without training, external memory, or context pruning. We also provide a theoretical analysis based on associative memory, which characterizes the context as a memory store, the question as a retrieval cue, attention as cue-trace association, and replay as trace reactivation. Experiments on eight long-context datasets with 128K context length show that RECONTEXT consistently improves evidence utilization across Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-8B, and Llama3-8B, achieving the best average rank on all three backbones. Code is available at https://github.com/Yanjun-Zhao/ReContext.

AI.tldr: RECONTEXT is training-free inference method that improves long-context reasoning by recursively replaying model-internal, query-conditioned evidence without training, using associative memory formalism; shows improvements across eight datasets and multiple backbones.
AI.motivation: Long-context models struggle to extract and leverage relevant evidence from very long inputs; there is a gap between context access and effective evidence use; a training-free, memory-free method to improve evidence utilization is desirable.
AI.method: Constructs a query-conditioned evidence pool using model-internal relevance signals, replays it before final generation, while preserving the full original context; recursive selection separates evidence organization from answer generation; no training, external memory, or context pruning; theoretical analysis via associative memory mapping.
AI.result: On eight long-context datasets with 128K context length, RECONTEXT improves evidence utilization across Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-3-8B, Llama3-8B; achieves best average rank across all three backbones; code released.
AI.conclusion: RECONTEXT demonstrates that recursive evidence replay can enhance long-context reasoning without training, offering a practical solution and theoretical grounding; suggests future directions in internal signal-based evidence curation.

title: Multimodal Fusion for Fine-Grained Classification of Breast Fibroadenoma and Phyllodes Tumors
summary: Breast fibroadenoma (FA) and phyllodes tumor (PT) are fibroepithelial breast lesions with highly overlapping appearances on B-mode ultrasound, making benign and borderline PT prone to being misclassified as FA and complicating preoperative decision-making. Existing computer-aided diagnosis methods commonly rely on single-modal imaging features and insufficiently exploit complementary clinical and textual information. To address this limitation, we construct the FAPT-M Dataset, a pathology-confirmed multimodal dataset comprising 910 patients with strictly reviewed ultrasound images, structured clinical attributes, and ultrasound diagnostic descriptions. Based on this dataset, we propose a clinically guided multimodal framework that integrates DenseNet-based visual encoding, CLIP-inspired text encoding, and lightweight clinical encoding, and further introduces clinical-conditioned adaptive modulation, cross-modal Transformer fusion, and dual-path representation learning to improve feature alignment and multimodal interaction. Under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, the proposed method achieves an accuracy of 77.64%, F1-score of 73.38%, and AUC of 89.74%, outperforming representative CNN-, Transformer-, and vision-language-based baselines. Ablation studies and class-balanced evaluations further confirm the contribution of three-modality fusion and the key architectural components. Overall, this work provides an effective multimodal approach for fine-grained FA-PT classification and establishes a high-quality benchmark for multimodal breast ultrasound analysis.

AI.tldr: Multimodal breast ultrasound framework (FAPT-M) combines DenseNet visual features, CLIP-like text embeddings, and clinical data with adaptive modulation and cross-modal fusion to classify fibroadenoma vs phyllodes tumor, yielding 77.6% accuracy, 73.4% F1, and 89.7% AUC on 5-fold CV, outperforming baselines; introduces a pathology-confirmed multimodal dataset (FAPT-M) of 910 cases.
AI.motivation: Fibroepithelial breast lesions FA and PT have highly overlapping B-mode ultrasound appearances, causing ambiguous preoperative decisions. Existing single-modal methods fail to exploit complementary clinical and textual information. A pathology-confirmed, multimodal dataset is needed to improve fine-grained FA-PT discrimination and establish a benchmark.
AI.method: Construct FAPT-M dataset with 910 patients including strictly reviewed ultrasound images, structured clinical attributes, and ultrasound diagnostic descriptions. Propose a clinically guided multimodal framework integrating DenseNet visual encoding, CLIP-inspired text encoding, and lightweight clinical encoding, with clinical-conditioned adaptive modulation, cross-modal Transformer fusion, and dual-path representation learning for improved modality alignment and interaction.
AI.result: Under patient-level five-fold cross-validation, the method achieves accuracy 77.64%, F1 73.38%, and AUC 89.74%, outperforming representative CNN-, Transformer-, and vision-language-based baselines. Ablation and class-balanced analyses confirm the contributions of the three-modality fusion and key architectural components.
AI.conclusion: The work delivers an effective multimodal approach for fine-grained FA-PT classification and establishes a high-quality multimodal breast ultrasound benchmark (FAPT-M).

title: Privacy-Preserving and Verifiable Approximate Distributed Coded Computing
summary: Distributed machine learning enables collaborative model training without centralizing data, but it also exposes learning processes to privacy leakage and malicious manipulation. Existing defenses typically address these threats in isolation and are often tailored to specific learning paradigms or model architectures, limiting their applicability in realistic deployments. In particular, federated learning and decentralized learning exhibit distinct adversarial surfaces that are rarely addressed within a unified framework. In this paper, we present a model-agnostic framework for adversary-resistant distributed learning that jointly addresses privacy preservation and malicious behavior across both federated and decentralized settings. Our approach combines paradigm-specific defense mechanisms with GPBACC, a privacy-enhancing coded computing technique applicable to arbitrary machine learning models. For federated learning, we integrate robust aggregation strategies to mitigate the impact of malicious participants, while for decentralized learning we employ approximate decode-and-compare and group testing techniques to enable lightweight verification and adversary isolation without relying on a trusted aggregator. Crucially, we evaluate the proposed framework through an explicit, attack-driven analysis. We implement representative privacy attacks and malicious behaviors, and empirically demonstrate that the combination of GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification mechanisms significantly reduces privacy leakage and improves resilience against active adversaries. These results suggest that privacy-enhancing coded computing, when combined with appropriate adversary-resistance strategies, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

AI.tldr: A model-agnostic framework combines privacy-enhancing coded computing (GPBACC) with adversary-resistance techniques for both federated and decentralized learning, aiming to reduce privacy leakage and improve resilience to active attackers. Evaluated via attack-driven experiments showing improvements over baseline defenses.
AI.motivation: Distributed ML faces privacy leakage and malicious manipulation; the threat surfaces differ between federated and decentralized settings, and existing defenses are usually paradigm-specific. A unified framework is needed for practical deployments.
AI.method: Integrate GPBACC (privacy-preserving coded computing) with paradigm-specific defenses: robust aggregation in Federated Learning to mitigate malicious participants; approximate decode-and-compare and group testing in decentralized learning for lightweight verification and attacker isolation without a trusted aggregator. Attack-driven evaluation with implemented privacy attacks and malicious behaviors.
AI.result: Empirical results show that combining GPBACC with robust aggregation and verification reduces privacy leakage and enhances resilience to active adversaries across both settings.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-enhancing coded computing, when paired with targeted adversary-resistance mechanisms, provides a practical and deployable foundation for secure distributed machine learning.

title: Online Safety Monitoring for LLMs
summary: Despite alignment training, LLMs remain prone to generating unsafe outputs at deployment time. Monitoring outputs online and raising an alarm when safety can no longer be assumed is therefore critical. We study a simple real-time monitor that turns a verifier signal from an external model into an alarm decision by thresholding, with the threshold calibrated via risk control. In experiments on mathematical reasoning and red teaming datasets, we show that this simple design is competitive with more advanced monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing.

AI.tldr: A lightweight real-time safety monitor for LLM outputs uses an external verifier signal thresholded and calibrated by risk control, achieving competitive performance with sophisticated sequential testing on math reasoning and red-teaming tasks.
AI.motivation: Despite alignment training, LLMs can produce unsafe outputs at deployment; a simple, online monitor is needed to detect potential unsafe outputs and raise alarms.
AI.method: Obtain a verifier signal from an external model; apply a threshold to convert it into an alarm; calibrate the threshold through risk control. Compare performance against monitors based on sequential hypothesis testing on math reasoning and red-teaming datasets.
AI.result: The simple threshold-based monitor performs competitively with the more advanced sequential hypothesis testing monitors on the evaluated datasets.
AI.conclusion: A straightforward, calibrated threshold monitor can effectively detect unsafe outputs in real-time and can rival more complex monitoring approaches.

title: LongEgoRefer: A Benchmark for Long-Form Egocentric Video Referring Expression Comprehension
summary: Egocentric videos capture rich and diverse human-object interactions and have emerged as a fundamental resource for understanding human activities related to objects. In this context, Video Referring Expression Comprehension (Video REC), the task of localizing the temporal and spatial extent of a referred object in video frames given a natural language query, plays a key role in linking textual descriptions to observed objects in untrimmed egocentric recordings. However, existing egocentric Video REC benchmarks primarily focus on short video clips, where some target object appears densely within frames. Such settings do not reflect real-world egocentric recordings, which are long-form, untrimmed, and characterized by sparse object occurrences and complex activity transitions. To address this limitation, we introduce LongEgoRefer, a novel and challenging benchmark constructed from long-form videos in the Ego4D dataset. LongEgoRefer contains 1,498 referring expressions with an average video duration of 45 minutes. The benchmark exhibits extreme target sparsity, detailed linguistic descriptions, and complex human-object interactions embedded in long, dynamic egocentric narratives. Consequently, it defines a demanding spatio-temporal grounding problem that requires models to identify both when an event occurs and where the referred object appears within extended video sequences. We evaluate existing Video REC approaches, including training-free baselines based on vision-language models combined with Grounded SAM2. Extensive experiments show that even advanced baselines and current state-of-the-art models struggle significantly on LongEgoRefer. These results highlight the intrinsic difficulty of long-form egocentric spatio-temporal grounding and emphasize the need for more robust video understanding models.

AI.tldr: Introduces LongEgoRefer, a long-form egocentric Video REC benchmark derived from Ego4D, with highly sparse targets in ~45-minute videos, challenging spatio-temporal grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing Video REC benchmarks use short clips with frequent target visibility, failing to reflect real-world long-form egocentric scenarios. There is a need to study spatio-temporal grounding under extreme sparsity and long narrative structure.
AI.method: Construct LongEgoRefer with 1,498 referring expressions from Ego4D, average video length ~45 minutes, emphasizing extreme sparsity and detailed linguistic descriptions; evaluate existing Video REC approaches including vision-language baselines and Grounded SAM2-based methods.
AI.result: Current baselines, including state-of-the-art models, struggle significantly on LongEgoRefer, indicating the intrinsic difficulty of long-form egocentric spatio-temporal grounding.
AI.conclusion: Long-form egocentric spatio-temporal grounding remains a hard problem; motivates development of more robust, temporally-aware video understanding models and possibly novel training strategies to handle sparse targets in long videos.

title: An Optimisation Framework for the Well-Conditioned Training of Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary:
Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a promising route to solve partial differential equations, yet they have struggled to reach the precision of classical solvers. The obstacle is increasingly understood to be one of optimisation, owing to the severely ill-conditioned loss landscape. We present $\textbf{DSGNAR}$: Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton with Adaptive Ratio, a scalable second-order optimisation framework that confronts this ill-conditioning and, in doing so, obtains unprecedented accuracy and speed. $\textbf{DSGNAR}$ couples a doubly-sketched Gauss-Newton model with a novel strategy that carefully controls both regularisation and step length. Across a suite of problems spanning nonlinear, chaotic, multi-scale, high-dimensional, and Navier-Stokes, the framework greatly improves on the state of the art: able to attain relative $\ell_2$ errors as low as $3\times10^{-16}$ in double precision, improve contemporary results by five orders of magnitude on the canonical Burgers' equation, and as much as eight orders on a high-dimensional Poisson problem, while remaining markedly faster. We further show that, in single precision, solutions at the limit of round-off error can be obtained very quickly: Burgers' equation to $\ell_2^{\text{rel}} = 4.75 \times 10^{-7}$ in under ten seconds. The framework is also robust to the choice of architecture, arithmetic precision, and initial hyperparameters.
  The code is available at https://www.github.com/wephy/physics-informed-neural-networks

AI.tldr: DSGNAR is a scalable second-order optimization framework for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) based on a Doubly-Sketched Gauss-Newton model with Adaptive Ratio, delivering unprecedented accuracy and speed across challenging PDE problems; code available.
